News.title: Betting shops ‘at heart of community life’ in Burnham’s own constituency, say voters
News.content:
Next

BETTING shops are at the heart of community life in PM Andy Burnham’s own seat — according to voters in his constituency.

They spoke out as bookies across the country blame shop closures on Labour tax hikes.



Pollsters Opinium found more than half the locals in Makerfield, Greater Manchester, believe the outlets made a positive contribution.

And one in four said they had placed a bet in the last year.



The findings come amid fears that another tax raid on gambling firms could hammer high streets and cost thousands of jobs.

Industry modelling claims higher Machine Games Duty could lead to as many as 1,470 betting shop closures, 34 casinos shutting their doors and almost 16,000 job losses.



Betting and Gaming Council Chief Executive Grainne Hurst said: “Makerfield tells a very human story about what betting shops mean to communities across Britain.

“The Prime Minister has said policies should face a ‘Makerfield test’ that if they don’t work for people here and don’t lift them up, they shouldn’t happen at all.”

Mr Burnham used the “Makerfield test” after winning the seat, saying policies that do not work for people in the constituency or “lift people up” should not happen.

Betfred founder Fred Done has also warned that further gambling tax rises in the upcoming Budget could devastate the high street betting industry.



The Sun’s Save Our Bets campaign is urging ministers not to hike betting duties at the Budget.

Chancellor John Healey will reveal his Autumn Budget on Wednesday, 28 October.

News.title: British Airways keeps Boeing 777 flying despite almost HALF the toilets being broken
News.content:
FAST AND LOOS British Airways keeps Boeing 777 flying despite almost HALF the toilets being broken







Next

BRITISH Airways is keeping a Boeing 777 flying — even though almost half its toilets are broken.

Passengers are having to queue for the loo at 30,000ft because four washrooms are locked.



Only two are working for the 84 First and Club passengers while the 170 in World Traveller class have to share three.

The plane, which does regular 11-hour flights from Heathrow to ­worldwide destinations including the US and India, also has no wifi.



In the next few days it has been scheduled to fly to and from the UK, New York, Los Angeles and San Francisco.

Passengers are not told of the problems before booking flights but get a scripted apology on landing.



One crew member said: “It’s unacceptable.

“Why are we hoodwinking passengers this way?”

Another said: “Staff are in the frontline of passengers’ upset at having splashed out on premium fares only to be offered a service that you’d be disgusted to experience on a cheap, no-frills’ carrier.”

BA said it had apologised to affected customers and “offered a gesture to help put things right”.



Sources said it hopes to repair the problem plane “in the next few days”.

News.title: Labour’s hated ‘holiday tax’ risks turning London into a tourism ‘ghost town’, top Tory warns
News.content:
Next

A PUNISHING holiday tax risks turning London into a tourism “ghost town”, a senior Tory says.

It could jeopardise the capital’s economic success if implemented by the Labour mayor Sadiq Khan.



The warning comes from Tory mayoral hopeful Sir James Cleverly after he put himself forward for the job.

He said: “I want to make sure that London is buzzing, London is vibrant, London’s attracting people, London’s contributing to the UK economy.



“The last thing we need is anything that would put that at risk, anything that would turn London into a ghost town.”

More than 20million foreign tourists visited London last year, contributing £40billion, he claimed.

He also said the PM’s “anti-London policies” were hurting the South.

The Sun has launched a Hands Off Our Hols campaign, warning it will price hard-working families out of staycations.



England’s local leaders are to get the power to introduce a fee per overnight stay.

Labour’s 10 regional mayors in England have committed to bringing in the visitor levy, but two Tory and two Reform mayors ruled out implementing the measure which could damage a city’s nightlife.

Mr Khan is enthusiastically pushing for the tourist tax to be charged at up to five per cent of the cost of a hotel room.

Trade body UKHospitality has warned it could add £100 to a family holiday.

Mr Cleverly quit Kemi Badenoch‘s top team to throw his weight behind running for London mayor.



If successful, he would be the first Tory to win the capital since Boris Johnson in 2012.

News.title: Jill Dando cops launch new probe into unsolved murder as hope CCTV could prove answers on mystery man
News.content:
Next

COPS have launched a fresh probe into the shocking unsolved murder of the adored TV star Jill Dando.

Detectives are re-examining CCTV of a mystery man who they believe could hold the key to cracking the 27-year-old case.



The Met is now using modern technology to enhance original footage from Putney Bridge Tube station, reports The Mirror.

It shows an unidentified man spotted around a mile from Jill’s Fulham home shortly after she was callously shot on her doorstep.



The force said: “In the 27 years since Jill Dando‘s murder, the investigation has been subject to numerous reviews, aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics.

“Recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology have provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station.



“This remains ongoing.”

The man, known as Man X, was filmed around 20 minutes after Jill was shot outside her home in Gowan Avenue, South West London, on April 26, 1999.



Cold-case officers are understood to have spent the past ten months finding and digitising the original footage.

It was believed to be buried among 223 boxes of material in police storage.

Now detectives hope clearer images could help establish who Man X was — and whether he was linked to the killing.

The footage is also being examined for possible links to Milorad Ulemek, a notorious Serbian paramilitary commander known as Legija.

Ulemek, a former French Foreign Legionnaire, led a unit involved in assassinations during the rule of former Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic.



A facial comparison expert previously identified similarities between Ulemek and Man X.

He said they had similar mouths, chins, hairlines and right sideburns.

Their noses and right ears were also said to be similar in shape and size.



A dent on Ulemek’s nose was also highlighted as matching one shown on a police e-fit released after Jill’s murder.

Two key witnesses have also said Ulemek resembled men they saw near the murder scene.

One woman was driving along Fulham Palace Road when she saw a man in a suit “running for his life”.

A month later, she picked out Man X in CCTV as the man she had seen.

But detectives dismissed her evidence, saying her original description did not match Man X.



Both men, however, were said to have been wearing suits and ties and had similar heights, builds and hair colour.

Jill’s neighbour Richard Hughes saw the gunman and believed he may have been carrying a mobile phone.

He said the killer “looked like” an e-fit produced by the female witness.

Another neighbour, Geoffrey Upfillbrown, also saw the killer and said the image looked “similar”, according to police notes.

A second key witness later said he was “80%” sure the man he saw near the scene was Ulemek.



Jill, 37, was ambushed from behind as she approached her front door.

She was killed instantly by a single bullet to her left temple.

At the time, Britain was bombing Serbia and Jill was one of the country’s best-known TV presenters.

She had fronted BBC shows including Crimewatch and Holiday.

Within hours of her murder, the BBC received a call claiming it was linked to a NATO attack on a Belgrade TV station.



There were also fears Jill had been targeted because she fronted a BBC appeal for Kosovan refugees 20 days before her death.

Nearly a year later, detectives focused on local man Barry George.

George, now 65, spent eight years behind bars after being convicted of Jill’s murder.

He was cleared at a retrial in 2008.

The case was moved to “inactive” in 2015 following a forensic review.



Ulemek is serving a 40-year sentence in Serbia after being convicted of helping to plan the assassinations of former Serbian president Ivan Stambolic in 2000 and prime minister Zoran Djindjic in 2003.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

George is currently facing trial over historical sex charges.

The Met investigation into Jill’s murder remains ongoing.

News.title: Afghan asylum seeker masterminded  crime ring which shipped £181million of stolen iPhones out of the UK
News.content:
PRISON CALLING Afghan asylum seeker masterminded crime ring which shipped £181million of stolen iPhones out of the UK







Next

AN AFGHAN asylum seeker masterminded a crime ring which shipped £181million of stolen iPhones out of the UK, a court heard yesterday.

Amir Khadikhel, his fellow Afghan Ismat Miakhel and Indian Mansoor Mohammed sent more than 62,000 to the Far East and Middle East using unwitting courier firms DHL and UPS.



The operation was uncovered ­following a tip-off from a victim who used the Find My Phone app to trace hers to a warehouse at Heathrow Airport.

A police raid recovered 3,000 stolen mobiles.



Suspects were later seen handing over phones and wads of cash outside a shop in North London.

A search of a London property led to phones being found under a hidden trapdoor and a further swoop recovered 299 more when some were heard ringing in sealed boxes.



Southwark crown court heard the phones had been stolen across the country.

They can be worth up to £3,700 in China because, unlike new phones, they are not subject to government restrictions.



Khadikhel’s lawyer said he came to the UK after fleeing Afghanistan in 2019, leaving behind his wife and child.

He said he was homeless and had mental health issues, and was lured into criminality by a person who housed him.

Khadikhel and Mohammed both admitted conspiring to receive ­stolen mobile phones, as well as participating in the criminal activities of an organised crime group.

Khadikhel also admitted conspiring to transfer the phones out of the UK.

Miakhel earlier admitted conspiring to receive and transfers stolen goods. Khadikhel, 35, of Wanstead, was jailed for 9½ years.



Miakhel, 33, of Walthamstow, got nine years and Mohammed, 30, of Wood Green, six years and five months.

News.title: Man denies attempted murder of two Jewish men stabbed in Golders Green
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

STAB DENIAL Man denies attempted murder of two Jewish men stabbed in Golders Green







Next

A MAN yesterday denied the attempted murder of two Jewish men who were stabbed in Golders Green.

Essa Suleiman, 45, also pleaded not guilty to attacking another man earlier the same day.

The case is no longer being treated as terrorism and Suleiman is currently being detained in Broadmoor secure psychiatric hospital, the Old Bailey heard.



Suleiman, of Camberwell, South London, is also accused of one count of possession of a bladed article in a public place following a series of attacks on April 29.



At 8.50am that day, a suspect armed with a knife arrived at an address in Great Dover Street, South London.

Ishmail Hussein received minor injuries and police carried out inquiries at an address connected to Suleiman.

Later that morning, he allegedly attacked two Jewish men in Golders Green, North London.



Shloime Rand, 34, and Norman Shine, 76, both received stab wounds.

Suleiman, a British national born in Somalia, appeared via videolink from Broadmoor hospital and spoke only to confirm his identity.

The case was adjourned for psychiatric reports and a three-week trial is due to go ahead from March 1.

The next hearing is due to be held on January 15.

News.title: Woman ‘raped by unknown man’ in city centre alleyway as cops share CCTV of person they want to speak to
News.content:
'ATTACK' HORROR Woman ‘raped by unknown man’ in city centre alleyway as cops share CCTV of person they want to speak to







Next

A WOMAN was allegedly raped by an unknown man in a city centre alleyway.

Cops have now released a CCTV image of a person they wish to speak following the attack in Staffordshire earlier this year.



Officers said a woman was approached by an “unknown man” near Bucknall Old Road in Hanley, Stoke-on-Trent at around 1pm on May 11.

The woman was then taken to an alleyway where she raped, police said.



Staffordshire Police has now released CCTV of a man they believe can help them in their investigation.

A force spokesperson said: “Detectives have been carrying out a number of enquiries as part of an ongoing investigation and are now able to release an image of a man we want to speak to.”



Any witnesses or anyone with information is urged to contact the police quoting incident 457 of May 11.

News.title: Man City found guilty of majority of 115 financial rule breaches
News.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching.

The Athletic , externalis reporting that the sanctions have not been decided but that the independent panel has reached its decision, finding the club guilty of all but one count.

The Premier League declined to comment.

Asked if the report was correct, City did not comment either way.

Instead they released a statement saying the "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality".

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence," it added.

BBC Sport has also been told that, in the event of being found guilty, City will appeal against the findings.

Other Premier League clubs are believed to have been informed about the independent panel's decision and have sought legal advice as to whether they would have a compensation claim.

News.title: Watch: What could the potential sanctions for Man City be?
News.content: Football finance expert Kieran Maguire says the potential sanctions for Manchester City will be 'significant' after the sources told BBC Sport that the club has been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching.

News.title: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
News.content:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.

Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that this could be done "if the necessary conditions are met" and said these were contained within the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June to extend a ceasefire that subsequently broke down.

Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official said positive discussions were taking place through mediators, including about nuclear issues, Reuters reported. Earlier this week Donald Trump threatened to "annihilate the Islamic Republic".

The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of prices.

It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.

"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States," Araghchi told reporters.

He did not specify what steps Iran wanted the US to take but added that "the actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU".

News.title: I'm not tempted to call an early election, Burnham says
News.content:
Andy Burnham has insisted he is not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process".

During a round of BBC interviews ahead of Labour's annual conference, the prime minister said his focus was on helping people with the cost of living and supporting businesses.

Recent polling has suggested Labour's position has improved since Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer in Downing Street in July, although Reform UK and the Conservatives are not far behind.

An early general election could give Burnham a mandate of his own and free him from commitments made in Labour's 2024 manifesto. The next general election must be held by August 2029.

Asked by ITV Calendar if the next election would be in 2029, he replied: "Yes, that's when the next election will be.

"All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead."

News.title: Daniel Thomas pleads not guilty after dinghy slashed
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has pleaded not guilty to criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the Channel with a knife.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, was arrested after the livestreamed video on Tuesday.

Thomas, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in Hampshire via videolink, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.

He pleaded not guilty to both charges and was remanded in custody until his next court appearance at Portsmouth Crown Court on 29 September.

News.title: U2 celebrate 50th anniversary at the school where they formed
News.content:
Exactly 50 years after they formed, U2 returned to Dublin to play a gig at the school where they met.

"We've escaped from the lab," declared Bono, as the quartet took to a stage in the playground. "How's the experiment working for you?"

The pupils of Mount Temple Comprehensive may not have been born when U2 were the worldâs biggest band, but they gave them a hero's welcome, waving signs that said, "I love U2", "It's a beautiful day - no school", and, "Bono, my mum says hi!"

The group treated them to a career-spanning set that included hits like I Will Follow, Vertigo and With Or Without You, as well as their latest single, Silencio.

As they played, teachers pulled down pupils whoâd climbed on their classmates' shoulders, before getting swept up in the moment and dancing along themselves.

As he looked out from the same stage where U2 made their debut in 1976, Bono became emotional.

"Thanks for, erâ¦ Yeah... I didn'tâ¦ Wow," said the frontman, temporarily lost for words.

News.title: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged' - US media
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

Police in the US state of Mississippi have said that they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" and placed hanging in a tree, the Associated Press reports.

The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune had been killed in a dispute related to drugs, US media reported.

The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree on the grounds of an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests.

The BBC has contacted the court, the medical examiner's office and Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey.

In a statement to the BBC on Friday, Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said "Our language has been consistent...Ms Fortune was found in a hanging position. We have not released any information contrary to that statement."

Brackney did not immediately respond to additional questions about the detective's disclosure in court.

Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging was staged.

The medical examiner confirmed earlier this month that Fortune's cause of death was homicide and said there would be a murder charge.

Jarques Ratliff, 51, was arrested and pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody in without bond.

A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in the case this week, while a third was reportedly being sought by authorities.

The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country.

Representative Ayanna Pressley, Democrat of Massachusetts, cites at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress, external, which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers.

The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has been ruled a suicide.

News.title: British climber dies after falling 60m on Spanish mountainside
News.content:
A 28-year-old British climber has died after falling about 60m (200ft) from one of the highest mountains in northern Spain.

The man fell into a gully while descending from the summit of Torrecerredo in the Cantabrian Mountains on Thursday, the Spanish Civil Guard said.

Police and an air unit were deployed to the scene after emergency services were called around 13:27 local time (11:27 GMT). The man's body was recovered by a mountain rescue unit.

The UK Foreign Office said it was in contact with local authorities "following reports of the death of a British national in Spain".

Spanish emergency services said they initially received a call saying that a person had fallen on the eastern face of the mountain and dispatched a rescue group aboard a medical helicopter.

A doctor among them confirmed the man's death at about 14:18 and remained at the scene to guard the body until a Civil Guard helicopter could arrive about an hour and 20 minutes later.

Specialist mountain rescuers were then lowered by winch to the site of the accident, where they recovered the man's body and belongings.

The identity of the climber, who Spanish authorities said was English, has not been given. The accident occurred when he was about 20 metres from the mountain's summit.

His body has been transported to the Institute of Legal Medicine, which provides forensic pathology services, in Asturias, the Civil Guard said.

Torrecerredo, which has an elevation of about 2,650m, is in the Picos de Europa, which is popular with climbers and walkers.

The region's tourism board describes the route up the mountain as "very difficult" with a demanding ascent, warning climbers to take particular care on steep and exposed upper sections on their way down.

Sepa Asturias - the body responsible for emergency services in the region - said it also transported a 54-year-old French woman to hospital after she suffered a leg injury on the mountain range on Thursday afternoon.

News.title: Noah Woods left playground through gap in fence, inquest hears
News.content:
Suffolk Coroner's Court heard from police that Noah had left the playground, walked into a memorial garden and left that through an open gate. He then ran down a path on a new housing estate towards nearby Decoy Pond.

Det Ch Insp Matt Connick from Suffolk Police told the court that CCTV showed Noah in the play area being looked after by a relative, which was "part of a normal routine".

The detective said Noah "left through a gap in the fence leading to the memorial garden where he left through an open gate".

After he had left the play area, he was closely followed by the relative trying to catch up with him, Connick added.

The inquest heard the relative had shouted out to Noah, who lived in neighbouring East Bergholt, but he went out of sight shortly afterwards.

Another man was said to have joined the search and then police were called.

At the time of the search, volunteers were told that Noah was non-verbal and partially deaf.

A statement from Brantham Parish Council, which maintains the play area at Merriam Close, said it was "deeply saddened by Noah's death and our thoughts remain with his family and all those affected at this extremely difficult time".

"The parish council understands that there was a break in the internal fencing, being constructed to separate the play area from the memorial garden, however the whole of the area at Merriam Close, including the play area and memorial garden are completely enclosed by appropriate perimeter fencing," it said.

"The council will co-operate fully with any investigation and, while inquiries are ongoing, does not consider it appropriate to comment further."

News.title: Some BBC channels and radio stations may well have to close, director general says
News.content:
Brittin took over as BBC director general in May after a decade as president of Google in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

Asked by Kuenssberg if he would allow a programme to be made and presented by AI, Brittin replied: "I would do, within guardrails."

He added: "We want to experiment with this technology and understand what it can and can't do, but I'm here because I believe in human creativity.

"I don't think anything we do should be replaced by AI. I think there are lots of places where AI can help us make the licence fee go further, but also help us in our decision-making and creativity. But it's not a substitute for humans."

He also warned of the danger of a handful of tech companies having too much control over information in the future.

"We're also in this moment where AI is in takeoff. So I think there's a danger that six companies will control access to information in future and the creation of information and misinformation," he said.

"Six companies, none of them European, let alone British. In that world, here's the BBC. It's the most trusted organisation by over half a billion people."

Asked if he trusted big tech companies he replied: "There's a lot of platforms out there, so I wouldn't trust any platform innately.

"And I think what you do is you keep under review how those things work and whether your content can show up in the right place and fulfil its mission.

"I think the BBC and our apps and services should be the antidote to the algorithm. Everywhere else you go is driven by some commercial interest."

The interview will be available on BBC Sounds and YouTube on Saturday 26 September, then on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg on BBC One and iPlayer at 09:00 BST on 27 September.

News.title: NHS to suspend staff suspected of snooping on patient records
News.content:
NHS staff in England suspected of looking at patient records without a valid reason will be immediately suspended as part of a "zero-tolerance crackdown" on snooping.

Those under suspicion will also be locked out of NHS computer systems, preventing any further viewing of confidential records, including from home.

NHS England chief executive Sir Jim Mackey has written to every trust, ordering the measures to be introduced immediately to strengthen protection against data breaches.

The move follows a series of high-profile incidents involving the records of Nottingham and Southport attack victims and a child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire.

This week, Bristol Foundation NHS Trust said it had launched an internal investigation after it emerged the medical records of an 18-year-old had been accessed years after his death.

The boy's mother, Paula McGowan, told the BBC she was "deeply concerned and hurt" and called for the NHS to do more to deal with the problem.

News.title: PM rules out giving Wales independence referendum powers
News.content:
The prime minister has ruled out handing powers to hold a referendum on independence to the Welsh government.

Andy Burnham said other UK nations do not have such powers and he did not "think we can create a different arrangement for Wales".

He added that the decision should be made jointly with Westminster, arguing that the UK Parliament has to have a "say on an issue of that magnitude".

Wales First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said last week he would seek powers to hold an independence referendum, although he ruled out staging one before the next Senedd election in May 2030.

Burnham also said he was open to looking at the Welsh government's "Cynnal" plans to trial offering Â£10 a week for 15,000 children aged under six, in households already receiving universal credit.

This would require the agreement of the Department for Work and Pensions and HMRC to avoid the payment being taxed or other benefits - paid for by the UK government - being reduced.

"I'll certainly ensure that there's a proper discussion about the issue," he said.

"I mean, I did things as mayor of Greater Manchester without there having to be any tax implications.

"So I'm not quite sure why that arises in this in this instance, but we will have a look at it for certain."

News.title: Jeffrey Donaldson victim describes 'profound impact' of child sex abuse
News.content:
The victims of child sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson have described the impact the abuse had on them.

Donaldson was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

The former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader appeared at Newry Crown Court for a hearing prior to his sentencing in October. He is seeking to appeal his convictions.

The prosecution barrister told the court that one of the women said her childhood had been stolen, while the second said the abuse affected her every day.

In her submission to the pre-sentencing hearing, Rosemary Walsh KC outlined what she described as the "salient facts" that were heard during the course of the trial.

She also described the impact the offending had on both victims, whom were described during the trial as Complainants A and B.

She said both complainants often wondered what life would have been like if they hadn't experienced the abuse.

In her victim impact statement, Complainant A described the "profound impact" the abuse had on her.

Walsh said the complainant believed her childhood had been "stolen" and that she felt an "enormous amount of anger that is always simmering away under the surface".

Walsh said the abuse Complainant B had suffered affected her "every day and every relationship", and that she had to fight on a daily basis the wish that she would die.

The prosecution barrister also outlined further aggravating and mitigating factors.

She said, in sentencing, the youth of the victims had to be taken account, as well as the "multitude of offences", which "spanned a considerable period of time", and the fact there were two victims.

Donaldson's defence barrister Keiron Vaughan KC told the court that the 63-year-old was "of previous good character" and that there had been no offending of this type over the last 18 years.

"In that period of time, Mr Donaldson has or did achieve significant things in his life," he said.

"I readily accept that these convictions obliterate all those achievements that he has made in his life, and that's certainly something he will have to live with."

Vaughan said he acknowledged the court would impose a "lengthy custodial sentence", but that he had complete confidence that the court would treat Donaldson in the same way it would any other defendant of a similar age and in similar circumstances.

Addressing Donaldson directly, Judge Paul Ramsey said: "Mr Donaldson, I will be sentencing you as soon as I can next month."

News.title: Contentious Orange Order parade can go ahead, commission says
News.content:
The Parades Commission has announced that a planned Orange Order parade is to be allowed on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown.

The commission said the parade on Sunday should start earlier than the Orange Order wanted and with fewer people - but can go ahead.

The decision is facing a legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition which opposes the march and has said the challenge will be heard on Saturday morning.

Rather than start at 13:00 BST on Sunday as intended, the commission has said the march can begin at 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested.

As it happened: Parades Commission says Orange Order Drumcree parade can go ahead

In a detailed document known as a determination, which was published on its website, external, the commission said: "This decision is not, and should not be perceived, as a victory for one side or a loss for another.

"It is the outworking of the application of the legal framework to the facts available to the commission."

News.title: PM says bailed sex offender case must be reviewed
News.content:
The prime minister has said that the decision to bail a sex offender and repeatedly allow him to return to his home overlooking the playground he targeted must be reviewed.

Zafer Dogan, 32, of Enfield, north London, was jailed on Thursday for two years and four months for taking thousands of pictures of children and using AI software to "nudify" them.

Andy Burnham called the case "disturbing", adding: "I would ask those working across the criminal justice system to look at it and to make any necessary changes as a result."

The Ministry of Justice said while the Crown Prosecution Service had the right to challenge them, final bail decisions were "made by the independent judiciary".

The ministry added: "The protection of victims, witnesses, and the public must always be considered when deciding whether or not an offender should be released on bail."

London's victims' commissioner Andrea Simon said victims and their families had been "grossly failed" by the court system that granted Dogan bail.

She said the case showed "the justice system did not centre victims" and called for a multi-agency review.

Speaking outside the court where Dogan was jailed, Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley criticised the "unfathomable decisions" of the justice system.

Burnham told BBC London's political editor Karl Mercer that Sir Mark "certainly has a point and it needs to be heard".

"It's a matter for the courts when these decisions are made," the prime minister said. "They need to hear the voice of the commissioner of the Metropolitan Police.

"This case is disturbing and I would ask those working across the criminal justice system to look at it and make any necessary changes as a result."

Burnham also told BBC London the plan to release some offenders before the end of their custodial sentences, to free up space in prisons, was "not an ideal situation".

"The failure to build prison spaces over a number of years has led to this unacceptable situation," he said.

Dogan had pleaded guilty to three counts of making indecent images of a child, which included 900 category C images, 294 category B images and 653 category A images, which are the most serious.

He also admitted possessing extreme pornography, possessing a prohibited image of a child, creating purported intimate images of an adult, obstructing a constable in the execution of their duty and a further two counts of making indecent photographs of a child.

According to the police, he had taken more than 5,000 pictures, many from his bedroom window.

Despite protests from the police and prosecutors, he had previously been bailed back to his flat, forcing one family who had fallen victim to his crimes to move into temporary accommodation.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today, Simon said: "I think victims and their families were grossly failed by the decision to allow this paedophile to return to an address where he was overlooking a playground near to his victims.

"The case [shows that] the justice system just does not centre victims. To know that the police and prosecutors opposed bail multiple times, but nevertheless, he was returned to the community, is an indication that the capacity pressures on prisons are not being balanced with the impacts that that's having on victims' lives.

"We seem to be lurching from one crisis to another, and victim safety and their rights seem to be put to one side, as the justice system struggles."

News.title: Ex-GTA developer's studio faces closure after debut game flopped
News.content:
Benzies set up Barb in 2016 - the same year he left Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar Games after a legal row over unpaid royalties.

It began work on Everywhere, intended to be a multiplayer role-playing game set in a futuristic city, before pivoting its focus to action-adventure MindsEye.

The project attracted a lot of interest and, according to company documents, external, Barb had managed to attract more than Â£233m of investment by 2024.

Former staff previously told BBC Newsbeat the development process had "no coherent direction" and accused senior managers of failing to listen to their concerns.

Following the game's turbulent launch, between 250 to 300 members of staff were made redundant.

Shortly before this, during an all-staff call, Benzies alleged "internal and external" forces had conspired to hinder MindsEye's release, and vowed to root out "saboteurs" within the company.

When Newsbeat asked Barb about this, it released a statement saying: "Leslie and the entire senior management team take full responsibility for the initial launch [of MindsEye].

"The version of the game that was released did not reflect the experience our community deserved."

Since its release, the company has failed to attract a bigger audience to the game with a series of fixes and content updates.

After further layoffs, reports last week suggested the remaining workers at the studio had also been let go.

The father-in-law of a murder victim has attacked the killer in the middle of his sentencing hearing.

Alberto Ontiveros-Sanchez, 55, had just finished delivering his victim impact statement in an Arizona courtroom Wednesday when he lunged at Abel Uribe, 33.

Nearly five years ago, Ontiveros-Sanchez’s son-in-law, 27-year-old Army Captain David Navidad-Parra, was found by Phoenix police dead on the ground with a gunshot wound. Uribe was quickly arrested in connection with his murder, and he has since pleaded guilty.

In a courtroom video, Ontiveros-Sanchez can be seen leaving the lectern and then pivoting right to the defense table, where he struck Uribe, who was restrained with handcuffs and leg chains, several times with his hand.

open image in gallery Alberto Ontiveros-Sanchez, the father-in-law of a murder victim, pictured, attacked the killer, Abel Uribe, in the middle of his sentencing hearing Wednesday ( Maricopa County Sheriff's Office )

Chaos erupted, with people seen pulling Ontiveros-Sanchez off of Uribe. Everyone then started clearing out of the courtroom.

Ontiveros-Sanchez was arrested, and then hours later he appeared for his own court hearing.

“After Mr. Ontiveros-Sanchez gave his remarks at the podium, he was very emotional," his attorney Christian Lueders told the judge at that hearing, per ABC15 Arizona.

"He came back and saw that the defendant who was there to be sentenced was laughing, snickering, and he lost it."

open image in gallery Ontiveros-Sanchez could be seen in a video, lunging to the defense table, where he struck Uribe, who was restrained with handcuffs and leg chains, several times with his hand ( Maricopa County Superior Court )

While the judge sympathized with what Ontiveros-Sanchez was feeling that day in court, he said violence would not be tolerated.

"I personally cannot imagine the emotions you were feeling today, but we cannot tolerate that kind of conduct in court," the judge said, according to the local outlet.

The judge allowed Ontiveros-Sanchez to be released, but he faces charges, including aggravated assault.

open image in gallery Ontiveros-Sanchez’s son-in-law, 27-year-old Army Captain David Navidad-Parra, was found by Phoenix police dead on the ground with a gunshot wound. Uribe was quickly arrested in connection with the murder, and he has since pleaded guilty ( Maricopa County Sheriff's Office )

While at the sentencing hearing before the incident, Ontiveros-Sanchez asked that Uribe receive the maximum punishment.

"I am asking for the gentleman who did this for him to be in jail for life. Not doing so would be to not do justice," he said, per local outlet KYMA.

After police found Navidad-Parra’s body on December 17, 2022, they learned of another call in the area about a man who went missing while giving a test drive of a car he was trying to sell to another guy.

Police confirmed the missing man was Navidad-Parra. That same day, Uribe was taken into custody.

When the sentencing hearing resumed, Uribe was given life in prison with the possibility of parole, according to reports.

A pumped-up Carlos Alcaraz delighted a London crowd containing Roger Federer to win in the Laver Cup doubles alongside Jakub Mensik and put Team Europe 3-1 up after day one.

Seven-time grand slam champion Alcaraz only returned from a four-month lay-off with a wrist injury at the US Open after he missed Wimbledon and Queen’s, but kept this Ryder Cup-style event on his calendar and was in the thick of the action on Friday.

World number three Alcaraz relished his opportunity to give out coaching instructions on a first appearance of 2026 in England before he ended up on the floor in celebration after a win for Casper Ruud during the day session.

Hours later, with a silver chain on show along with a white compression sleeve on his right arm, Alcaraz brushed off a couple of early wayward volleys to sparkle at The O2 with an array of forehand winners and deft touches at the net during 87 minutes on court in front of all-time great Federer.

Alcaraz and partner Mensik downed Taylor Fritz and Alexander Bublik by a 6-4 6-4 score to bring the curtain down on an entertaining and successful first day for Team Europe after earlier wins for Ruud and Rafael Jodar.

“I am trying to have fun every place I go and every court I play on and especially doubles,” Alcaraz said during his on-court interview.

“I try to enjoy, try to be better and try to improve my tennis, my things and a couple of adjustments.

“I am trying to enjoy as much as I can and having a partner like Jakub, it is really easy to have fun on the court.”

Mensik added: “We didn’t do it that much to be honest during the week, and especially me.

“For Carlos, it doesn’t matter if he plays singles or doubles, I think he could be world number one even in doubles!”

Ruud kicked off the action and marked his sixth appearance for Team Europe with a 6-7 (4) 6-4 10-8 victory over Francisco Cerundolo to floor a jubilant Alcaraz.

Alcaraz was in the ear of the two-time French Open runner-up Ruud during a difficult first set and the Norwegian eventually clinched the opener in London after a tense final point in the match tie-break.

It ended with Alcaraz in a heap on top of team-mates Jodar and Flavio Cobolli after a Ruud winner before the Spaniard got up to join the celebrations, but Team World debutant Brandon Nakashima got Andre Agassi’s men on the board with win over Mensik.

After Nakashima was victorious by a 6-1 3-6 10-7 score, the American was labelled “AI” by captain Agassi.

“He’s rock solid,” Agassi said. “I’m not convinced he is real. I think he is AI. He just goes about his business point after point after point.”

Spanish sensation Jodar dismantled Bublik in emphatic fashion but only after he required the help of captain Yannick Noah to assist with more shoelace issues in the third game.

Jodar has risen up the rankings during the past 12 months and yet caused occasional ire with frequent problems with his trainers. After he resolved this issue and received encouragement from Alcaraz, the big-hitting 20-year-old smashed his way to a 6-2 6-3 win in front of Federer.

“I’m very happy to represent (Team Europe) and I also want to thank Roger who was in the stands watching me. It’s a pleasure,” Jodar said.

All eyes were then on Alcaraz and he did not disappoint.

An early bullet forehand down the line was a sign of things to come and a succession of volleys at the net, including on match point, inspired Team Europe to a 3-1 lead after day one.

At a Catholic home south of Argentina’s capital, residents with disabilities are eagerly preparing to welcome Pope Leo XIV as their caregivers struggle to secure medicine, diapers and other essentials.

Leo will visit the home in Claypole, a working-class suburb of Buenos Aires, on Nov. 9, a day after meeting President Javier Milei. The back-to-back stops will take him from the presidential palace to a home whose staff say the libertarian leader’s spending cuts threaten the round-the-clock assistance residents need to walk, talk, eat and bathe.

Home to about 400 people with disabilities, the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione resembles a small town, with roads connecting dozens of residential buildings, classrooms and therapy rooms around a central square and church. Beyond basic care, it helps residents develop skills and pursue their own goals through cooking workshops, gardening and dance classes. Families often turn to the institution when they cannot afford care or are unable or unwilling to provide it themselves, caregivers say. Most residents receive no family visits.

For years, the home also served as a training ground for future priests. As archbishop of Buenos Aires, Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, encouraged seminarians to spend a month at the Cottolengo before ordination, putting their faith into practice through service to people on society’s margins. Francis never returned to Argentina during his 12-year papacy, disappointing many of his compatriots.

Now Leo’s visit promises to draw international attention to the home at a critical moment, said Fernando Montero, who oversees its disability services. Since government deliveries of medicines, diapers, dressings and food stopped in November 2025, the home has relied on its own funds and donations to fill the gap.

"Pope Leo’s visit gives us great hope that this problem — and people with disabilities themselves — will gain visibility,” Montero said.

___ Associated Press writer Isabel DeBre in Buenos Aires, Argentina, contributed to this report.

An 18-year-old has been arrested after he was spotted allegedly moving a tub that contained a dismembered torso at an apartment in Smyrna, Georgia.

Kingston Bradley has been charged with concealing the death. He was taken into custody on Wednesday and is being held without bond at the Cobb County Jail, according to 11Alive.

Bradley was allegedly spotted moving a plastic tub through an outdoor area at the Park Valley Apartments around 8:15 p.m. on Wednesday.

When Bradley noticed that he was being watched, he allegedly dropped the tub in a dirt walkway and ran into his apartment, which is in the same complex.

Police received a missing person's report directing them to the complex. When officers arrived at the scene and opened the tub, they discovered a dismembered human torso inside.

Kingston Bradley, 18, was charged with concealing the death after police allegedly found a tub containing a woman's torso near his apartment, as well as blood, carpet cleaner, and a strong scent of bleach inside his Smyrna, Georgia apartment ( Cobb County )

Investigators then searched Bradley's apartment and allegedly found multiple bloodstains inside as well as a large, blood-covered saw. Police said in a report that a strong bleach smell was present in the apartment. They also allegedly found a mop, a bucket of water, and a carpet cleaner.

The victim was identified as a woman, but her name has not been released to the public. The victim's family told 11 Alive that the woman who was killed was Shanteria "Tia" Mosely.

They said they filed a missing person's report after she left home to make DoorDash deliveries and did not return home. The family members claim they tracked Mosely's phone to the apartment complex and even spoke to Bradley, who allegedly told them he had not seen the woman.

Michelle Weaver, Mosely's aunt, said she is the one who saw Bradley allegedly moving the tub.

The Smyrna Police Department is still investigating the incident.

Bradley has a previous, unresolved case that involves a fight with his father in late 2024. He was charged with two counts of terroristic threats, battery, simple battery, and criminal trespass-damage to property.

According to a warrant in that case, Bradley allegedly hit his father with an Xbox controller, breaking down his bedroom door, and then pushing "a 15-year-old male juvenile" into a window, breaking it in the process.

The terroristic threat charge comes from him allegedly "suggesting the death" of his father.

Bradley pleaded not guilty in that case in April and will face his next hearing for that matter on October 6.

A powerful nor’easter storm on track to lash the East Coast this weekend is being fueled by climate change, according to scientists.

Even though a super El Niño climate pattern has suppressed hurricane formation in the Atlantic so far this year, the ocean’s exceptionally warm waters have helped the storm’s formation.

These water temperatures have been made 10-50 times more likely due to human-caused climate change, according to the non-profit Climate Central.

And it’s not just ocean temperatures that have been influenced. Rising sea levels and flooding linked to the storm are also exacerbated by climate change.

Delaware would only experience minor flooding from the nor’easter without sea level rise and New York City wouldn’t see flooding at all without climate change, the group said.

open image in gallery John Garrisi, left, and Gaige Graf move an outdoor table away from the shorefront during the early stages of the nor'easter storm on Friday in Gloucester, Mass. Impacts from the nor’easter are expected into next week ( AP )

“Climate change is raising sea levels along the East Coast, so coastal communities are starting every storm from a higher water level,” Dr. Zachary Labe, a climate scientist at Climate Central, said in a statement.

“That makes flooding and erosion from nor’easters like this one more likely and more severe,” he added.

A wind gust of 52 mph was recorded on the north side of Long Island on Friday afternoon, according to The Weather Channel.

Coastal flooding is expected from the Mid-Atlantic up to New England, with some flooding already affecting parts of Virginia and North Carolina on Friday.

Rip currents are expected at beaches, and heavy rain and strong wind gusts will make travel difficult.

Ahead of the storm, states of emergency were declared by the governors of New York and New Jersey.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul urged residents to “take this storm seriously” on social media, declaring an emergency for Nassau, Suffolk, New York City and Westchester.

“We’re expecting dangerous coastal flooding, strong winds and potential power outages through the weekend,” she said in a post on X.

In New York City, the annual Global Citizens Festival, featuring artists and celebrities including Lauryn Hill, John Legend, Shaboozey and Korean boy band Tomorrow X Together was cancelled and tickets were refunded.

Con Edison, New York City’s largest utility, said the energy company was “preparing additional crews to respond around the clock” in a post on X.

Notably, there are no lifeguards on duty at New York’s public beaches this weekend, because the season ended on September 13.

open image in gallery New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency ahead of the storm ( Getty )

In neighboring New Jersey, Gov. Mikie Sherrill wrote on X that a state of emergency was effective starting at 5 p.m. in Atlantic, Burlington, Cape May, Cumberland, Middlesex, Monmouth, Ocean and Salem counties.

The state’s largest utility, PSE&G, also said its crews were prepared to work “24/7” to restore any service, should outages occur.

“As the storm’s track continues to evolve, the company has activated its storm response plan, positioned additional crews and resources throughout its service territory, alerted customers, and is prepared to respond safely and efficiently should severe weather cause power outages,” the company wrote in a release.

Impacts from the nor’easter are expected into next week, federal forecasters cautioned.

“In addition to the rain, wind gusts in excess of 50 mph are likely for eastern Long Island and southeastern New England, which will lead to power outages and tree damage in some areas,” the National Weather Service said.

Gucci creative director Demna moved beyond the strict archetypes of his debut collection and fixed his gaze on the fashion house’s luxe heritage for his all-important second collection, previewed Friday during Milan Fashion Week.

The runway was transformed into a luxury Gucci boutique, where Cardi B, wrapped in white faux fur, and Donatella Versace, wearing a stole from Demna’s first Gucci collection, sat on cushioned sofas. Brand ambassador Jannik Sinner took a seat beside Vogue’s Anna Wintour.

Models broadcast nonchalance as they strolled through the boutique, casting their eyes over jewelry cases, shelves of handbags and racks of ready-to-wear.

At a moment when the luxury business is struggling, the setting made the commercial imperative unusually explicit: These were clothes intended not merely to project an image, but to move from rack to wardrobe. And the runway offered flexible propositions for eager consumers.

“Gucci is about luxury that wants to be seen,” Demna wrote in show notes.

A bold silhouette made the first pitch, before the details became apparent. Men’s suits had exaggeratedly broad shoulders, while pagoda shoulders shaped women’s jackets and dresses. Collars were turned up, adding to the attitude. The styling remained Italian: cropped pants and elongated loafers with no socks for him, a cinched trench coat over a blouse and skirt for her.

References to Alessandro Michele’s eccentricity and Tom Ford’s sexualized silhouettes were less stark than in Demna’s debut. Instead of asking customers to embody one of his sharply drawn Italian “famiglia” archetypes, the collection proposes borrowing elements without becoming captive to them.

Layering made those identities harder to pin down. Low-slung trousers held precariously in place by three belts suggested the swagger of a maranza, or troublemaking urban youth. But a bourgeois tartan skirt of an impeccably groomed Milanese woman was destabilized by a leather bomber worn over a plaid shirt and finished with an oversized necklace.

The collection’s strongest looks had undoubted commercial appeal: A double-breasted navy peacoat paired with high-heeled equestrian boots — with spurs for a Demna flourish — and a rugby shirt with Gucci stripes for him layered under an Oxford shirt and Gucci logo jacket.

Moschino puts fashion back on the street.

At Moschino, Loris Messina and Simone Rizzo brought the cult credibility they built at Sunnei to their debut as creative directors, taking up founder Franco Moschino’s legacy of intellectual wit.

Their debut show was set on the top floor of a parking garage overlooking the 2026 Olympic ice hockey venue just as the setting sun created a pinkish sky in the background.

The runway was flanked by hundreds of people in their own clothes walking in the opposite direction throughout the show, creating a stream of personal styles that situated the collection among everyday wardrobes.

The house’s irony remained, but it felt less dependent on quirk and gimmick than in recent iterations. Grass fringe punctured the preciousness of luxury, while cartoonish graphics functioned more as art than as characters or caricatures.

Still, humor came through the clothes themselves: exaggerated side bustles brought Marie Antoinette proportions to skirts worn like denim, while padding turned the enhanced backside to suggest a female ideal. It was still recognizably Moschino, but the joke didn’t overwhelm the clothes.

Fans who look to Moschino for novelty bags shaped like milk cartons or cooking pots may be disappointed by the pared-down aesthetic. The bag of the season was a very practical, large bucket bag and the only nod to novelty was a bag shaped like a cat that perched on a model's shoulder.

The designers said they are forging a modern version of the fashion house that isn't stuck in previous decades.

“We want Moschino to become a cultural loudspeaker again,” Rizzo said. “We have the same urgency in terms of creativity and breaking walls, but it's 2026.”

The Supreme Court will let Donald Trump’s administration implement an expansive government database that collects citizenship data, Social Security numbers and other sensitive information for millions of Americans, a powerful tool that federal agencies and state officials could use to hunt for ineligible voters.

Voting rights groups fear that the database could be used to wrongfully purge eligible voters without an opportunity to correct mistakes, opening the door for unnecessary confusion and illegal disenfranchisement.

The high court’s ruling will likely not have any significant impact on this year’s midterm elections; justices stressed that the administration must comply with the National Voter Registration Act, which bars any major changes to registration rules within 90 days of a federal election.

“Today’s Supreme Court order is a serious blow to voter privacy and civil rights, but it changes nothing about what the law requires before the midterms,” said Tim Harper with the Center for Democracy & Technology.

Still, voting rights advocates and elections experts fear that the conservative majority court has opened the door for the administration to put millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable database.

open image in gallery The Supreme Court will let the Trump administration implement an expansive DHS database that collects Social Security data and other sensitive information in an effort to root out noncitizen voters ( Getty )

A federal judge had previously blocked use of the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, or SAVE, arguing that it likely violated Americans’ privacy rights and could end up wrongly removing eligible voters from state databases.

Homeland Security has even admitted that the data isn’t perfect, and analysts have uncovered numerous significant errors, including incorrectly flagging recently naturalized citizens as noncitizens who are ineligible to vote.

“While states are prohibited from conducting mass removals during the current statutory 90-day ‘quiet period,’ they should exercise extreme caution with any use of this database,” Verified Voting president Pamela Smith said.

“Now more than ever, voters must check their registration well in advance of Election Day to ensure they are not swept up in a flawed system through no fault of their own,” she said Friday.

States are not currently required to use the SAVE system, and it’s unclear whether there’s an appetite for an unwieldy and unreliable database within a critical period before national elections with no room for error.

"This decision will not have any significant impact on the 2026 election, as systematic voter list maintenance is prohibited within 90 days of a federal election, which the Supreme Court explicitly confirmed,” said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research.

“The most important thing for voters to know is that they will continue to experience the same safe, secure, and reliable voting process in 2026 that they have in past elections,” he said.

open image in gallery The DHS database under Secretary Markwayne Mullin won’t change any rules before midterm elections, but critics fear the Supreme Court has opened the door for the Trump administration to begin identifying allegedly ineligible voters for mass purges ( AFP/Getty )

Friday’s emergency ruling was unsigned, but the court’s three liberal justices joined a 12-page dissent that warned that any program that disenfranchises “even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take.”

The decision is a victory for Trump after a series of losses at the high court, including in his attempts to overhaul election administration — efforts that dovetail with his government-wide anti-immigration campaign.

The administration has justified the citizenship database as part of an ongoing effort to identify noncitizen voters, fueled by the president’s baseless claims that millions of ineligible voters have cast ballots against him.

But critics argue that the database puts the burden of protecting the right to vote on voters themselves, forcing new citizens and other people who would be wrongfully removed to prove they belong.

Jacqueline De León, senior staff attorney with the Native American Rights Fund, argued that the SAVE tool won’t have any “meaningful” impact on removing ineligible voters from rolls but could end up having “a devastating impact on removing voters who are indeed eligible to vote.”

“At the very least, it will sow confusion among voters nationwide, which may be part of its intended purpose,” she said Friday.

“SAVE was never designed to verify citizenship: it relies on outdated and inaccurate data that produces false matches, risks disenfranchising eligible voters, and exposes sensitive personal information to misuse and bad actors,” added Harper with the Center for Democracy & Technology.

“To be clear: claims that SAVE has uncovered widespread noncitizen voting or proven fraud in past elections are not supported by the evidence,” he said. “Noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare, and states already maintain their rolls through more accurate and privacy-protective methods.”

James Percival, general counsel for Homeland Security, appeared to celebrate the court’s ruling. “Yes, you read that right. We had to file an emergency petition in the Supreme Court just so we could use government data to help states stop noncitizens from illegally voting,” he wrote on X.

News.title: Carreras’ try-of-season contender helps Bath eclipse Harlequins
News.content:
And they kept playing, it was not until Richards scored in the 72nd minute that the game was decided. Still for Bath, a five-try victory away from home, felt like a decent return.

If they were to stand any chance of finding a way back into the game, Quins had to score first after the restart. They were rewarded for their attacking intent after running from a scrum deep in their half, with Murley cutting a brilliant line before Pedro Delgado drove over for his side’s third try.

Quins had the opportunity to further cut the deficit when first Sam Riley carried down the left wing and Cameron Anderson drove into the Bath 22. But as Quins looked to pick and go, Beno Obano and Guy Pepper combined to hold the ball up over the line.

It felt like a significant moment and when Riley was shown a yellow card for a high tackle on Obano moments later, the odds against a Quins comeback lengthened again. Yet there was something sticky about their resilience.

“I am really happy with the grit and the fight that they showed, particularly in the second half,” said Gilmore. “We had some massive defensive sets on our goal-line which we withstood. I reckon they were the moments last year that Bath would probably run in three tries really quickly and kick the score out, which is good.”

Bath emptied their bench, including the introduction of England flanker Pepper, but they could not pull away as expected in the final quarter, despite some impressive contributions by Tom de Glanville.

It was left to their line-out maul to score their first points of the second half, with Richards touching down to seal Harlequins’ fate. Still, there were enough promising glimpses to give Harlequins supporters hope that more encouraging days lie ahead.

News.title: Manchester City found guilty of 114 charges
News.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules. It is a decision that, if upheld, would equate to one of the biggest scandals in football history.

City face a range of sanctions from a fine to points deductions and even expulsion from the Premier League. Or a combination of all, under rule W51 of its handbook. No punishment has yet been announced.

If the verdict is upheld, with City expected to appeal, it will also raise question marks over the 20 trophies the club have won under Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, whose Abu Dhabi group took over in 2008.

The charges can be broken down into five categories and relate to a period from 2009-23 in which City won six League Cups, three FA Cups, seven league titles and the Champions League. There is the provision for removing past titles, but that would appear remote.

Of the 115 charges:

Fifty-four were for failing to provide accurate financial information from 2009-10 to 2017-18

Fourteen were for failing to provide accurate details for player and manager payments from the same period

Five were for failing to comply with Uefa’s rules from 2013-14 to 2017-18

Seven were for breaching Premier League profitability and sustainability rules from 2015-16 to 2017-18

Thirty-five were for failing to co-operate with the investigation from 2018-23.

City have been the dominant force in English football for most of that time, but that status is under threat with a verdict that will send shockwaves around Europe and could have huge ramifications for the club.

That is unless they can win an appeal, with sources cautioning it still may take up to another two to three years for the case to be resolved, following on from an already five-year investigation.

Case is far from being resolved

The Premier League’s rules provide for an independent appeal board with broad powers, including the ability to uphold, vary or overturn the independent commission’s decision.

It would therefore appear that despite the verdict, the case is far from being resolved and punishment decided. The details of the commission’s findings, when published, will be crucial to determining what happens next.

But if it is upheld, the verdict also opens up the possibility of City facing legal action from other clubs who feel they missed out on trophies and even merit money from league placings.

It is understood Premier League clubs are already discussing legal action and possible compensation claims as a result of the guilty verdict.

News.title: Britain sends team to South Sudan as country braces for Ebola
News.content:
British Ebola specialists have been deployed to South Sudan because of fears the haemorrhagic fever will spread from neighbouring Congo.

A rare form of Ebola, known as the Bundibugyo species, is spreading rapidly in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where more than 7,800 people have caught the virus since May, 3,700 of whom have died.

To prepare for the threat of imported cases, Britain has positioned three experts in and around the South Sudanese capital, Juba. They will assist and train local authorities on infection control, set up awareness campaigns for local communities, and test people crossing the border for the virus.

The team is employed by the UK Health Security Agency’s (UKHSA) Public Health Rapid Support Team (PHRST), which is regularly sent to the epicentre of disease outbreaks overseas – for instant the cruise ship at the centre of a deadly hantavirus in the South Atlantic earlier this year.

The current Ebola outbreak is the fastest-growing ever recorded and is on course to become the largest in history, overtaking the 2014-16 West Africa Ebola outbreak, in which around 30,000 people contracted the haemorrhagic fever and roughly a third died.

Experts fear it is only a matter of time before the virus spreads to South Sudan, which shares a 500-mile border with the DRC. Thousands of people cross the frontier each day to work, attend school and trade goods, mostly fish, in lucrative markets between the two countries.

If the virus gained a foothold in South Sudan, which became the newest country on earth after severing ties with Khartoum in 2011, experts fear the consequences would be catastrophic and worsen an already dire humanitarian situation.

“It’s so variable as to where the outbreak is spreading at the moment, there are cases from some of the border towns [with South Sudan],” Ed Newman, director of the PHRST, told The Telegraph.

“There’s a feeling [Ebola could spread] any day. Maybe you could say we’ve been lucky so far,” Mr Newman said, on the sidelines of a UKHSA conference in Manchester.

News.title: Russell capitalises on Antonelli error to take Azerbaijan GP pole
News.content:
Russell – who begins the weekend 81 points behind the Italian – simply has to capitalise. And he really should do. Even if Antonelli hadn’t crashed out, he has looked on a different level this weekend, dominating practice and qualifying. Russell topped Q1, Q3 and Q3, securing the 12th pole of his career with a lap which was nine tenths quicker than his best lap in Q2 and eight tenths quicker than Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, the next fastest driver. He could hardly believe it himself.

“That was a pretty decent lap,” he told his team over the radio on his cooldown lap. “How much was [the gap]?”

“Just over eight tenths to Leclerc.” came the response. “Woah!”

This has not been the easiest season for Russell, who began the year the overwhelming favourite for the title, having dominated his younger team-mate over the course of last season. So he could be forgiven for feeling proud of having done such a good job.

“It’s been a while so it definitely feels good,” he admitted. “This was probably the biggest pole margin of my whole career, including my F2 and F3 days.

“The lap felt really sweet, car’s been feeling really great this weekend. On a track like this where you can hug it, it feels amazing.”

News.title: Buttler injury derails England chase and sends Sri Lanka series to decider
News.content:
Enter Buttler to play a wonderful counter-attack, whacking Wellalage for four and six and dumping leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage over the rope twice as he raced to 41 off 22 balls.

Buttler was at a crossroads after the T20 World Cup in February. Despite England making the semi-finals, he averaged just 10 in the tournament to complete a third poor World Cup in a row. A break with his family, and a very good Indian Premier League, where he made a crucial technical correction, changed his fortunes.

Matthew Hayden, the batting coach at the Gujarat Titans, asked him whether he was watching the ball closely enough. Buttler discovered that, now 36, he is a right-eye dominant batsman, so with Hayden’s help he opened up his stance to give himself a better view of the ball. A summer rich in runs has followed with an average of 51 for England and a strut back in his body language. The injury has surely ended Buttler’s summer and there are worries that he could be out of the Pakistan ODI triangular tournament next month as well, just to add to the night’s woes.

This was not a vintage England performance. Atkinson made a crucial error on the boundary, dropping a straightforward chance off Kusal Mendis on 17. It kickstarted Mendis, who went on the charge smashing 51 in 24 balls. He put on 137 in 120 balls with Kuminda Mendis. Josh Tongue had an off day going at seven an over and Jofra Archer was given similar treatment, although he bowled better than figures suggest, as anything wayward with pace on the ball was hit away.

Overton was more effective with his cutters and slower balls, while Ahmed did at least bag a couple of wickets, credit for keeping his head after some early rough treatment. Kusal Mendis was given out leg before on 99 but overturned the decision and stroked a four next ball for a deserved hundred.

Thanks for joining me. A global rout in bond markets deepened overnight as traders expect the US to keep raising interest rates.

Japan’s 10-year bond yield surged to 3.08pc on Thursday, its highest level since 1996, as markets responded to stronger than expected US economic data and higher oil prices.

It followed sharp rises in the US on Wednesday, when the yield on 10-year Treasuries – a benchmark of global borrowing costs – surged as high as 5.12pc, up from 4.96pc. It was the biggest jump since the “liberation day” tariff turmoil in April last year.

Bonds were sent into turmoil as traders bet that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates three times by April next year in an effort to bring down inflation. Money markets suggest there is a 70pc chance of the Fed following this month’s first rate rise in three years with a second in October.

This followed closely watched industry data on Wednesday, known as PMIs, showed US private sector activity jumped unexpectedly to a five-year high in September.

Meanwhile, oil prices spiked 3.9pc on Wednesday to move back above $100 a barrel, risking an inflationary spiral in the world economy.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “The main driver was a strong batch of PMIs, along with a rebound in oil prices, which both led to mounting speculation about faster rate hikes.” Here is what you need to know.

What happened overnight

Debt markets were in turmoil after Japanese bond yields hit 30-year highs.

Japan’s benchmark stock market, the Nikkei 225 rose 1pc to 65,645.10, as some chipmakers got a boost from the recent interest in AI. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.7pc to 8,702.00.

News.title: Zelensky lashes out at EU
News.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky lashed out at the European Union over its moves to weaken sanctions on Russian oligarchs.

In his address to the UN General Assembly, the Ukrainian leader warned that beyond making life “more comfortable” for Russians, “it also gives the war more time for Putin to send poor people into the kill zone. So Russia’s revenues must remain a target.”

His criticism came after France and Luxembourg successfully pushed for sanctions exemptions for Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, Russian oligarchs, on Tuesday.

Kyiv branded the decision “shameful and unjustifiable”. The men are known to share close ties to Vladimir Putin and have net worths of $14bn and $16bn, respectively.

In his fourth address to the UN as a wartime leader, Mr Zelensky said it was paramount that the international community increased pressure on the Kremlin to stop “the madness” of the war spreading.

Under pressure from Donald Trump to halt attacks on Russian energy targets, Mr Zelensky defended his country’s aerial offensive for successfully depriving Putin of revenue for his war.

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said.

‘End the war before winter’

Washington has recently attempted to revive the long-stalled negotiations between Ukraine and Russia. On Tuesday, Mr Zelensky implored Mr Trump to help Kyiv end the war “before winter”.

Mr Trump appeared optimistic, suggesting an agreement would happen “more quickly than people understand”.

Sergei Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that Russia was prepared to negotiate for a lasting peace but would not “pause the war”.

Mr Zelensky sought to remind world leaders that the conflict was not constrained within Ukraine’s borders at a time when the global community was distracted by a myriad of conflicts and crises.

Citing the support of Iran and North Korea for Russia, he warned that Putin’s war kept “spreading further”.

“Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and take another country instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” Mr Zelensky said at the UN.

He noted that fighters from at least 47 countries were helping to prosecute Moscow’s war against Ukraine and urged leaders to prevent their citizens from being dragged into the conflict.

After Mr Zelensky’s address, reports emerged that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s envoy, was on his way to the US where he would meet Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Trump administration representatives.

Sources told Reuters that the meeting would take place in New ‌York on the sidelines of the UN summit.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, also confirmed Mr Trump had invited his Russian counterpart to attend the G20 summit of world leaders in Miami in December.
