World.title: Marineland belugas that died in Chicago had chronic inflammatory disease, preliminary necropsy findings show
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Post-mortem examinations of two former Marineland belugas indicate the whales were sick when they arrived last month at their new home at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago.

Peekachu, 23, and Rain, 20, arrived on Aug. 13 as part of a massive operation to rehome 30 belugas and four dolphins from Niagara Falls, Ont., to four aquariums in the U.S. and one in Spain. The moves took place in six stages this summer.

Preliminary medical findings “identified significant, chronic gastrointestinal disease,” according to a Shedd Aquarium release on the two whales’ deaths.

“The disease had likely been present for an extended period,” according to the aquarium, due to “the significance of the inflammation, the types of immune cells present” and other signs.

“These changes develop over time, potentially months or years, indicating that the disease began before the whales arrived at Shedd and compromised their health rendering them more vulnerable and sensitive,” said the statement.

Rocks among foreign objects in stomachs

Examinations on the female belugas also revealed foreign materials in their stomachs, including “bird feathers, sticks and large, porous rocks” in Peekachu, and “small flecks of material that may be paint” in Rain.

In the case of Peekachu, “she could not have ingested these materials while at Shedd, and they are believed to have been present before her rescue,” said the statement.

Peekachu, a 23-year-old beluga whale from Marineland, died suddenly on Aug. 25 at the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago. (Shedd Aquarium)

“It's just one of the things that happens to bored, intelligent animals,” said Naomi Rose, marine mammal scientist for the Animal Welfare Institute in Washington, DC.

"If nobody's there to sort of keep an eye on that and remove those objects, then they'll play with them in that way. And every once in a while, they ingest them.”

Shedd said it doesn’t believe the foreign materials were directly related to their passing. The necropsy also found no evidence of communicable disease.

Marineland, the permanently closed theme park and zoo, threatened to euthanize the animals last fall, writing at the time that it was running out of money to care for them.

Another female beluga, 26-year-old Osiris, also died after arriving at Shedd Aquarium, but necropsy results aren’t currently available.

Two other former Marineland animals ‒ Jelly Bean, a 19-year-old beluga, and Echo, a 30-year-old bottlenose dolphin ‒ also died, after being rehomed to Oceanogràfic de València in Spain. Post-mortems are also being done in these cases.

The Marineland belugas were transported by cargo plane to Chicago on July 21. (Shedd Aquarium/ Brenna Hernandez)

Ottawa cites apparent 'neglect' of whales

A statement from the office of Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said the preliminary necropsy findings reveal “an unacceptable neglect for their health and well-being prior to their relocation.”

It added that “we continue to be grateful to the experienced professionals who have played a role in this operation, helping provide a dignified last chapter to these whales and supporting many others in their new homes.”

WATCH | Concerns over the death of another Marineland beluga: CBC's Aarti Pole talks to Valeria Vergara about concerns over the recent death of a Marineland beluga. | Duration closed caption 7:36 Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis.

In a statement to CBC News on Friday, Marineland called the deaths of the two whales "extremely unfortunate, and our thoughts are with those who cared for them at Marineland and Shedd."

"We acknowledge and appreciate the DFO’s [Department of Fisheries and Oceans'] concern and note that they had no oversight, role, responsibility or expertise in or for animal care at Marineland."

Citing Shedd's early indications that the whales died from inflammation, Marineland said it agrees that the materials found in their digestive tracts weren't the cause.

A Marineland beluga whale is transported onto a truck, destined for the U.S., via a sling in Niagara Falls, Ont., on July 20. (Shedd Aquarium/ Brenna Hernandez)

"Belugas are naturally curious animals that investigate and occasionally swallow objects in their environment, both in human care and in the wild, just like the family dog does from time to time.

"Our veterinary and animal care teams successfully cared for Peekachu for 23 years and Rain for 20 years, for every day of their lives with us, in a large outdoor habitat alongside the social group they had always known," the statement said.

"We are focused on supporting the ongoing care of the rehoused animals and improving their lives while the process of investigation continues."

The Chicago aquarium said in a statement that Peekachu and Rain “came to Shedd from a facility where provincial authorities had repeatedly documented environmental concerns… Shedd understood that some whales could arrive with serious, long-standing health needs that could in no way be fully assessed before the rescue.”

‘I'm still expecting more of these whales to die’

Camille Labchuk, executive director of Animal Justice, questioned whether the whales were healthy enough to be moved.

“And I think that's something that experts should have detected beforehand,” said Labchuk.

She said her group has been warning the federal and provincial governments for years that at some point, Marineland would close and the whales would need to be moved.

“There should have been a lot more diligence years ago to get these whales into a healthier condition so… they could have survived the move without paying the price with their lives.”

“This was a slow-moving disaster that everybody saw coming,” said Labchuck, “I'm still expecting more of these whales to die.”

World.title: Trump's top trade envoy says U.S. 'comfortable' with state of relationship with Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump is "comfortable" with where things stand with Canada — his country's once closest ally — and is in no rush to reach a new trade deal, according to his top trade envoy.

"The reality is President Trump is comfortable where we are on Canada," United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a Friday morning interview with the American network CNBC.

"They call us now and then and we have good conversations about potential deals. But there's no urgency on our side."

The two countries have been embroiled in a trade dispute since Trump was re-elected, but the relationship further soured after talks to reach a deal collapsed at the 11th hour last month.

The U.S. side maintains Canada walked away from a good deal. The Canadian side has accused the Americans of not negotiating in good faith and encroaching on Canada's sovereignty.

Greer, who mainly spoke to CNBC about new trade negotiations with Chinese President Xi Jinping, was asked about the state of the trade relationship with Canada.

"We're still getting what we need from them in terms of oil, gas, potash, all of these things. We're shipping [agricultural products] back and forth across the border, so there's still a lot of strong trade between the two countries," he said.

The U.S. slapped 50 per cent duties on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods on Aug. 22. Canada started collecting retaliatory tariffs Sept. 8. The summer measures are on top of existing levies on Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and lumber.

Starting next week, the Trump administration plans to ban the import of certain products including Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and molasses.

Trump has also ratcheted up his jabs at Canada since trade talks fell apart, including posting to social media a map of North America with the U.S. flag covering Canada and another post showing a cartoon version of himself standing over a sprawled out Prime Minister Mark Carney during a hockey game saying, "Get up, governor."

He has also signed an order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

LeBlanc says he talks to Greer a few times a week

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Greer's comments are consistent with his conversations with the U.S. trade representative — adding he talks to his counterpart a few times a week including later Friday afternoon.

"We'll continue to do the good faith work to try and get the agreement, but I'm not waiting by my phone to see if I have a text from [U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard] Lutnick on Mr. Greer," said LeBlanc from Moncton, N.B.

"We're continuing to do the work, but we are always ready to talk to the Americans about trying to find the right agreement."

Former Canadian ambassador to the U.S. Frank McKenna said he'd be careful with the rhetoric coming from the south that there's no sense of urgency for a deal.

WATCH | LeBlanc on his conversations with Greer: Canada not 'desperate' to get a U.S. trade deal 'at any cost,' says minister | Duration closed caption 1:27 Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says comments from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer that the Trump administration is not in a rush to make a deal with Canada are 'consistent with the conversations' he's had with his U.S. counterpart. LeBlanc says the government will keep working to reach an agreement, but 'we're not waiting by the phone.'

"I would think in terms of some of the states in play in this midterm election — which is starting to swing pretty sharply blue — there would be some urgency because the affordability issue is the big issue, and trade is associated with affordability," he told CBC's Rosemary Barton Live.

The former diplomat said that with the two parties still in contact, "at some point, this will become ripe and some kind of a trade deal will be done."

McKenna, who is also a former premier of New Brunswick, said it's "a logical imperative" that two countries bound as closely as Canada and the U.S. "would end up eventually having a trade deal."

World.title: Liberal MP says he was demoted for supporting NDP bill targeting arms export controls
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Charlottetown MP Sean Casey says he was removed from his position as parliamentary secretary to the minister of veterans affairs because he supported an NDP private member's bill that targeted arms exports to Israel.

In March, Casey said he was warned by the Liberal whip that if he supported NDP MP Jenny Kwan's Bill C-233, known as the No More Loopholes Act, then he would be relieved of his duties.

Although 15 Liberal MPs broke rank and supported the bill, Casey was the only parliamentary secretary to do so.

"The bill was targeted at closing the loopholes that allowed for Canadian military equipment to be sold to another country but end up in Israel, so end up being used to kill Palestinians," said Casey in an interview with CBC News.

"That was the goal of the legislation. And that's what my constituents were concerned about."

Casey said he received a call from the Atlantic desk of the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) on Thursday saying that he was being replaced. He described the conversations with both the whip and the PMO as "direct" and clearly referencing his support for Kwan's bill.

On Friday, the PMO announced that Quebec MP Sophie Chatel will replace Casey.

Parliamentary secretaries make $20,900 above their base MP salary of $217,700 and represent the minister at public events.

Casey said over the past six months, he began to wonder whether he'd be disciplined at all.

"I kept my word to my constituents and I voted in favour of the legislation and didn't hear anything from anyone until yesterday," he said.

"It took so darn long, I was kind of wondering if they forgot about me."

Departure from Trudeau platform

Casey said his understanding was that Liberal MPs outside of cabinet were entitled to a free vote on private member's bills, except in cases that involve implementing the Liberal platform, traditional confidence matters like the budget or instances that affected protections guaranteed in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

This was explicitly laid out in the 2015 Liberal platform that brought the Trudeau Liberals to power.

"Based on everything I knew in my 15 years here, there was a rule change that was unbeknownst to me and to many of my colleagues," he said.

The Prime Minister's Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The vote did not appear to be whipped, given that more than a dozen Liberal MPs did support Kwan's bill, which ultimately failed.

In a statement, Kwan said what happened to Casey is "distressing and should concern all Canadians."

She said it raises questions about the Liberal government's commitment to allowing MPs to exercise their judgment and represent their constituents freely.

"The prime minister talks a good talk, but in reality, he will wield his power to shut down dissent," she said.

Casey said this will not prevent him from reflecting the will of his constituents in the House, saying "if anything, I'm freed a little bit to not have to toe the party line as strictly as is now apparently required."

But he said he continues to have "tremendous" respect for the prime minister and affection for the Liberal Party.

"What has happened doesn't change that one iota," he said.

World.title: Taylor Swift dropped 4 new songs. Here's what fans are sleuthing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If there’s one thing guaranteed to turn the internet into a room full of amateur detectives, it’s a new Taylor Swift track. Make that four and they go full-blown CSI.

The pop star dropped The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, the extended version of her 2025 album that includes four new tracks.

It's part of a broader trend of pop artists releasing an extension of their album as a deluxe, with experts speculating it is done to boost streaming revenue, or sell more units as physical media makes a comeback. Artists like Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo, Zara Larsson and Charli XCX have all done the same.

Swift says the new tracks came together after she went to Sweden to celebrate the success of The Life of a Showgirl with collaborators Max Martin and Shellback.

All four songs have since charted in the Top 10 on Apple Music but have been receiving mixed reviews, with some Swifties expressing letdown over the star's output.

"As a Swift fan, I find the four new songs quite disappointing," one fan wrote on X.

"I guess this era isn’t really just for me ," another wrote on Instagram. " NO ITS SO SO GOOD," a third commented.

We scrubbed through the internet to find out what fans are thinking. Shall we dive into the rumour mill? Let's go track by track.

Patient Zero

This is the lead single, she announced the other day on Instagram.

On first listen, fans think this one puts Swift in the role of "patient zero," and that she seems to be talking to an ex's new partner, singing: "I've been there. Felt the reeling, done the healing," and, "If he’s killing you, I see you. I was patient zero.”

Some speculate it could be Sofie Turner and Joe Jonas, who Taylor Swift also dated way back when. But fear not: Swift herself confirmed the meaning to Capital FM radio Friday.

“I was hanging out with a bunch of friends, and one of my friends told us that she had been reached out to by the new girlfriend of an ex of hers, asking for guidance on if she had had the same experiences with this guy that this new girlfriend was having,” Swift told the station.

“And everyone in our group just immediately started saying like, 'Oh, I've been through that too,' and telling the stories of when this kind of reach-out had happened for them.”

A music video for the song will air at this weekend's MTV VMAs, starring Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell.

Cleveland!

It doesn't require much decoding to decipher the subject of this song as Swift's husband Travis Kelce. The two got married at Madison Square Garden earlier this year. Fans think she's speaking to her critics in this one.

"He already took me to Cleveland and showed me The Heights," she pens. "And now I'm wearing white, so hate all you like this is the love of my life."

Its simplistic lyrics have Swifties spinning, some upset with her output.

"Cleveland … we need to talk," one user wrote on X. Others are coming to her defence. "Cleveland is corny and THANK GOD IT IS!!!!!!" wrote another .

Pink Clouding

This song seems to be a lyrical apology for being a "liar" in a previous relationship.

“Years later, I still wonder how to tell you sorry,” Swift sings.

Many fans are theorizing it's a message to Tom Hiddleston because of its apparent callbacks to songs from her catalogue like Getaway Car, which fans also think is about Hiddleston. The two were briefly coupled up in 2016.

“Having a Taylor Swift song about Tom Hiddleston in the big 2026 feels like sleeping with a cold pillow,” one user wrote. “Didn’t expect a hiddleswift apology in the year of 2026 i love her bad,” wrote another .

Babylon

Thing is, even Swifties can't pin down exactly what this one is about.

"Am I stupid what is she trying to say in Babylon," one fan wrote on X. "I have no idea what Taylor Swift is singing about in Babylon, but it’s my favourite movie of the year," wrote another.

A look at the lyrics tells you it's about a person who left their small town in Virginia, having regrets at a casino and on a train.

"You never knew that it was Babylon 'til it was gone," Swift writes, leading some to believe it's a message about nostalgia.

World.title: Why the viral clip of 'multitasking mom' at a baseball game has enraged people online
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A woman with a baby strapped to her chest, a diaper bag on her back, and her arms full of food at a Major League Baseball game has inadvertently become a metaphor for the disproportionate load mothers carry — in this case, literally.

The woman was singled out by two legendary broadcasters at Tuesday's game between the Giants and the Twins at Oracle Park in San Francisco as she sidestepped back toward her seat balancing three trays of food.

"Holy smokes, Mike! Look at this," Duane Kuiper says as the woman makes her way across the aisle.

"If there's ever a true definition of a multitasking mother, that is the deal right there," Mike Krukow responds in the broadcast.

The clip, which has since gone viral, shows the man in the seat next to the "multitasking mother" staring at his phone until the woman is nearly beside him, standing up to move a coat out of her seat, then digging into his food while the woman shrugs the diaper bag off her back, still holding the grinning baby and two full trays.

"Did I just hear that guy say, 'Did you forget something?'" Kuiper asks, as the two broadcasters joke that maybe he she didn't bring any ketchup.

The broadcast returned to her a few more times between pitches while Kuiper and Krukow expressed disbelief at the scene, exclaiming, "are you kidding me?" and "bless her heart" as the man popped some fried food in his mouth.

"Well, that’s mom of the year right there!" Krukow said.

"She’ll be the last one to eat, too," added Kuiper.

Neither the woman nor the man sitting beside her have been identified. In a statement to CBC News, a communications manager for the San Francisco Giants said that they don't plan to identify her because "we respect the privacy of all our fans."

"We hope she and her family enjoyed their night at Oracle Park — and we think that moms are amazing," the spokesperson said in a written statement.

A screen grab of a video posted to X on Tuesday showing the scene in the stands at the San Francisco Giants game against the Minnesota Twins. (@nocontextsfg/X)

Visual of a familiar sentiment

Without hearing from the people involved, observers can't know the context of the situation — like whether the man is her partner, or whether or not help was offered.

But while some have argued you can't judge a situation based on a short clip, for many others, "multitasking mom" represents invisible labour, the mental load of motherhood, and weaponized incompetence.

"How do I divorce someone else’s husband?" one person asked in the comments of an ESPNW Instagram reel of the clip viewed 40 million times by Friday. The comment was "liked" nearly 115,000 times.

"Let us stop normalizing this," someone else commented.

The clip is resonating because it gave a visual to a familiar sentiment — that women do more household labour and family management, explained Shana MacDonald, the O'Donovan Chair in communication at the University of Waterloo, who researches social and digital media.

"This showed that in a very direct but almost comical way," she told CBC News.

On a broader scale, the past year has seen a significant increase in conversations around motherhood, MacDonald added. Some parts of society are emphasizing motherhood as "womens' central calling," she noted, while in other spheres, we're hearing more concerns about burnout and lack of support.

That includes some of the recent conversations about Lindsay Clancy, the U.S. mom who was on trial for the deaths of her three children, MacDonald said.

WATCH | Social media drives obsession with Lindsay Clancy trial: How social media drives toxic obsession with the Lindsay Clancy case | Duration closed caption 3:41 The online obsession with the Lindsay Clancy trial has turned a horrific tragedy into a frenzy of speculation, misinformation and conspiracy theories. For The National, CBC's Ashley Fraser examines how social media's insatiable appetite for the case both raises, and undermines, awareness about postpartum psychosis.

Clip is triggering for many: sociology prof

The clip from the Giants game offers people a chance to voice their frustrations, Lisa Strohschein, a sociology professor at the University of Alberta and editor-in-chief of the journal Canadian Studies in Population, told CBC News.

She cautioned people against rendering judgments without knowing any of the context, while adding that the clip has tapped into the anger about structural inequalities in our society.

In the U.S., for instance, reproductive rights are being rolled back, she noted, and so-called "trad wives" that glamourize domestic life are on the rise.

In Canada, w hile some studies have found that fathers are taking on more parenting than they have in the past, others have found mothers are still generally the managers of the household. Women also still consistently take on a larger share of unpaid household work, including chores and child care, according to a 2022 Statistics Canada report.

All that to say, a woman balancing trays of dinner and a baby while a man next to her eats seems to be triggering for a lot of people, Strohschein said.

"Women, when they see this — I think it's kind of like the last straw."

World.title: Police investigating threatening email sent to Muslim schools across Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A number of regional police forces in Ontario and Quebec have launched an investigation into an email sent to Islamic schools across Canada over the course of this week, which threatened to kill Muslims unless they are deported.

The Muslim Association of Canada, which runs the nine private schools that received the email, said they alerted municipal police in Ontario, Vancouver and Montreal, as well as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, on Thursday morning.

The MAC schools follow standard provincial educational curricula, on top of Islamic, Quranic and Arabic-language education.

The email — which CBC News has seen — was fired off from a party identifying themselves as "Jehu, Citizen Vigilante" and came from an account titled "exposingNWO@protonmail.com." It was time-stamped last Sunday, Sept. 20.

Using dehumanizing language against Muslims, it says "millions on top of millions of people in the nation of Canada are ready to take up arms."

The email alludes to the upcoming Alberta referendum, which includes a question asking voters there to decide if the province should remain a part of Canada or eventually hold a vote on secession, and states Muslims will be "deported or slaughtered" once "Alberta becomes its own nation."

It then says this will happen "regardless of the election results," and "you won't be warned again."

Investigations underway

CBC News reached out to the RCMP and the six local forces where the eight schools are located.

In a statement, the London Police Service said it is investigating a threat to a local school and "collaborating with partner law enforcement agencies to gather information and assess any potential connections." Potential criminal code offences may include uttering threats, criminal harassment, or inciting willful hatred, the service said.

In the Greater Toronto Area, Peel Regional Police also posted a statement on the social media platform X, saying its hate crime unit is actively investigating. It said it beefed up officer presence overnight near local mosques and schools, and patrols will continue over the weekend.

Waterloo Regional Police said its officers visited a school after receiving notification of an emailed threat and conducted safety planning. The Ontario service's hate crime unit has launched an investigation, and are aware of emails sent to other jurisdictions as well.

The Ottawa Police Service confirmed it received a complaint and said it is working with law enforcement partners as part of an ongoing investigation.

"As a precaution, police visibility remains increased around religious institutions and the educational facility that received the complaint," the OPS said in a statement. "At this time, we have no information indicating a specific or imminent threat to religious or educational institutions in Ottawa."

Montreal's police service confirmed in an email to CBC News its hate crime unit is aware of the incident and will lead their investigation.

Scope of threat unprecedented: MAC

Nabil Sultan, a spokesperson for the Muslim Association of Canada, said while the organization has received "hate comments and emails on social media" in the past, a single note targeting many of its schools is something it has never experienced before.

"Such a disturbing email to be received by teachers and administrators, and families and children, really makes it difficult for us to live as a community feeling good about ourselves, feeling that we are welcomed in this society," he said in an interview with CBC News from London, Ont., where two of the schools that received the email are located.

Sultan said it was hard not to think of the Afzaal family, which lost four of five members after a man deliberately drove his truck into the group while they were out on an evening stroll in June 2021. London police called it a hate-motivated crime and a sentencing judge said it was a terrorist attack.

"A part of you wants to move on, and a part of you wants to believe that it was a lone wolf incident, and that something like this should not happen again," he said. "And this is a reminder that that is not the case, and we're still under threat."

CBC News visited one of the two Ottawa schools that received the emailed threat, Abraar Elementary, on both Thursday afternoon and Friday morning, around the times parents were picking up or dropping off their children.

An Ottawa Police Service vehicle was parked outside the school on Thursday.

Mohammed Saleem, the principal of Abraar Elementary School in Ottawa, said the level of violence in the email was a shock. (Pierre-Paul Couture/CBC)

Sara Omar, who had just dropped her five-year-old daughter, spoke to CBC News outside the school on Friday.

"Definitely me and my husband, and other moms in group chats, we were worried and anxious. But at the same time, honestly, we won't be intimidated," she said.

"We have confidence in our schools, in our community. So we won't stop living and bringing our children to school because of these threats."

Omar said she and her husband are still trying to figure out how to have a conversation with their daughter about the threat.

"If there is a lockdown, what does that look like? How to listen to her teachers in that moment — in such an intense moment. How do you even have these conversations with a five-year-old?"

The school's principal, Mohammed Saleem, said getting the note in his inbox was a "total shock," given the "explicitly violent language" and clear threats to children in the email.

Parents at the school were notified by email and teachers were preparing to have classroom talks with students on Friday, he said.

Saleem said he is unsure how long heightened security measures, including police stationed in front of the school and patrolling the neighbourhood, might last.

"Usually, we will work with the police, consult with them to see, because they will let us know from time to time what they are hearing on their radar, what they're seeing," he said.

The school recently temporarily hired security guards, he said, after gunmen killed three people during a mosque shooting in San Diego last May in what police have called a hate-motivated crime .

Push for more government action

Statistics Canada reported in March that police-reported hate crimes in Canada more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, jumping from 1,817 to 4,882. Incidents involving Islamophobia in Canada nearly tripled, growing from 84 reported crimes to 229 over the same period.

The agency also noted a tripling of reported hate crimes targeting Jews from 2020 to 2024, rising from 331 incidents in 2020 to 920 in 2024.

Concerns over the email come on the heels of a shooting near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., which police have said was a deliberate, hate-motivated attack aimed at the Jewish community.

Saleem said the incident highlights a hole left behind when the federal government scrapped two offices — focusing on combating Islamophobia and antisemitism respectively — earlier this year . They were replaced with an advisory council that is meant to combat all forms of hate .

"It was the wrong move," Saleem said. "It's important that we kept that office to make sure that proper interventions, policies are being enacted to combat Islamophobia."

Amira Elghawaby, in her former capacity as Canada's special representative on combating Islamophobia, speaks during a news conference in Ottawa on Dec. 10, 2024. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

In an interview, Amira Elghawaby, the former special representative on combating Islamophobia, did not go as far as saying her office should be restored, but said that the federal government needs to continue to "meet and uphold its commitments on human rights, which includes making sure that Canadians of all backgrounds, including faith minorities like Canadian Muslims, have the protections and supports and the solutions they need to live lives of dignity in Canada."

She spoke to CBC News from New York City, attending meetings on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly, where she said it was clear to her that both Islamophobia and antisemitism continue to be dangerous at the global level.

World.title: Hawaii readies for arrival of Hurricane Nolo amid risks of catastrophic flooding
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

People on Hawaii's Big Island are preparing for another potentially life-threatening and catastrophic storm, with Hurricane Nolo expected to bring flash floods and extreme surf as it churns just south of the islands through the weekend.

Nolo was expected to strengthen to a major hurricane on Saturday. Its maximum sustained winds increased to 165 kilometres an hour on Friday. The storm's centre was located about 300 kilometres south of Hawaii's southernmost point.

Tropical storm conditions expected to begin on land in the evening, with hurricane conditions possible by early Saturday, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. It was expected to take a turn west Saturday and avoid directly hitting the islands.

Forecasters warned parts of the Big Island could see rainfall totals up to 38 centimetres, with a possibility of up to 64 centimetres. That was down from an earlier forecast that called for up to 89 centimetres.

"People are going to want to kind of shelter in place on the Big Island, be in their safe place, certainly by later today, tonight, well into Saturday," Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, said Friday.

"Don't venture out if you don't have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down."

Heavy rainfall possible elsewhere

Heavy rainfall also was possible on Hawaii's other islands, the hurricane centre said. Maui also could see heavy rainfall and potential life-threatening flooding and mudslides, forecasters said.

Crews on the Big Island spent hours Friday trying to build berms to guide water and move large debris ahead of the worst of the rain, said Erika Kapu, Hawaii program manager for the humanitarian non-profit CORE.

Darren Montalvo loads sand bags onto his truck in Hilo, Hawaii, on Friday, amid the approach of Hurricane Nolo. (Gregory Bull/The Associated Press)

Hawaii officials told residents to put together emergency kits and the governor issued an emergency proclamation, activating more than 230 Hawaii National Guard members. Schools were closed in some areas.

Hawaii County officials on the Big Island were urging residents in flood-prone areas to consider taking refuge at shelters being set up or other locations.

The heaviest rain from Nolo is likely to fall over the same southeastern region of the Big Island that was hit in August by Hurricane Lala and where grounds are still wet from additional precipitation. The storm surge could hit 30 to 91 centimetres, creating large and dangerous waves and coastal flooding, the hurricane centre said.

Hawaiian Electric, the state's primary utility, said crews that had been helping restore power in Kauai after this month's Hurricane Lowell would return to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in preparation for the coming storm.

Residents and tourists on the Big Island were busy preparing.

In Hilo, where light rain was falling Friday, residents filled bags with sand and gravel at Francis Wong Stadium, where authorities set up a sand distribution centre.

Dean Taise said water was starting to get into his driveway from the street, so he decided to get a few sandbags ready ahead of possible floods.

"They say, prepare for the worst, right? Hope for the best," Taise said.

Hawaii Gov. Josh Green has requested an emergency disaster declaration for four Hawaii counties.

Polo gaining strength

Meanwhile, Mexico is under the threat of Hurricane Polo as it heads toward the Baja California peninsula after bringing storm conditions to the southwestern coast.

The hurricane centre said Polo gained significant force overnight into Friday morning and doused parts of Mexico's Pacific coast. No major damage or flooding was reported along the coast overnight into Friday.

By midday Friday, attention turned to the peninsula, where the hurricane was slated to arch back and hit between Monday and Tuesday. Local authorities were preparing shelters. Mexico's government announced Friday afternoon that they were closing ports in the region as dark clouds swirled overhead.

Palm trees sway in Armeria, Mexico, on Thursday, as Hurricane Polo moved through. (Dante Alfaro/Reuters)

The latest estimated sustained winds were 290 kilometres an hour.

Residents stacked sandbags to fortify beachfront shops and evacuated their homes in some coastal areas on Thursday. Mexican authorities opened shelters and cleared people from beaches, and 15,000 security personnel were deployed across the coast. Schools were closed.

In the port city of Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán, seawater swept through homes and left wooden planks and furniture strewn on the streets. Locals and government officials were clearing debris and shoveling thick mud coating much of the town.

Alicia Contreras said the walls and roof of her restaurant had been severely damaged by 4.5-metre waves. As officers and family helped pick through the damage, Contreras worried about how she would recover economically.

"This is huge because we have no other source of income. Now we're just surviving," Contreras said.

Brennan said some moisture associated with Polo will be pushed into parts of the southwestern U.S. by Monday, possibly producing scattered flash flooding in the Four Corners region, particularly portions of Arizona and New Mexico.

El Niño prompts global shifts

El Niño is prompting major environmental shifts across the world, fuelling drought in some areas and flooding in others. It traditionally dampens the Atlantic hurricane season, while it tends to rev up tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific with moist air and little wind shear.

A third storm in the Pacific, Hurricane Odalys, was at Category 4 status and was still far from land, roughly 1,537 kilometres west-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula.

LISTEN | Will our weather always be like this?: What on Earth? 25:02 Is this Super El Niño a peek into forever weather?

Two other powerful storms were churning in the Atlantic Ocean, but were not near land.

In the northern Atlantic, Tropical Storm Fay reformed early Thursday. As of Friday, it was about 1,674 kilometres west-southwest of the Azores, the hurricane centre said. Off Africa's western coast, Tropical Storm Gonzalo strengthened early Friday as it approached the Cabo Verde Islands.
