World.title: Meeting in Mexico City, Sheinbaum and South Korea’s president pledge deeper ties
World.content:
Listen to this article

Visiting South Korean leader Lee Jae Myung and his Mexican counterpart, President Claudia Sheinbaum, agreed Thursday to deepen their bilateral relationship through a new roadmap focused on economic and financial cooperation, trade and technology.

In a joint press conference at Mexico City’s National Palace, the two presidents announced the signing of 17 agreements that included expanded cooperation in artificial intelligence, aerospace, energy, defense and supply chains.

Lee’s visit took place as Mexico seeks to diversify its economic relations amid international trade tensions and negotiations with the United States, its main partner, and as it promotes Sheinbaum’s Plan México to attract investment and increase national production.

During the press conference, Sheinbaum highlighted that bilateral trade reached US $27 billion in 2025, pointing out that South Korea is one of Mexico’s top five trading partners worldwide, while Mexico is the Asian nation’s main partner in Latin America.

“The goal of greater complementary economic cooperation between our countries will generate shared prosperity and benefits for our people,” Sheinbaum said, adding that South Korean investment since 2006 topped US $11.5 billion.

Lee — the first South Korean leader to visit Mexico since 2010 — said both countries agreed to finalize the review of their reciprocal investment promotion and protection agreement, in order to strengthen economic ties.

“Mexico, the world’s 10th-largest economy and a hub of the global supply chain, is a highly important strategic partner for Korea,” Lee said.

The agreements signed range from economic and financial cooperation, to science and technology, as well as agriculture, security, intellectual property, culture, tourism and academic exchange.

Sheinbaum and Lee committed to promoting trade and investment and facilitating the integration of Mexican small and medium-sized enterprises into the supply chains of South Korean companies operating in Mexico.

Both governments also adopted a Mexico-Korea Action Plan 2026-2030 and will seek to complete the review of the agreement on the promotion and reciprocal protection of investments “in the short term … in order to facilitate trade.”

Lee also announced talks to create a US $100 million credit scheme to facilitate Mexican companies’ acquisition of goods and services from Korean companies and to support South Korean firms operating in Mexico.

Yes, K-pop was on the agenda

At the same time, the two countries agreed to expand their cultural and educational exchanges, including the possibility of establishing a K-pop culture center in Mexico and a Mexican cultural institute in South Korea.

On that topic, Sheinbaum announced that K-pop superstars BTS will return to Mexico next year, adding that Stray Kids (a popular South Korean boy band) was to perform at Mexico City’s Estadio GNP Seguros on Friday.

Although BTS has not officially confirmed a return visit to Mexico, Sheinbaum said the group had accepted her proposal during their visit to the National Palace in May.

With reports from EFE, El Universal and Billboard

World.title: Tabasco homicides dropped over 50% since 2024, officials report: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📍 Sheinbaum on tour: As is often the case on Fridays, President Sheinbaum held her press conference outside Mexico City. Her mañanera today was held in Villahermosa, the capital of the Gulf coast state of Tabasco.

As is often the case on Fridays, President Sheinbaum held her press conference outside Mexico City. Her mañanera today was held in Villahermosa, the capital of the Gulf coast state of Tabasco. 📉 Homicides down 54% in Tabasco : National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported Tabasco’s daily homicide rate hit 1.6 in August, a 54% drop from the November 2024 peak of 3.5 per day.

: National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported Tabasco’s daily homicide rate hit 1.6 in August, a 54% drop from the November 2024 peak of 3.5 per day. 🚔 Over 6,500 arrests since October 2024 : Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 6,527 people were arrested in Tabasco between October 2024 and September 15, 2026. He said that 2,053 firearms and nearly 13 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period.

: Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 6,527 people were arrested in Tabasco between October 2024 and September 15, 2026. He said that 2,053 firearms and nearly 13 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period. 🔻 La Barredora “greatly diminished” : Asked about the criminal group once allegedly led by Tabasco’s ex-Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena, García Harfuch said the organization has been “greatly diminished” and “practically split in two.”

: Asked about the criminal group once allegedly led by Tabasco’s ex-Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena, García Harfuch said the organization has been “greatly diminished” and “practically split in two.” 🗨️ Sheinbaum weighs in on Trump-Xi meeting: The president called Thursday’s meeting in Washington between Trump and Xi “very interesting.” She warned that rivalry between the two powers creates global uncertainty and reaffirmed Mexico’s preference for “peace and cooperation for development.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Villahermosa, capital of the Gulf Coast state of Tabasco.

Security officials presented data showing that the federal government has made significant progress in combating violence in the state, including through the arrest of alleged criminals accused of fueling it. Officials reasserted that the government’s security strategy is yielding results in Tabasco and across the country.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s comments on the meeting in Washington, D.C., on Thursday between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Sheinbaum will join both leaders, and various others, at the APEC Summit in China in November.

Government reports 54% reduction in homicides compared to 2024 peak

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that the daily homicide rate in Tabasco in August was 1.6, a reduction of 54% compared to November 2024, the month with the highest murder rate —3.5 per day — since the current federal government took office in October 2024.

“Thanks to the strengthening of the national public security strategy and coordination with the state government, a reduction in this crime has been achieved,” she said.

According to the data Figueroa presented, the year-over-year decline in homicides in August was 16%.

Figueroa also reported that Tabasco has recorded an average of 10.3 high-impact crimes per day so far in 2026.

That figure represents a decline of 12% compared to 2025 and a reduction of 18% compared to 2024. Among the offenses classified as high-impact crimes are homicides, kidnappings, acts of extortion, violent robberies and rape.

More than 6,000 people arrested in Tabasco since October 2024

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported that more than 6,500 people — 6,527 to be exact — were arrested in Tabasco between Oct. 1, 2024 and Sept. 15, 2026.

Data he presented showed that 2,053 firearms and 12.97 tonnes of drugs were seized in the state in the same period.

García Harfuch said that the arrest of “important targets” in Tabasco has had a “direct impact on the reduction of violence.”

He mentioned a number of the most significant arrests that have been made in the state, including that of a man accused of nine homicides.

García Harfuch: La Barredora has been weakened

A reporter asked García Harfuch about the current strength in Tabasco of La Barredora, a criminal group that was formerly allegedly led by ex-Tabasco Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena.

Bermúdez, who served as security minister in the state government led by former Governor Adán Augusto López Hernández, was arrested in Paraguay in September 2024 and subsequently extradited to Mexico, where he is in prison awaiting trial. López, a Morena party senator and former federal interior minister, has faced claims from opposition parties that he was also involved in La Barredora when the group was allegedly led by Bermúdez.

García Harfuch said there have been “a lot of arrests” of people linked to the criminal group. He subsequently praised the Tabasco state police for their efforts to combat organized crime.

“This organization is greatly diminished,” he said, referring to La Barredora.

“It’s practically split in two,” García Harfuch said.

Sheinbaum comments on Trump-Xi meeting

A reporter asked the president about the meeting on Thursday between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, noting that the latter stated that China and the United States must maintain a peaceful relationship and engage in “healthy” competition.

Sheinbaum described the meeting between the U.S. and Chinese presidents as “very interesting.”

“… The idea of rivalry between two important nations such as China and the United States creates uncertainty in the world,” she said.

“And what Mexico has always sought is peace and cooperation for development,” Sheinbaum added.

She said that her government’s view is that economic competition shouldn’t create “rivalries between countries.”

Mexico has important economic relationships with both the United States and China. Mexico and the United States are each other’s largest trading partner, while China is a large exporter of goods to Mexico.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Cano’s ‘Malinche’: A musical that’s not all song and dance
World.content:
Just about every evening for the past year and a half, more than 1,000 people have made their way to El Frontón, a century-old Art Deco theatre in Mexico City’s small but historic enclave, Tabacalera.

There, the musical, “Malinche,” has been in full swing, having recently kicked off its second run on Aug. 15, with more than 80 cast members singing and dancing flamenco, urban, hip-hop and contemporary to the vision of Jesús Carmona, donning face paint, leather crop tops and fringed two-pieces in an auditorium seating 1,299.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MALINCHE EL MUSICAL (@malinchethemusical)

Created, written and directed by Nacho Cano, the show entered the Mexican theatre scene in March 2025 after a two-and-a-half-year run in Madrid, where it was housed in the IFEMA complex.

It wasn’t exactly Cano’s vision, who unsuccessfully pitched for a 30-meter Aztec-inspired pyramid in Hortaleza, but the venue was still kitted out with a small pyramid, cenotes, pyrotechnics and live bands, making a sizeable impression in Spain’s commercial theatre market.

Since its opening night, though, “Malinche” has faced backlash for what some consider historically insensitive depictions of the 1519 Spanish Conquest, including its retelling of Aztec emperor Moctezuma’s Christian awakening.

The controversy surrounding “Malinche” requires a discussion that centers not only its account of the titular Nahua woman, but also the political background of those who paved the way for its success.

Navigating the history and identity of Malinche

Much of popular art cannot be separated from its contemporary political milieu, both socially and geographically, and Nacho Cano’s work is no exception.

It was just seven years ago that then-President Andrés Manuel López Obrador sought an apology from Spain’s King Felipe VI over the colonial treatment of Indigenous Mexicans. After he failed to deliver such an apology, the king was subsequently excluded from President Claudia Sheinbaum’s inauguration, though he has since acknowledged that “there were significant abuses.”

Often described to those who don’t know her as the “Mexican Pocahontas,” it is widely understood that Malintzin, Doña Marina (her Christian name), or Malinche was an Indigenous woman who became Hernán Cortés’ interpreter and thus played a critical role during Spain’s conquest. Around 14 years old when she met Cortés, Malinche would eventually give birth to their son.

In no uncertain terms, Malinche’s history has been written for her. There is no surviving account from her own voice, only skewed and holey Spanish and Nahuatl accounts of the conquest. As an interpreter pushed into slavery, a potential informant of the Cholula massacre, or a willful lover — depending on who you ask — Malinche’s story becomes warped and warbled on the tongues of many.

A contested icon across modern political agendas

Like any cultural paradigm, scholars have attempted to categorize her perception and presentation both temporally and by groups supporting varying ideologies.

A traditional nationalist slant views Malinche as a traitor, “La Chingada,” taking on an Eve-like persona in her betrayal of the nation for the conquistadors, ultimately facilitating the tragic end of the Mexica. Others stress her victimhood not only at the hands of her oppressors but also in her literary portrayal as a traitor.

Here we see, through the abstraction of Malinche, the reduction of the female to a single narrative. Her portrayal even inspired the neologism “malinchista,” which refers to those favoring foreign cultures and ideals.

Meanwhile, feminist and Chicanx discourse have outlined Malinche’s dynamic representation in alignment with varying political agendas and strived to empower her agency. Many view her as a victim of colonial patriarchy who, as scholar Gloria Anzaldúa described it, exists beyond the “traditional/treacherous binary,” and chose to “be a survivor” who “cast her lot with the Spaniards to ensure survival of a race.”

Other postcolonial scholars take on such subaltern perspectives but question Malinche’s true autonomy, often highlighting the backdrop of religious colonial values of benevolence that Malinche was constructed and demonized against.

Acutely relevant, a pro-Hispanic and contemporary transformation of the narrative sees Malinche much like Disney portrays Pocahontas — a young woman whose love for the heroic Western explorer enabled the birth of the mestizaje, making her the “mother” of Mexico.

And so enters Nacho Cano, creator of “Malinche.”

Nacho Cano’s path from pop star to controversy

Ignacio “Nacho” Cano is a former member of the popular band Mecano, a luminary of Spain’s ’80s music scene and one of the biggest Spanish pop stars of the time. The band’s debut album sold 1 million copies in Spain alone, and they have since sold more than 30 million records worldwide.

Cano went on to develop the wildly influential “Hoy No Me Puedo Levantar,” a musical exploring Madrid’s post-Franco countercultural movement, La Movida, and one of the most financially successful Spanish musicals to date.

Despite his status as a 20th-century pop idol, Cano also established himself as a controversial political figure. He’s an avowed ally of the right-wing president of the Community of Madrid and People’s Party, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, who presented him in 2021 with the Order of the Second of May.

Ayuso herself was described by Politico as being in a “nationalistic showdown with Mexico.”

Such political dissension stems from her admiration of Cortés and defense of the Spanish Conquest as a civilizing mission, perhaps most notably at this year’s “Celebration of Evangelization and Mestizaje in Mexico.”

Sheinbaum has rebuked Ayuso’s characterization of the “conquest as salvation,” while Ayuso has been dubbed by Morena party members “the heir to the Spanish Falange,” a far-right fascist political movement founded in Spain in the 1930s.

Cano has similarly argued that “without Cortés there would be no Mexico,” a sentiment reflected in the feathers and flashlights of his extravagant musical production.

Divided perspectives and powerful corporate backing

In July 2024, Cano was arrested for alleged improprieties and poor working conditions for the performers in Madrid’s “Malinche,” including undocumented immigrants. The charges were dropped the following year, with Cano insisting that left-wing leaders led an alleged coordinated attack.

Beyond the show itself, Cano offers viewers a more detailed insight into the 10-year process behind his play in the 2021 Netflix documentary, “Making Malinche,” a name whose very essence speaks volumes. Malinche is once again a woman methodically remade and reduced, this time to an unwavering, consensual lover.

In an interview with El Mundo, Cano argued that Mexico’s history has been told “deliberately poorly,” and claimed in the documentary that his work is more historically accurate.

The overarching narrative he perpetuates is that Malinche was not a betrayer, but a woman whose passionate love for a Spaniard gifted humanity the New World.

We have seen a correlation between Malinche’s shifting portrayal and shifting Mexican cultural identity, as critics argue Cano has both sanitized and romanticized the violent reality of Spanish conquest.

Left-wing critics have argued the musical erases Indigenous trauma and experience in its “perpetuat[ion] of a Eurocentric narrative,” describing it as a “spectacle of postmodern Falangism.”

On the other end of the spectrum, conservative critics have chided Cano for doing a disservice to Catholicism, accusing him of not pushing far enough “an authentic ode to the history of Spain, against ideological revisionism and the Black Legend,” a reference to a school of thought that suggests “anti-Catholic” and “anti-Spanish” narratives deliberately position the Spanish Empire as singularly motivated by cruelty and greed.

However, these are not the only reasons many people in the left-wing community have boycotted “Malinche.”

The champions of ‘Malinche’

Ricardo Salinas Pliego, a Mexican television magnate and chairman of Grupo Salinas whose net worth is estimated to be US $5 billion, is responsible for bringing “Malinche” to Mexico and promoting it on his network, TV Azteca. His wife, María Laura Medina de Salinas, served as an executive producer during its opening in Mexico last year, after falling “in love” with it in Madrid and “form[ing] a synergy” with Cano, according to José Manuel Azpiroz, the director of communications at Salinas’ Grupo Elektra.

What’s more, the show is officially “presented” by Banco Azteca, part of Salinas’ conglomerate.

Much like Cano, Salinas is no stranger to controversy, having been accused of tax evasion to the tune of US $3 billion while also flirting with a presidential run.

Once labeled “the newest face of the Mexican new right,” he is an outspoken critic of Sheinbaum and supporter of the National Action Party (PAN), with a political temperament that follows in the footsteps of Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Salinas and Cano also have close ties to Juan Miguel Zunzunegui, a Mexican historian and avid rejector of the Black Legend. He defends the Spanish empire and upholds a history that dismisses Indigenous suffering and denies the mass violation of women.

In an interview with El Mundo, he said, “[t]he Spaniard who thinks they did horrible things in America does so out of ignorance.”

Cano recently wrote the prologue to Zunzunegui’s book, “Hernán Cortés,” and Zunzunegui is involved in the current run of “Malinche,” making a special appearance as Spanish friar and translator Jerónimo de Aguilar.

Turning historical violence into a love story

Malinche’s representation has been utilized as a vehicle to express specific sociopolitical ideologies within Mexican society, both at home and abroad. The question now is why proponents of “Malinche” feel a desire to promote a history of colonial violence as a love story that’s couched in consent and results in creation?

Some have asked a similar question of Disney’s romanticization of colonial relationships in its 1995 adaptation of “Pocahontas,” with the understanding that depicting a “mutually satisfying encounter” legitimizes what they describe as the violence of Western history.

“Malinche” too warrants consideration as part of a broader ideological posture seeking to sublimate Spain’s imperial legacy. However, with its second season running through January 2027, its popularity, devoid of nuanced conversations about who gets to write and rewrite history, speaks for itself.

Millie Deere is a freelance journalist.

World.title: The Mexico City neighborhoods where earthquakes are barely felt
World.content:
Mexico City was built over five ancient lakes. Those bodies of water were systematically drained in the centuries following the invasion of Tenochtitlán, the ancient imperial capital of the Mexica, and 500 years later, we’re still grappling with the consequences of that lacustrine past.

The soil in the Mexican capital is remarkably uneven — so much so that the local government classified the city into “zones,” distinguishing the soil types found in each borough.

Zone II, for example, is characterized by sandy soils, meaning earthquakes are felt with greater intensity at the surface. What’s more, this type of soil makes buildings prone to collapse if civil protection measures are not followed.

According to a UNAM Global report, the Roma, Condesa and Juárez neighborhoods fall within this zoning area. As such, they are among the neighborhoods that sustained the most structural damage during the 2017 and 2019 earthquakes.

Unfortunately, the Cuauhtémoc borough is among those that have been most ravaged by Mexico City’s earthquakes. Despite being one of the city’s major tourist draws — home to the Historic Center and the iconic Roma and Condesa neighborhoods — it has historically been devastated by these natural disasters, followed by the Benito Juárez, Coyoacán and Xochimilco boroughs.

Which neighborhoods, then, have suffered the least damage from earthquakes? Read on to find out if you live in one of them.

Safest neighborhoods during earthquakes in Mexico City

If you are looking to escape earthquakes in Mexico City, I have bad news for you: it isn’t possible. However, there are neighborhoods, many of which are located in the city’s southern reaches, where the movement is barely perceptible.

This is because, around 1,770 years ago, the Xitle volcano erupted in what is now the city’s south. Even today, the area retains this natural advantage, resulting in stable ground, as documented by the Mexico City government.

Having established that areas in Mexico City’s south, with its preserved volcanic soils, tend to be safer during earthquakes, which neighborhoods experience the least seismic activity?

Colonia Jardines del Pedregal

One of the most famous neighborhoods for being “safe during earthquakes” is Jardines del Pedregal. Designed by Diego Rivera and architect Luis Barragán in the 1940s, this area is recognized as one of the city’s wealthiest neighborhoods.

Characterized by huge houses and spacious pavilions and gardens, it sits on volcanic rock terrain that absorbs much of the seismic shock.

As mentioned, the neighborhood features natural volcanic stone details integrated into its urban architecture — and sometimes even into the houses themselves. So, in addition to being one of the city’s most exclusive areas, it also has the wonderful advantage of being barely affected by earthquakes.

Ciudad Universitaria at UNAM

In addition to being home to one of the most beautiful ecological reserves in the south, UNAM’s Ciudad Universitaria (CU) is one of the places in Mexico City where earthquakes are least perceptible.

As seen in El Pedregal, it is common to find large chunks of volcanic rock embedded in the ground, forming part of the area’s natural beauty.

Often, because these materials are so ancient, age-old trees have grown atop the volcanic rocks, providing shade to the university’s community. So yes, you can stroll through its vast green spaces and enjoy its UNESCO World Heritage-listed views in complete tranquility.

Colonia Guadalupe Inn

Known as the “little queen of the south,” the Guadalupe Inn neighborhood is one of the most traditional in the southern part of the city. Like its neighbors Chimalistac and San Ángel, it retains a colonial charm in its homes and businesses — a quality few places in the capital have preserved so gracefully.

Established in the mid-20th century on the grounds of the former Hacienda de Guadalupe, its streets bear the names of famous Mexican composers and are often lined with beautiful jacaranda trees, as well as other species found only in southern Mexico City.

Beyond its remarkable architectural and natural beauty, the neighborhood also tends to be spared during earthquakes.

Colonia San Ángel

If Guadalupe Inn is the “little queen of the south,” San Ángel is the empress. Classy, ​​upscale and undeniably stylish, it is another neighborhood where Mexico City’s tremors are barely felt.

Like the other southern colonias mentioned in this article, it is situated on volcanic soil, which absorbs much of the seismic impact.

During the colonial era, San Ángel was a small village in its own right, and it shows. The neighborhood boasts a Baroque church at the heart of a stone-paved plaza, a magnificent flower market, and fantastic cobblestone streets. What more could you ask for?

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: More than 7,000 ignore clouds to gather at Chichén Itzá for the equinox
World.content:
Thousands of people gathered in the esplanade in front of the great pyramid of Kukulcán in the Chichén Itzá archaeological site in the state of Yucatán on Monday and Tuesday to witness the famous descent of the serpent.

The spectacular light and shadow phenomenon takes place during the spring and autumn equinoxes each year when afternoon sunlight hits the pyramid at a particular angle. As a result, the silhouette of a serpent is projected on the wall of the north balustrade of the structure known as El Castillo.

The intricate design of El Castillo, also called the Temple of Kukulcán, allows for the projection of seven isosceles triangles of light which appear to the observer as a luminous and magical serpent moving down the pyramid toward the carved serpent head near its base.

This fascinating interplay of light and shadow — known as the hierophanies of the equinoxes — typically lasts from 10 to 30 minutes.

This year, the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) implemented a special operation to receive tourists beginning on Sunday as the interplay of light and shadow was visible from Sunday through Tuesday.

El Castillo was built in a geometric pyramid shape with nine truncated levels, superimposed and progressively smaller with a small temple at the top.

Central staircases on each of the four sides, each with 91 steps. allowed access to the temple. In total, there are 364 steps, but including the platform on which the pyramid rests, the result is 365, precisely the length of the Maya civil year.

“It reminds us of the admirable precision with which the ancient Maya observed the movement of the sun and the cycles of the seasons,” the INAH said in a statement, adding that the calculations were fundamental to Maya agriculture.

INAH said the instant of the equinox this year occurred at 3:51 p.m. on Monday. In all, INAH recorded more than 7,000 visitors at Chichen Itza from Sunday through Tuesday.

Because autumn starts before the rainy season ends, there are often clouds at the equinox hiding the effect. This year was no exception, but there were enough breaks in the cloud cover for the visitors to get good looks at the phenomenon.

Last year, Chichen Itza surpassed Teotihuacán and Tulum as the most popular cultural tourism site in Mexico, according to the Tourism Ministry.

With reports from La Jornada Maya, National Geographic and Yucatán Magazine

World.title: Brazil’s Top Prosecutor Survives 5–4 Council Vote on Inquiry Over Jailed Banker
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

BRAZIL · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The country Brazil has about 213 million people and Latin America’s largest economy, roughly US$2.3 trillion a year, close to Canada’s. Its federal prosecutors, not the government, decide whom to charge.

— Why it matters The central bank shut Banco Master in November 2025. Repaying savers there and at two sister banks will cost the deposit guarantee fund about R$51 billion (about US$9.9 billion).

— Why now Police found messages mentioning Paulo Gonet, the prosecutor-general handling the case, on the phone of the bank’s jailed former owner, Daniel Vorcaro. A photo shows the two together in London.

— What happened On Friday 25 September 2026 the prosecution service’s governing council voted 5 to 4 to shelve a request to look into Gonet’s conduct. It voted 9 to 0 against removing him from the case.

— Who is involved Gonet, prosecutor-general since December 2023. Vorcaro, jailed since 4 March 2026. Ciro Soares, a lawyer police say relayed most contacts. Nicolao Dino, who chaired the session.

— What it means for you Deposits in Brazil are insured up to R$250,000 (about US$48,000) per person per banking group. The fight is over who prosecutes the collapse, not over savers’ money.

— Still open Four members wanted a senior prosecutor to examine the material first. Any bias question belongs to the Supreme Court, the rapporteur said.

Paulo Gonet, Brazil’s prosecutor-general, is in charge of the criminal case over the collapsed Banco Master. On Friday 25 September 2026 the prosecution service’s governing council, which he normally chairs, decided by 5 votes to 4 not to have his conduct examined.

Francisco Sanseverino, rapporteur for the prosecution service’s governing council, found no minimum evidence of a crime. Three members sided with him and four went against, leaving a 4–4 tie until the session’s chair, Nicolao Dino, voted last to make it 5 to 4.

The headquarters of Brazil’s Prosecutor-General’s Office in Brasília, seen from the road. The Superior Council of the Federal Prosecution Service met here on Friday. (Photo: Luis Dantas, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

How the council voted

The council voted on two questions. All nine voting members rejected removing Gonet from the Banco Master cases at the Supreme Federal Court (STF).

The second question split them. Sanseverino, Celso de Albuquerque Silva, Alexandre Camanho de Assis and Vice Prosecutor-General Hindenburgo Chateaubriand voted to shelve the request.

Janice Ascari, Samantha Chantal Dobrowolski, José Adônis Callou de Araújo Sá and Ana Borges Coelho Santos wanted a senior prosecutor appointed to examine it first. Dino, who voted last, made it 5 to 4 for shelving, g1 reported.

Dino said there had been no prevarication, and that Gonet could not have foreseen that a man he met socially in 2024 would later be investigated. Nothing in Gonet’s actions, he said, pointed to conduct serving “a personal interest or sentiment”.

Dobrowolski said Gonet should not have acted in the proceeding where he was mentioned, because “no one is judge or prosecutor of their own conduct”. She pointed to his request to annul a police report that dealt with him.

Callou said a prosecutor cannot seek to annul investigation reports “in which he himself is mentioned”. Ana Borges Santos said there were enough elements to examine whether Gonet had committed prevarication, meaning failure of official duty for personal reasons. She said nothing so far linked him concretely to that crime.

Chateaubriand saw no such case. “I cannot see what interest he has” that would justify a prevarication inquiry, he said, and he found no proof of a close friendship with Vorcaro.

What the rapporteur decided

Sanseverino holds the rank of subprocurador-geral, the top grade of the federal prosecution career. He split his vote into two questions.

The first was whether the council should take Gonet off the Banco Master case for possible bias. Sanseverino said that question lies outside the council’s powers.

He said the bias claim “should be raised in those case files” at the Supreme Federal Court (STF), Brazil’s highest court. It would then be “for the STF itself to decide.”

In practice, that keeps Gonet at the head of the Banco Master proceedings unless the STF orders otherwise.

The second question was whether to open a criminal inquiry into Gonet. Sanseverino said no, finding no minimum evidence that a crime occurred or that Gonet committed one.

“Phrases or exchanges of messages cannot be examined in isolation or out of context,” he said. Doing so, he argued, creates “an artificial situation” that does not match the facts.

No direct conversation, the rapporteur found

Sanseverino said police found no contact saved as “Paulo Gonet” or “Gonet” on Vorcaro’s phone. Nor did they find any record of a direct conversation between the two men.

Most references to Gonet appear in chats between Vorcaro and Ciro Soares, a lawyer who once worked for Banco Master. For the rapporteur, the lack of direct contact “already weakens” the claim of a close friendship.

He called the April 2024 meeting in London “isolated” and “superficial”, a social occasion with other people present. He noted that Gonet admits speaking to Vorcaro once more, by phone, on 15 March 2025.

On messages about a London trip in 2025, he found no request for any advantage by Gonet. “These are conversations between third parties, without any direct or indirect participation by the prosecutor-general,” he said.

He also said Gonet backed the case prosecutors in Brasília and São Paulo from July 2025. That was when Gonet learned of the suspicions around the bank.

What the police messages say

The material comes from Vorcaro’s phone, seized by the Federal Police in Operation Compliance Zero, their investigation into Banco Master. The messages cover 2024 and 2025.

In April 2024 Soares told Vorcaro that “Gonet is firm” and that “friendship is everything”.

In March 2025 Soares sent the banker a photo of himself with Gonet, with the words: “Call here. He wants to talk to you.”

Phone calls followed, one lasting three minutes and 49 seconds. Police did not establish what was said.

Soares also forwarded messages he attributed to Gonet. One read: “I already miss you! I’m boarding for Rome. Send him this message.”

Other messages concern the prosecutor-general’s son, Pedro Gonet, joining a trip to London in April 2025. According to the police material, Vorcaro authorised paying his expenses.

In a message to Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, Vorcaro asked whether they could “reverse this with Paulo and Andrei”. Investigators read that as Gonet and Andrei Rodrigues, head of the Federal Police.

Then came the photo, published by O Globo on 18 September. It shows Gonet holding a cigar at a London table, with whisky glasses and Vorcaro seated nearby.

The prosecutor-general’s office confirmed the picture is genuine. Its background is set out in Paulo Gonet and Vorcaro Photo Tests Brazil’s Biggest Bank Fraud Case.

Gonet’s defence

Paulo Gonet denies any wrongdoing and sent the council a 37-page written defence on 15 September. “I have no friendship at all with Mr Daniel Vorcaro,” he wrote.

He added that he has no “personal interest” in cases where Vorcaro is a party or under investigation. He says he met the banker once, at a London legal event with other officials present.

At a Supreme Court session, he called a single phone contact arranged by a lawyer “very brief and banal”. He has also asked the court to annul the police report that names him.

He argues that Justice André Mendonça, then in charge of the case, overstepped by ordering inquiries that prosecutors had not requested.

Why the prosecutor-general matters so much

The Federal Prosecution Service, known in Portuguese as the Ministério Público Federal (MPF), brings federal criminal cases in Brazil. The constitution makes it independent of the government, the courts and Congress.

The prosecutor-general heads it. The president nominates a career prosecutor, and the Senate must approve him for a two-year term.

Only the prosecutor-general can bring criminal charges before the STF against the most senior officials, such as ministers and members of Congress. Any charge in the Supreme Court side of the Master case would come from his office.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva first appointed Gonet in December 2023. The Senate approved a second term on 12 November 2025, by 45 votes to 26.

Removing a prosecutor-general early takes a request from the president and an absolute majority of the Senate, in a secret ballot.

The bank behind the case

Banco Master grew by selling deposit certificates that paid well above market rates. Savers were protected by Brazil’s deposit guarantee fund, the FGC, which insures deposits up to R$250,000 (about US$48,000).

The central bank ordered Master and other group companies into liquidation on 18 November 2025. Investigators put suspected fraud in credit portfolios the bank sold at about R$12 billion (about US$2.3 billion).

Conversions use 5.175 reais per US dollar, the open.er-api.com rate for 25 September 2026. The FGC’s expected bill of about R$51 billion (about US$9.9 billion) covers Master and two sister banks.

Vorcaro was arrested in November 2025 at São Paulo’s main airport as he prepared to leave on a private jet. A court ordered him freed under electronic monitoring on 28 November 2025.

Justice Mendonça ordered him back to jail on 4 March 2026. Police allege he led a criminal organisation that included a group used to watch and intimidate opponents.

Delays sought by his lawyers are covered in Brazil: Jailed Banker Vorcaro Asks Top Court to Delay Police Interviews.

How the council vote works

The Superior Council is the prosecution service’s top decision-making body. It has ten members: the prosecutor-general, his deputy and eight elected senior prosecutors.

Gonet normally chairs it but is barred from his own case, so nine members vote. Nicolao Dino, the council’s vice-president and brother of Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino, chaired the session.

After the rapporteur, members vote from most junior to most senior, and Dino votes last. The council has never before weighed an inquiry of this kind into a prosecutor-general.

The next member to speak, Janice Ascari, said the mentions of Gonet did not, on their own, prove he received any advantage, or that he or his son knew of any expenses being paid. She called the London photo “a clear moment of social relaxation”. She still voted for a senior prosecutor to examine the material first.

The request came from federal deputies of Novo, a pro-market party in Congress. They asked for another senior prosecutor to take over the Master files at the Supreme Court.

What comes next

The decision shelves the request inside the prosecution service, and Gonet keeps the Banco Master cases. No senior prosecutor will be appointed to examine his conduct.

Any bias question belongs to the STF itself, the rapporteur said. Gonet’s own request to annul the police report that mentions him is also pending there.

The margin was narrow. Four of the nine voting members wanted the facts examined before any decision to shelve.

The vote is not a finding that Gonet did nothing wrong. The majority found no minimum evidence of a crime to justify examining his conduct.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Brazil’s Federal Prosecution Service?

The Ministério Público Federal (MPF) investigates and prosecutes federal crimes and defends the public interest in court. It is independent of the government and is headed by the prosecutor-general.

Is Paulo Gonet under investigation?

No criminal inquiry has been opened. On 25 September 2026 the council voted 5 to 4 to shelve the request to look into his conduct, and 9 to 0 against removing him from the Banco Master cases.

What was Banco Master?

A Brazilian lender that sold high-yield deposit certificates backed by the national deposit guarantee. The central bank shut it on 18 November 2025, and its former owner, Daniel Vorcaro, is in jail.

Does the vote affect money held in Brazilian banks?

No. The vote concerns who prosecutes the case; deposits remain insured up to R$250,000 (about US$48,000) per person per banking group.

World.title: Essequibo: Guyana Urges Venezuela at 81st UN Assembly to Heed Coming ICJ Ruling
World.content:
GUYANA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — What happened President Irfaan Ali urged Venezuela at the UN on Thursday 24 September 2026 to abide by the coming ICJ ruling.

— Update, 25 September Supporters of the opposition WIN party picketed outside the UN during Ali’s speech, News Americas reported.

— Venezuela’s line A day earlier, acting President Delcy Rodríguez asked Guyana to return to negotiations under the 1966 Geneva Agreement.

— The case Guyana wants the court to confirm the 1899 award that fixed the border; hearings ended in May 2026.

— The catch No judgment date has been set, and Venezuela still rejects the court’s jurisdiction.

— What is at stake Essequibo covers more than two-thirds of Guyana, and Venezuela’s sea claim reaches into the Stabroek oil block.

— What comes next Guyana expects a ruling between November 2026 and January 2027; the sea border needs separate talks.

On the UN stage, Guyana and Venezuela restated opposite paths for Essequibo while the world court prepares its judgment.

The ruined gateway of Kyk-Over-Al, a Dutch colonial fort on an island near the Essequibo River, in the region Venezuela claims. Photo: Dan Lundberg, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Guyana has used the UN General Assembly to press Venezuela over Essequibo, a vast region Caracas has long claimed. President Irfaan Ali urged Venezuela on Thursday 24 September to abide by the International Court of Justice’s coming ruling.

“We urge Venezuela to abide by the forthcoming ruling in accordance with their obligation under the UN Charter, as Guyana will do,” Ali said in New York.

What Ali Said About Essequibo

Ali said Guyana went to the court only after decades of trying to settle the dispute bilaterally. That included a mixed commission and the good offices of the UN secretary-general.

He called the 1899 Arbitral Award “the full, perfect, and final settlement” of the border. Guyana had “endured long and repeated provocations and aggression”, he added.

It was his first address to the Assembly since the court finished hearing the case in May 2026. He said both countries had taken part in those hearings.

“We look forward to a new era of neighbourly relations,” he said. He tied that hope to the development of both countries and the stability and prosperity of the region.

Ali said Guyana has “always advanced the peaceful settlement” of the border controversy. It took part in the case in full respect for international law, he added, and encouraged Venezuela to do the same.

Venezuela’s Answer, a Day Earlier

Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, spoke from the same podium on Wednesday 23 September. She reaffirmed what she called Venezuela’s historic rights over Guyana-Essequibo.

“Here, I appeal to the Cooperative Republic of Guyana to resolve the issue and to return to negotiations,” she said. In Venezuela’s view, that is what the Geneva Agreement requires.

Agreements reached bilaterally last longer and work better than those imposed by outside bodies, she argued. She wore a brooch showing a map of Venezuela that included Essequibo.

Rodríguez took over after US forces removed Nicolás Maduro on 3 January 2026. She was previously responsible for Venezuela’s case at the court, AFP noted.

She said Venezuela wants to rebuild ties with its South American neighbours and the United States. Those ties must rest on respect and equality, she added.

She did not criticise the United States or ExxonMobil, Demerara Waves noted. Instead she thanked President Donald Trump and his government for their readiness to resume diplomatic relations and cooperation.

She called a recent US–Venezuela agreement “one of the most all-encompassing and significant ever signed”. It will help ensure the hemisphere’s energy balance, she said.

Where the ICJ Case Stands

The border dates from the colonial era. An arbitration tribunal in Paris fixed it in 1899.

The Geneva Agreement was signed in February 1966 by the United Kingdom, Venezuela and British Guiana, three months before Guyana’s independence.

Venezuela says the 1899 award is null and void. In its view the Geneva Agreement requires a practical settlement negotiated with Guyana.

Guyana filed the case in 2018 after the UN secretary-general referred the dispute to the court under the Geneva Agreement. It asks the judges to confirm that the 1899 award and its boundary are valid and binding.

The court ruled in 2020 that it had jurisdiction and rejected a further Venezuelan objection in 2023. It has also twice granted Guyana’s requests for provisional measures.

The latest, in 2025, ordered Venezuela not to hold, or prepare to hold, elections in the disputed territory.

Venezuela boycotted the court’s 2018–2020 jurisdiction phase but has taken part since then, while still rejecting the court’s authority.

No judgment date has been announced, and the court gives two weeks’ notice. Guyana’s government has estimated a ruling between November 2026 and January 2027.

Why Essequibo Matters

Guyana is a small English-speaking country just east of Venezuela. Essequibo makes up more than two-thirds of its territory of about 83,000 square miles.

Oil was discovered offshore in 2015. Venezuela’s maritime claim reaches into ExxonMobil’s Stabroek Block, Guyana’s main oil area.

That is why the dispute weighs on investors as well as diplomats.

The land boundary is what the court will rule on. The maritime boundary would need separate talks, because Venezuela has not signed the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.

The United States has said it is willing to help settle that maritime line after the ruling, Demerara Waves reported. ExxonMobil hopes to resume exploration in parts of the Stabroek Block nearer Venezuela afterwards.

Maduro’s repeated calls to annex the territory once raised fears of armed conflict. Ali and Maduro met in Argyle, St Vincent, in December 2023 and pledged not to threaten or use force.

Why It Matters If You Invest in Guyana

For oil companies, contractors and investors, a clear ruling could reduce a major political risk over Guyana’s offshore boom. That depends on Caracas accepting it, and the ruling would not settle the sea border.

Guyana is also a founding member of Trump’s Shield of the Americas, a US-led security coalition against drug cartels. Venezuela, under Rodríguez, is rebuilding relations with the US at the same time.

Outside the Hall: Opposition Supporters Protest

While Ali spoke on Thursday 24 September, supporters of the opposition We Invest in Nationhood (WIN) party protested outside the UN, News Americas reported. Members and supporters of the party’s New York chapter, launched in late August, staged the picket.

Signs read “Let the Courts Do Their Jobs, No to Victimization” and “More Democracy, No to Dictatorship”. The chapter listed seven grievances, from alleged persecution of Opposition Leader Azruddin Mohamed to accountability for the MV Barima ferry disaster in July, which killed more than 70 people.

Its statement also cited an Inter-American Development Bank estimate that 58% of Guyanese lived on less than US$6.85 a day. The estimate rests on 2021 survey data, and the government says it is out of date.

The group picketed again that evening outside Ali’s meeting with the diaspora in Queens, News Americas reported. At the Queens event, Ali urged US-based Guyanese to invest in the country’s farm sector, calling himself a farmer of ten years, Demerara Waves reported.

No direct government response to the protest had been reported by Friday. At the Queens event, though, Ali said without naming Mohamed that “you can be my best friend but if you do the crime, you have to do the time,” Demerara Waves reported.

Mohamed cannot travel to the United States, where he and his father are wanted over alleged financial crimes and are fighting extradition. WIN won 16 seats in the September 2025 election and is the main opposition party.

What Comes Next

The next milestone is the court’s announcement of a date to deliver its judgment. Both governments have now set out their positions before the full UN membership.

Watch too for any US move on the maritime boundary. Another question is how Rodríguez’s government would respond to an adverse ruling.

Venezuela case page; AFP via RTL Today, Guyana urges Venezuela, 24 September 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Essequibo dispute?

Venezuela claims the Essequibo region, which makes up more than two-thirds of Guyana. Guyana says the 1899 Arbitral Award settled the border for good and has asked the ICJ to confirm it.

What did Guyana say at the UN?

President Irfaan Ali urged Venezuela to abide by the ICJ’s forthcoming ruling, as Guyana will do. He said Guyana went to court only after decades of failed bilateral efforts.

When will the ICJ rule on Essequibo?

The court finished hearings in May 2026 but has not set a date. Guyana’s government has estimated November 2026 to January 2027.

What does Venezuela want?

Venezuela wants direct negotiations under the 1966 Geneva Agreement and rejects the court’s jurisdiction. It has nevertheless taken part in the proceedings since the jurisdiction phase.

World.title: Colombia Bonds Get Bank of America Overweight Call on 3.1% Primary Deficit
World.content:
COLOMBIA · MARKETS

Key Facts — What happened Bank of America raised Colombia’s external sovereign debt to overweight from marketweight, Valora Analitik reported on 25 September.

— The reason It sees the new government’s fiscal adjustment as sustained and structural, built mainly on spending cuts.

— The numbers BofA now sees the primary deficit at 3.1% of GDP in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028.

— The valuation Colombian bonds trade like BB- credits, 1.7 notches below an average rating of BB+ to BB, BofA says.

— The catch The call rests on execution, and El Niño, wage rises and August quake costs could get in the way.

Colombia bonds have won a vote of confidence from Bank of America, which likes the new government’s deficit plan.

Bogotá seen from the eastern hills. The capital is home to the finance ministry, which manages Colombia’s public debt. Photo: Jusezam, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Colombia bonds sold abroad in foreign currency have a new backer. Bank of America has raised its call on them to overweight from marketweight.

Valora Analitik reported the change on Friday 25 September 2026. It covers Colombia’s external sovereign debt.

An overweight call means the bank advises clients to hold more of the bonds than a benchmark index does.

The reason is fiscal. BofA says the new administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella is committed to an adjustment it sees as sustained and structural.

What Bank of America Changed

The bank lowered its forecasts for the central government’s primary deficit, the gap before interest payments. It now sees 3.1% of GDP in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028.

It also expects the overall deficit, including interest, to fall step by step to 6% of GDP by 2028.

The key point for BofA is how the gap will be closed. Past reforms leaned almost entirely on higher taxes, the bank noted.

Why Colombia Bonds Look Cheap to BofA

The planned rescue bill, the Ley de Rescate, envisages an effort of 4.7 points of GDP over four years, BofA says. About 70% comes from spending cuts and 30% from revenue measures, according to BofA.

Adjustments driven by spending cuts tend to hurt growth far less than tax rises, the bank argued. BofA sizes this year’s budget-cut decree at 0.7% to 1.1% of GDP, mostly in capital spending.

BofA called the initial target conservative, leaving room for positive surprises. It says the bonds trade at a discount equal to 1.7 rating notches.

In other words, they are priced like BB- debt, against an average rating of BB+ to BB.

If the plan stays on track, the bank expects rating agencies to keep Colombia’s ratings stable. It sees that as a clear entry point for investors.

A New Way of Borrowing

The report also highlights a change in how the government funds itself. Colombia is returning to its historical mix and relying less on the local market.

External funding rises back to about a third of the total, BofA noted.

That should ease pressure on domestic interest rates, the bank said. Multilateral lenders such as the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and CAF would play a bigger role.

BofA also mentioned a possible contingent programme with the International Monetary Fund. Multilateral and bilateral lenders offer longer maturities at lower cost, it noted.

The government is dropping what BofA called purely accounting operations used before, such as total return swaps. It is instead swapping short-term TCO notes due in 2026 and 2027 for debt due in 2027 and 2028.

How Colombia Got Here

The upgrade follows a difficult year for the public accounts. Colombia triggered the escape clause of its fiscal rule in June 2025, suspending its targets for 2025 to 2027.

The central government’s primary deficit reached 3.5% of GDP in 2025, up from 2.4% in 2024, the fiscal watchdog CARF said.

On 28 August, Finance Minister Miguel Gómez Martínez warned bankers that urgent action was needed to avoid an abyss. He set out a 21.9 trillion peso (about US$6.6 billion) spending cut for 2026.

The official 2026 target for the primary deficit is 3.3% of GDP. BofA’s forecast of 3.1% is slightly better than the government’s own goal.

Not everyone is as upbeat. On 4 September the CARF estimated the 2026 primary deficit at 3.9% of GDP, above both the official goal and BofA’s figure.

On 11 September the CARF warned that the overall deficit could come close to 10% of GDP in 2027, Portafolio reported.

Fitch rates Colombia BB with a stable outlook after a downgrade in December 2025. On 9 September it warned that a failure to consolidate could put new pressure on the rating.

The rescue bill has been announced but not yet filed in Congress. Gómez Martínez said on 14 September that the government would present it in October.

What the Markets Already Show

BofA says the shift in expectations is already visible. Davivienda’s manufacturing PMI rose to 54.7 in August, and business confidence in the survey hit a seven-year high.

BofA also says yields on peso government bonds due in 2030 have fallen more than 300 basis points since May 2026. Those bonds are known as TES.

Risks to the Call

The bank also noted headwinds, though it says confidence is holding despite them. The earthquake of 10 August 2026 will bring moderate reconstruction costs that weigh on the 2026 accounts temporarily.

Inflation should ease gradually towards 2028, BofA expects. But El Niño could push up food and energy prices, and past minimum-wage rises still feed through.

Why It Matters

For investors in Colombia, a major bank calling the dollar debt cheap can lower the state’s costs abroad if others follow.

Local loan rates track peso TES yields and the central bank’s policy rate more closely, so the effect at home is indirect.

For people earning or spending pesos, a stronger fiscal story can support the currency over time. For now global dollar strength dominates.

The official rate rose to 3,329.61 pesos per US dollar on Friday, from 3,151.73 a week earlier.

What Comes Next

The test is delivery. Watch whether Congress and the government stick to the spending cuts in the planned rescue bill and the 2027 budget.

Also watch the rating agencies, and whether an IMF contingent programme takes shape.

Sources: Valora Analitik, Bank of America raises its bet on Colombia, 25 September 2026; Portafolio, Colombia moves away from the fiscal rule, 4 September 2026; Portafolio, CARF warns on the deficit, 11 September 2026; La República, the fiscal adjustment bill, 1 September 2026. Exchange rate: Colombia’s official TRM for 25 September 2026, 3,329.61 pesos per US dollar.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Bank of America change on Colombia?

It raised its recommendation on Colombia’s external sovereign debt to overweight from marketweight. Valora Analitik reported the change on 25 September 2026.

Why is Bank of America more positive on Colombia bonds?

It sees the new government’s fiscal adjustment as sustained and structural. About 70% of the planned effort comes from spending cuts, which the bank says hurt growth less than tax rises.

What deficit does Bank of America expect for Colombia?

It sees a primary deficit of 3.1% of GDP in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028. The overall deficit should fall to 6% of GDP by 2028.

What could go wrong?

The bank points to reconstruction costs after the August 2026 earthquake. It also flags inflation risks from El Niño and from minimum-wage rises, and the rescue bill is not yet in Congress.

World.title: Braskem Mexico Freeze: Brazil Court Halts Idesa Funding, Summons Petrobras
World.content:
BRAZIL · BUSINESS

Key Facts — The country. Brazil has 213.6 million people and the region’s largest economy and stock market. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has governed since 1 January 2023, and the first election round falls on 4 October 2026.

— The money. The currency is the real (BRL), about 5.18 to the US dollar on 25 September 2026. Braskem is renegotiating about US$10.9 billion of financial debt, much of it in bonds sold abroad.

— The background. Braskem is a Brazilian petrochemical group controlled by the state oil company Petrobras and the private equity firm IG4 Capital. On 24 August 2026 it filed for extrajudicial recovery, an out-of-court restructuring under Brazilian bankruptcy law.

— What happened. On 24 September 2026 a São Paulo bankruptcy court barred Braskem from sending new money to Braskem Idesa, its Mexican joint venture. Creditors put the total potential commitment at up to R$4.1 billion (about US$800 million).

— What is disputed. Prosecutors argue creditors cannot vote on an incomplete balance sheet or on projections that ignore large extraordinary obligations. They also state there is still no definitive proof of asset stripping, conflict of interest or abusive management.

— What it means for you. For residents of Brazil or Mexico the direct effect is small: Braskem Idesa runs a petrochemical complex in Veracruz and sells to industry, not households. The bondholder group behind the request holds roughly US$7 billion of notes.

— The catch. The freeze is temporary. On 25 September Braskem told the market it knew of the ruling but had not yet been formally notified. Petrobras and IG4 Capital must explain how the Mexican deal was approved. Braskem must show majority creditor support by 22 November 2026; it had 39.6% when it filed.

A São Paulo court has frozen new Braskem money for its Mexican unit, as creditors and prosecutors asked. Petrobras must now explain how the deal was approved.

São Paulo Court Grants Braskem Mexico Freeze Before Creditor Vote

A São Paulo court granted a Braskem Mexico freeze on 24 September 2026. The order suspends new money flowing to Braskem Idesa, the company’s petrochemical joint venture in Mexico. It also orders Petrobras and IG4 Capital, Braskem’s controlling shareholders, to explain how the deal was approved.

What changed on 24 September

Judge Tainá Maria Leonardo de Oliveira of São Paulo’s 2nd Bankruptcy and Judicial Recovery Court granted an urgent injunction on 24 September. It answered a request from Braskem bondholders and debenture holders that São Paulo state prosecutors had backed.

Braskem and its subsidiaries must stop new payments, capital injections, guarantees and share options tied to Braskem Idesa’s restructuring. The block lasts until further notice, and breaches can bring fines and liability for company managers.

Petrobras and Shine I, IG4 Capital’s fund holding its Braskem stake, must explain the corporate and contractual approvals behind the deal. Braskem has 15 days to file a detailed report on the Mexican operation.

Creditors also question whether trade credit from Petrobras may have funded the Mexican rescue. The judge named ACFB Administração Judicial as court administrator, as prosecutors had recommended.

What the Braskem Mexico freeze request asks for

São Paulo’s state prosecutors filed an opinion in Braskem’s out-of-court restructuring case. They asked the judge to suspend new money flowing to Braskem Idesa, the company’s Mexican joint venture.

The request covers new disbursements, capital injections, asset transfers and the conversion of credits into shares. It also covers new guarantees and any purchase or sale options over the Mexican stake.

The move follows a petition from an ad hoc group of Braskem bondholders and debenture holders. That group holds roughly US$7 billion of notes issued abroad.

Prosecutors also asked the court to summon Braskem, its subsidiaries and Petrobras for documents and explanations. Petrobras and the private equity firm IG4 Capital are Braskem’s two controlling shareholders.

The opinion came from the Promotoria de Justiça de Falências, the bankruptcy unit of the São Paulo state prosecution service. It is a state case, not a federal one, and is separate from the Maceió ground damage in Alagoas.

The company supplies electricity and other inputs to second-generation producers; sells utilities, such as steam, water, compressed air and industrial gases; industrial services; and engages in the production, supply, and sale…

Why the timing matters for the creditor vote

Braskem filed for extrajudicial recovery on 24 August 2026 and the São Paulo court accepted the case on 28 August. That gave the company a 90-day standstill that runs to 22 November 2026.

Braskem had already won a 60-day court shield in late June 2026, before the August filing. The new standstill replaced it under Brazil’s bankruptcy law.

Inside that window Braskem must win support from a majority of the affected creditors. It had 39.6% when it filed, below the level a judge needs to confirm a plan.

Prosecutors argue that creditors cannot vote properly without full information about the Mexican commitments. Creditors cannot decide, they wrote, on an incomplete balance sheet or on projections that ignore large extraordinary obligations.

The opinion does not ask the court to cancel the restructuring. It asks for a pause until the information gap is closed.

How the money going to Braskem Idesa is built

Braskem Idesa filed a prepackaged Chapter 11 case in the United States in mid-August 2026. Chapter 11 is a US court process that lets a company reorganise while shielded from creditors.

Under that plan Braskem committed about US$476 million of fresh capital, including money advanced before the filing. The plan cuts more than US$920 million of the Mexican unit’s debt.

Prosecutors put the wider economic commitment at up to R$4.1 billion (about US$800 million). That figure uses about 5.18 reais to the dollar, the rate on 25 September 2026.

Brazilian press reports put the amount directly at stake at more than US$400 million. The larger totals include loans, guarantees and options that may never all be drawn.

Most of the US$476 million had already been paid before the order. Estadão reports that about US$70 million due in the coming months is now held back.

The plan keeps Braskem as majority shareholder of the Mexican unit. Grupo Idesa, its local partner, becomes the largest minority holder.

What Braskem and the court have said so far

Braskem declined to comment on the ruling to Reuters and Estadão on 24 September. People close to the company told Estadão it is expected to appeal.

On the morning of 25 September, Braskem told the market it had learned of the decision but had not yet been formally notified. It is “assessing the consequences and next steps” and will keep the market informed, Valor Econômico reported.

Petrobras and IG4 Capital had not commented on the order in reports published by 25 September 2026.

The judge wrote that final US approval would lock in commitments and could drain cash irreversibly. That could stop Braskem rebuilding its assets if Brazilian creditors are later found to have been harmed.

She also ended creditor protection for Braskem Netherlands B.V. and Braskem America Finance Company. Neither had shown the one-third creditor support required, and both have 15 days to prove it.

Prosecutors were careful about their own language. They said there is still no definitive proof of asset stripping, conflict of interest or abusive management.

What this means for expats and investors in Latin America

Braskem is renegotiating about US$10.9 billion of financial debt, much of it in bonds sold abroad. The freeze order changes how those holders judge their chance of repayment.

For expats living in Brazil or Mexico, the direct effect is small. Braskem Idesa runs a petrochemical complex in Veracruz state and sells to industry, not to households.

The wider signal is about creditor rights in cross-border cases. A Brazilian court is now policing cash moving into a subsidiary that is already under US bankruptcy protection.

What is not yet known is whether an appeal will succeed. It is also unclear how the order will affect the Mexican plan in the US court.

What to watch in the coming days

The US Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas had set Braskem Idesa’s plan confirmation hearing for 24 September 2026. Its outcome had not been widely reported by 25 September.

The São Paulo ruling landed the same day. The two courts are separate, and neither one is bound by the other.

The freeze may force Braskem to rework the timing of its Mexican rescue. That could make the 22 November deadline in Brazil harder to meet.

For now new money is blocked while both cases keep moving. The next signals are Braskem’s 15-day report, the Petrobras and IG4 answers and any appeal.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who asked for the freeze?

A group of Braskem bondholders and debenture holders asked first. São Paulo’s state prosecution service, through its bankruptcy unit, backed the request.

Has a court blocked the money?

Yes. On 24 September 2026 a São Paulo bankruptcy judge suspended new Braskem payments, guarantees and share options for Braskem Idesa until further notice.

How does this affect Braskem’s restructuring?

The Braskem Mexico freeze does not cancel it. Braskem still has until 22 November 2026 to win majority creditor support for its plan.

World.title: Brazil: Vasco da Gama SAF Auction Won by Lamacchia’s Almirante in US$386 Million Deal
World.content:
Football Business: Brazil

Key Facts —Auction. Almirante Participações S/A, the company of businessman Marcos Lamacchia, won the auction for 90% of Vasco da Gama’s football corporation (SAF) at Rio de Janeiro’s Court of Justice on 25 September — as the sole bidder. —Money. Lamacchia committed a R$500 million injection into the football department, paid in five annual R$100 million instalments and barred from servicing old debts; the total operation exceeds R$2 billion. —Who. Lamacchia, 47, is the stepson of Palmeiras president Leila Pereira and son of Crefisa founder José Roberto Lamacchia — a family link that the regulator Anresf will examine for conflicts of interest. —Not done yet. The sale still requires approval by Vasco’s Deliberative Council, an extraordinary general assembly of club members and Anresf clearance. —Background. Vasco has been in judicial recovery since 2024; the SAF’s shares are split between the club (30%), 777 Partners (31%, bought in 2022) and a 39% block disputed in arbitration.

Vasco da Gama’s long search for a new owner has crossed its decisive hurdle: Marcos Lamacchia’s Almirante Participações won the court-run auction for 90% of the club’s SAF on Friday — a R$2 billion-scale deal that still faces votes and a conflict-of-interest review.

São Januário, Vasco da Gama’s historic home in Rio de Janeiro. (Photo: The Rio Times archive)

What Happened at the Auction

The auction of 90% of the Vasco SAF’s shares was held on the afternoon of Friday 25 September at the 4th Business Court of the Rio de Janeiro Court of Justice (TJRJ), within the club’s judicial recovery proceedings. The result favouring Almirante Participações S/A was homologated shortly before 3pm, Estadão reported.

There were no rival bidders. Lamacchia’s company had entered the process as the “stalking horse” — the baseline bidder entitled to make the first proposal and to cover any higher offer. None materialised, so the prerogative was never needed.

Lamacchia did not attend the hearing in person. He was represented by his partner at Almirante, Mário Junqueira, and by lawyer André Sica, according to Estadão’s court coverage.

The Money on the Table

The centrepiece of the winning proposal is a R$500 million capital injection, paid in five annual instalments of R$100 million. The money is destined exclusively for the football department and is explicitly forbidden from being used to pay off pre-existing debts — a clause designed to ensure the funds rebuild the squad rather than service the past.

Beyond that, the bid commits to investing R$120 million over ten years in the club’s training centre and R$30 million over two years in the youth categories. It also covers payments to creditors in the judicial recovery plan, plus tax, social-security and non-judicial debts. Adding all obligations, the total value of the operation surpasses R$2 billion, Estadão and ge reported.

The court had dispensed with an independent prior valuation, treating the auction itself as the “market test”. After the final bid, court assistants are still to produce a comparative study to validate the price and fend off any claim of a cut-price sale.

Who Is Marcos Lamacchia

Marcos Faria Lamacchia, 47, is a São Paulo-based investor with a discreet public profile. He is the son of José Roberto Lamacchia — founder of financial group Crefisa and husband of Palmeiras president Leila Pereira — making Marcos her stepson. His mother, Junia Faria, is the daughter of the late banker Aloysio de Andrade Faria, who appeared on Forbes’ billionaire list.

Trained in business administration with specialisations in accounting and corporate law at the University of Miami and at Fundação Getulio Vargas, he worked at Eagle Bank, Conglomerado Alfa and Fiesp and was a Crefisa director between 2004 and 2009. Since 2008 he has been a founding partner and CEO of Blue Star, a financial consultancy and investment firm in São Paulo.

That family tree is also the deal’s biggest legal question: the national football regulator Anresf is examining whether being the stepson of another club’s president constitutes a conflict of interest under Brazilian football’s ownership rules.

Why Vasco Got Here

Vasco’s SAF was created in 2022 when 777 Partners bought a 31% stake; the associative club kept 30%, while a further 39% remains tied up in an arbitration dispute. After 777 was removed from the SAF’s command amid its own collapse, the club’s finances deteriorated into judicial recovery.

The Lamacchia orbit has been financing the club through the crisis: Crefisa agreed an R$80 million loan in October 2025, Almirante lent R$40 million in July, and on 10 September the court authorised a further R$150 million financing line from Almirante — released in monthly tranches under judicial supervision — to keep the club solvent through the auction.

The same 10 September decision, by judge Simone Gastesi Chevrand, settled conflicts with former investor 777 Carioca LLC, which formally declared it would not oppose the recovery plan or the creation of the new SAF — clearing the path to Friday’s auction.

What Happens Next

Winning the auction is a decisive step, but not the last one. The operation must still be submitted to Vasco’s Deliberative Council and to an extraordinary general assembly where club members vote. It also faces scrutiny from Anresf, the national football regulation and sustainability agency, on the conflict-of-interest question.

The legal debate turns on Article 1,595 of the Civil Code, which counts a stepson as a first-degree relative by affinity, and on the CBF-linked regulation defining “significant influence” over a club. Anresf must decide whether the Leila Pereira connection disqualifies or merely conditions the purchase.

No completion date has been set. But the parties involved consider that the hardest stage — finding and validating a buyer inside a court-supervised process — has now been overcome.

What We Could Not Confirm

We could not confirm the exact per-year schedule of the creditor payments bundled into the R$2 billion total, nor how the disputed 39% arbitration block will be resolved into the new SAF’s final share structure.

It is also unclear when Anresf will rule on the conflict-of-interest question, and what conditions — if any — it might impose. We will update this report when the council vote and the regulator’s decision are published.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who won the Vasco da Gama SAF auction?

Almirante Participações S/A, the company of businessman Marcos Lamacchia, won the 25 September auction at Rio’s Court of Justice as the sole bidder, acquiring the right to 90% of the SAF’s shares pending internal approvals.

How much is the Vasco SAF deal worth?

The headline commitment is R$500 million for the football department over five years, plus R$120 million for the training centre, R$30 million for youth football and coverage of recovery-plan creditors and tax debts — bringing the total operation above R$2 billion.

Is the sale of Vasco’s SAF final?

Not yet. The deal still needs approval from Vasco’s Deliberative Council and an extraordinary members’ assembly, plus clearance from regulator Anresf, which is examining a possible conflict of interest because Lamacchia is the stepson of Palmeiras president Leila Pereira.

World.title: Cuba Military Planning: US Army Reserve Canvasses 6 Unit Types, CBS Reports
World.content:
CUBA · SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened On 25 September 2026 CBS reported the US Army Reserve is checking which support units it could give Southern Command.

— The units A military police brigade, a medical brigade, a surgical detachment, engineers, a logistics battalion and a sustainment command.

— The Cuba link The message never names Cuba, but several US officials told CBS the planning is aimed at the island.

— The catch The document shows no sign of deployment orders, and gives no troop numbers, destination or mission.

— The timing The units are “possibly needed in 90–120 days”, and commands had to reply by 25 September.

— Havana’s stance In an NBC interview before the report, Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez said the US could never justify an attack.

Cuba military planning has reached the US Army Reserve, days after Donald Trump told the UN the island’s government would fall.

The fence line at the edge of the US naval base at Guantánamo Bay, the only US military foothold on Cuba. Photo: Ivan Curra, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
