Cuba military planning in Washington is continuing, and has now reached the Army Reserve. The US Army Reserve is checking whether it can give Southern Command police, medical and other support units within four months.

CBS News reported this on Friday 25 September 2026, citing an internal Army message.

The message does not mention Cuba. Several US officials told CBS, speaking anonymously, that the request is part of continued military planning aimed at the island.

There is no sign in the document that any unit has received deployment orders. CBS published the report days after Trump told the UN General Assembly that Cuba’s communist government “will fall”.

What the Army Reserve Message Asks For

Army Reserve headquarters asked its subordinate commands to report whether six types of formations could be made available. All six would come under US Southern Command, which covers Central and South America and the Caribbean.

The units include a combat sustainment support battalion, which coordinates transport, maintenance, fuel and supplies. It also includes an engineer battalion and an expeditionary sustainment command to oversee logistics across a whole theatre.

Two medical elements are on it: a medical brigade and a forward resuscitative and surgical detachment for emergency surgery near troops. The list also includes a military police brigade, used for security, detention and law enforcement.

The units would be “possibly needed in 90–120 days”, the message says. Commands were told to send their answers to Army Reserve headquarters by 25 September.

What the Document Does Not Say

The message gives no number of troops. It does not say where the forces would go or which operation they would support.

The Army Reserve did not respond to CBS before publication. A Southern Command spokesperson said the command does not comment on movements or deployment timelines, citing operational security.

The spokesperson added that Southern Command “continuously coordinates with the Joint Force to assess a range of potential requirements” in its area. The statement neither confirms nor denies a Cuba mission.

Months of Contingency Planning in Cuba Military Planning

This is not the first sign of planning around Cuba. Earlier this year, US forces carried out reconnaissance of the seafloor and sea approaches around the island, US military personnel told CBS.

US air units were also put on heightened readiness and told to pre-position personnel for a possible deployment. Those plans did not go ahead, CBS said.

In May, CBS reported that US intelligence officials were assessing how Cuba would respond to possible US military action. In July, it reported that planners had examined options including an air assault by thousands of soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division.

Officials stressed in July that those briefings did not mean President Trump or the Pentagon had decided to act. CBS found no sign of deployment orders in the new message either.

The Pressure From Washington

The planning comes as the Trump administration squeezes Cuba’s economy and presses for political change. On 17 September it sanctioned eight Cuban entities and three officials, the State Department said.

Four of the entities are nickel-sector companies and four are military research enterprises.

At the UN on 22 September, Trump said his administration sought a “fundamental change” in Cuba. He added that “freedom will be coming to Cuba”.

The Cuban delegation walked out during his speech.

Trump also said Secretary of State Marco Rubio was “deep into negotiations” with Havana. In March, he said he expected to have “the honor of taking Cuba”, and later that “Cuba’s going to be next”.

Washington has also enforced a de facto oil blockade since January. President Miguel Díaz-Canel calls that “economic warfare” and has vowed to resist any US attack.

What Havana Says

Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez spoke to NBC News in New York this week, before the CBS report. He said the US would never find any justification for attacking Cuba, EFE reported.

Cuba poses no threat to US security, he argued. It has raised its defensive capacity with the participation of the whole people, he said.

In the same interview, he said he did not expect a raid like the one that seized Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro in January. He added that Havana takes the threats “very seriously”.

He confirmed “some episodes of conversations” with Washington but gave no details. His deputy, Carlos Fernández de Cossío, told Prensa Latina this week that there had been no progress.

Why It Matters

For anyone with family, business or travel plans in Cuba, the report adds a security question to an economic crisis. International visitors fell 64.4% in January–August 2026 from a year earlier, according to the statistics office ONEI.

The planning also fits a wider US military push in the region. US strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific have killed more than 230 people, CBS said.

That toll covers about 70 strikes since the campaign began in September 2025.

Joint US–Ecuador operations against armed groups began in March. On Thursday, US troops and DEA agents helped Ecuador arrest more than 30 people linked to Mexico’s Jalisco cartel.

What to Watch

The first marker is whether any of the six unit types receive orders. Counted from this month, the window of 90 to 120 days points to around the turn of the year.

The second is diplomacy. Rodríguez says Havana is willing to keep talking, while Trump says Rubio is negotiating.

Any shift in that channel matters as much as troop movements.

Sources: CBS News, US military lays groundwork for potential action around Cuba, 25 September 2026; Infobae (EFE), Cuban foreign minister on a possible attack, 25 September 2026; CiberCuba, Fernández de Cossío on talks with the US, 25 September 2026; NBC Miami, Cuba’s foreign minister pushes back on Trump, 24 September 2026; US State Department, sanctions fact sheet, 17 September 2026; EFE, Cuba tourism January–August, 24 September 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the US about to invade Cuba?

There is no sign in the document of a deployment order. CBS reported planning for support units, with no troop numbers, destination or named operation.

What units is the US Army Reserve checking?

It is checking six types of formation. They are a sustainment battalion, an engineer battalion, a sustainment command, a medical brigade, a surgical detachment and a military police brigade.

Does the Army message mention Cuba?

No. Several US officials told CBS News that the request is part of continued military planning aimed at Cuba.

What has Cuba said?

In an NBC News interview before the report, Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez said the US could never justify an attack. He said Cuba takes the threats very seriously and is ready to keep talking.

Connected Coverage

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief — Friday, 25 September 2026

The Capitol in Washington. The Senate refused by fifty votes to forty-nine to order the fighting in Iran stopped, with four Republicans crossing and one Democrat voting against. Photo: Martin Falbisoner, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

USA & Canada Intelligence Dossier — Friday, 25 September 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web and updated through the day. Read the web dossier → · Every edition on the dossier page →

The war vote — Weary, and one senator short of ordering the fighting stopped. The seized ballots — Taken on an outsider’s fraud claim, and ordered back by a unanimous court. Canada’s worst case — Calm about the unthinkable, and willing to say so out loud. Quebec’s ballot — Hungry for a change of government, and unconvinced by everyone offering one.

The American mood this morning is fatigue with a war nobody can vote away. The Senate was asked on Thursday to order the fighting in Iran stopped, and it declined by a single vote.

What makes the fatigue political is who is complaining now. Republican candidates in Iowa and Michigan spent this week telling shoppers that the war has to end, and blaming the price of fuel.

The cost is counted at the pump before it is counted anywhere else. The American Automobile Association, the motoring club whose daily price report is the national standard, put regular petrol at US$4.48 a gallon on 24 September, against US$3.16 a year earlier.

Two courts spent the same Thursday telling American officials they had gone too far. One ordered a sheriff to hand back more than 650,000 ballots; the other set a permanent limit on crowding in immigration cells.

Canada’s temperament this week is a strange calm about the worst thing imaginable. The Prime Minister told an American newspaper he had studied the risk of an American invasion, and his defence minister said the next day that such work is ordinary.

What steadies the picture is that each of these fights is running through an institution rather than around one. Two courts ruled, a chamber voted, a foreign ministry made an offer, and three provinces are about to put questions to voters.

Key Facts — The Senate war vote. The Senate refused by 50 votes to 49 on 24 September to order an end to the fighting in Iran, four Republicans joining the Democrats. — Petrol at the pump. The American Automobile Association put regular petrol at US$4.48 a gallon on 24 September, its highest ever for the time of year, against US$3.16 a year earlier. — The seized ballots in Riverside. California’s Supreme Court held unanimously on 24 September that Sheriff Chad Bianco broke state election law by taking more than 650,000 ballots, and must return them. — The New York holding rooms. Judge Lewis Kaplan permanently ordered fifty square feet a person and unmonitored lawyer calls at 26 Federal Plaza on 24 September, calling the conditions unconstitutional. — Deportations at the Supreme Court. The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on 24 September to suspend an appeals ruling of 18 September requiring notice before removal to a third country. — Carney on the worst case. Canada’s Prime Minister told the New York Times, published 23 September, that he studied an American invasion as an extreme tail risk; his defence minister called such work normal. — Quebec before the vote. Léger put the Parti Québécois on 29 per cent and the Liberals on 23 before the 5 October election, with 65 per cent wanting a change of government. — Alberta’s referendum polling. Research Co found 74 per cent of Albertans would stay in Canada and 22 per cent would start leaving, from 750 likely voters questioned in late August.

Worn Down By A War The Senate Would Not Halt

The one thing the Senate decided this week, it decided against itself. Stars and Stripes, the newspaper that serves the American armed forces, and CBS News both record Thursday’s count as 49 in favour and 50 against.

Stars and Stripes describes the measure as non-binding, so it would not have compelled the President even had it passed. It was a war-powers resolution, the instrument by which Congress can instruct a president to withdraw forces, and the House had passed the same resolution in July.

Four Republicans voted with the Democrats and one Democrat voted with the Republicans. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Thom Tillis of North Carolina backed it, and John Fetterman of Pennsylvania opposed it.

The war it concerns began on 28 February, which puts it in its seventh month. Senator Andy Kim of New Jersey told the chamber: “It’s cost us American lives. We’ve lost at least 19 service members, brave men and women, over 750 injured.”

The Pentagon has put a price on it. Stars and Stripes gives its estimate of the war’s cost as about US$42 billion.

The public accounting is not settled. PBS News puts the cost so far at US$43.5 billion, and reports a further US$87.6 billion sought from Congress for the war, American farmers and an Ebola response.

The resolution’s author framed it as a question of who decides. Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia said of the President: “We’ve never had a president who talks like this, and we never should again. But it is not his decision; it’s our decision.”

The Republican who runs the chamber read the mood as economic rather than moral. John Thune called it “an economic frustration” and said he hoped the administration was “laser-focused on trying to get the strait open”, CBS News reports.

Two Republican candidates for the Senate spent the week campaigning against their own President’s war. Ashley Hinson, running in Iowa, wrote that Iowans “shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran”, NPR reports.

Her Michigan counterpart made the same case in a supermarket. Mike Rogers said that “Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life” and that the war “needs to end and end quickly”, NPR reports.

The drift is measurable in the lower chamber as well. Seven House Republicans now support a resolution to remove American forces from Iran, up from four over the summer, NPR reports.

Voters are telling pollsters that this election is about the President rather than about Congress. The NPR, PBS News and Marist survey of 1,280 registered voters on 14 and 15 September found 45 per cent calling their vote opposition to Trump, and 54 per cent of independents agreeing.

The price those candidates point at is on the motoring club’s own board. The association put regular petrol at US$4.4825 a gallon on 24 September, up from US$4.4386 a week earlier and US$3.1634 a year ago.

The club said as much in its own words, in its price report of 24 September. It stated that “at $4.48 per gallon, this is the highest the national average has ever been for this time of year”, and that the month was on course to set a September record.

Freight feels it harder than families do. The association’s diesel average reached US$6.528 a gallon on 22 September, US$2.84 above a year earlier, FleetOwner, an American trucking trade title, reports.

The White House answer on fuel is about supply rather than about the war, and the conservative Fox Business channel reported it on 4 September. Its spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said the President “remains committed to unleashing American energy dominance, cutting costs, and putting more money back in the pockets of hardworking American families”.

The oil market itself has stopped pointing one way. November Brent settled at US$106.60 a barrel on Thursday and was reading US$105.35 at 13.58 UTC on Friday.

Underneath that, buyers are still paying more for oil now than for oil in December. The gap between the two contracts was US$6.38 on Thursday’s settlements against US$4.96 on Wednesday’s, so the premium for immediate delivery has widened rather than eased.

Tehran has put a timetable in front of Washington. Iran’s Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the Strait of Hormuz would reopen seven days after fighting stops and the United States lifts its naval blockade and oil sanctions, Al Jazeera reports.

The strait is the narrow sea lane at the mouth of the Gulf through which much of the world’s oil is shipped, and Iran’s offer treats it as closed. Washington had not accepted the offer by 14.55 UTC on Friday.

Araghchi presented the terms as old ground, drawn from the Islamabad memorandum that paused the fighting earlier this year. He said Iran’s conditions “are nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad MOU, which was signed by the US President”, the Arab Times, a Kuwaiti daily, reports.

The administration’s own reading is cooler than the offer. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at the United Nations this week that he did not “want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough”, Al-Monitor reports.

He allowed the contact itself some weight. Rubio added that “at the same time, I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation”, Al-Monitor, a Washington-based news site covering the Middle East, reports.

A Sheriff Who Stopped Trusting His County’s Ballots

The week’s most striking American ruling came from a state court. California’s Supreme Court held unanimously on Thursday 24 September that a county sheriff broke state election law by seizing more than 650,000 ballots.

The court ordered him to return them and to stop his investigation. Chad Bianco, the elected sheriff of Riverside County in southern California, had taken the ballots in February and March 2026, KQED and Fox News report, after a special election held in November 2025.

The vote he was investigating had national consequences. Proposition 50 was a redistricting measure Californians approved, redrawing five Republican-held seats in the federal House of Representatives to favour Democrats, CBS Los Angeles reports.

Bianco’s own account of why he took them is plain. Fox News, the conservative American network, reported in March that he had said: “This investigation is simple: Physically count the ballots and compare that result with the total votes recorded.”

The claim behind the seizure came from outside his office. A group calling itself the Riverside Election Integrity Team said it had found about 45,000 excess votes in the November 2025 count, Fox News reported.

The county’s own election office rejected the claim. Art Tinoco, Riverside County’s registrar of voters, said the group “had misinterpreted how votes are counted on Election Day”, and put the final gap at 103 votes, or 0.16 per cent, Fox News reported.

California’s chief election officer said much the same. Shirley Weber, the Secretary of State, said the sheriff’s office “has taken actions based on allegations that lack credible evidence and risk undermining public confidence in our elections”, Fox News reported.

The court did not weigh that claim at all. Chief Justice Patricia Guerrero wrote that state law “unambiguously prohibits the removal of ballots from an elections official’s custody”, KQED, a public broadcaster in San Francisco, reports.

She gave a second reason that does not rest on the statute. Letting police have unfettered access to ballots, Guerrero wrote, “itself creates a substantial risk to election integrity”, CalMatters, a non-profit news service covering the state government, reports.

The sheriff did not concede the point. In a video statement, CalMatters reports, he said: “We are very disappointed and wholeheartedly disagree with the court’s ruling.”

His written statement went further. Bianco called the inquiry “a lawful and legal investigation into potential election fraud” and the case “an obvious legal attempt to prevent the investigation from occurring that was successful”, CalMatters reports.

He says he will obey it all the same. KQED reports that he would comply with the ruling while exploring options of assistance from the federal courts, and he complained that “Sacramento shut it down”.

He had signalled in August that a ruling would not stop him. CalMatters reports that he said then his office would continue its investigation into the 2025 election, whatever the court decided.

California’s governor treated the ruling as a win for the machinery of the state. Gavin Newsom’s office published a statement on 24 September saying it “affirms that in California we will defend democracy — using every branch of government”.

The attorney general who brought the case was harsher. Rob Bonta said Bianco “willfully defied my direct orders, misused criminal investigative tools and created a constitutional emergency in the process”, KQED reports.

Bianco is not a marginal figure, which is what gives the case its weight. He ran for governor of California this year as a Republican and lost, CalMatters reports, and he remains the county’s elected sheriff.

What happens next is not fully settled, and the ruling closes only this challenge. Bianco has signalled he may turn to the federal courts, and no federal filing had been reported by 14.55 UTC on Friday.

Enforcement That Outran The Rules It Wrote

The second ruling of that Thursday was about rooms rather than ballots. Judge Lewis Kaplan of the federal district court in Manhattan issued a permanent injunction on 24 September over the immigration holding rooms at 26 Federal Plaza in lower Manhattan.

The building is a processing centre rather than a prison, and that is the point. Its holding rooms were designed for stays of twelve hours or less, and Kaplan found that people were kept in them far longer and in far greater numbers, Axios reports.

The agency involved is Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which arrests and removes people without legal status. The number of people held in those rooms rose from fewer than ten to upward of a hundred between May and August 2025, Newsweek reports.

The judge’s findings go to intent. Kaplan wrote that the agency “knew, or should have known, that how it was treating detainees was wrong, yet it continued to do it anyway”, Newsweek reports.

He then put a motive on it. It did so, Kaplan wrote, “to inflict punishment on detainees and induce them to self-deport”, Newsweek reports.

One phrase in the ruling is blunter than the rest. Kaplan wrote that the building “essentially was a black site” before his earlier orders, Newsweek reports.

The order is unusually specific about ordinary things. It requires at least fifty square feet of floor space for each person and temperatures kept between 68 and 74 degrees Fahrenheit, Axios reports.

The rest of the list is equally plain. Three meals a day with bottled water, soap and toilet paper, licensed medical staff on site, clean bedding and unmonitored telephone calls to lawyers are all now court-ordered, Axios reports.

The judge also found his own earlier orders ignored. Kaplan wrote that the agency had repeatedly ignored them and that officials had at times “intentionally concealed or recklessly disregarded the truth”, Axios reports.

The department’s standing position is that the place is not a jail. In August 2025 the Department of Homeland Security said that “26 Federal Plaza is not a detention center” but a processing centre for brief holds before transfer.

It rejected the overcrowding account outright at the time. The claims were “categorically false”, the department said, ABC7 New York reported.

The department has not said what it will do next. Axios and Newsweek both asked on Thursday and had no reply, and no statement had been made by 14.55 UTC on Friday.

The agency’s political defence is being made elsewhere, and not about these rooms. Tom Homan, the White House official who directs border policy, told the first Attorney General’s Summit on Victims of Violent Crime on Thursday that enforcement would go on.

His words were aimed at the reporters in the room. “We’re gonna keep pushing. We’re not gonna apologize. The media back there, you can hate us all you want, we’re not going anywhere,” Homan said, The Hill reports.

He also put a number on the agency’s work the day before. “Over 60% of ICE arrests are criminals. That’s just a stone-cold fact,” Homan said on the Fox News programme The Will Cain Show on 23 September, Breitbart, a conservative American news site, reports.

While a district judge narrowed what the agency may do, the government went upstairs. The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on 24 September to suspend a ruling that requires notice before a person is deported to a country that is not their own, the Associated Press reports.

The ruling it wants lifted is recent and unanimous. The First Circuit appeals court in Boston held on 18 September, by three votes to nothing, that the policy conflicts with the rules governing claims of a fear of torture, the Associated Press reports.

The appeals court put the principle in a single sentence, which the Associated Press quotes. Judge Seth Aframe wrote that the right to contest removal “means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination”.

The government’s case is about volume and speed. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the court had “in the dark of night” robbed the government of “an entirely legal and valuable tool to stem the tide of illegal immigration”, the Associated Press reports.

His solicitor general gave the court a scale. D. John Sauer wrote that the government “has been able to remove thousands of aliens to third countries in recent months, and thousands more are eligible for such removal”, the Associated Press reports.

The case now has a clock on it. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who handles emergency applications from that circuit, asked those challenging the policy to reply by 4 p.m. Eastern time on Monday, and the court had not ruled by 14.55 UTC on Friday.

Parliament Hill in Ottawa. The prime minister has described American military action against Canada as an extreme tail risk that it would be irresponsible not to plan for, and his defence minister called such planning normal.

The Badges Came Back, The Dinner Did Not

Thursday’s unfinished business in Washington has largely been finished. Reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were readmitted to the White House grounds a little over two hours after the White House was told of Judge Timothy Kelly’s order, PBS News reports.

The delay had a mechanical explanation. Judge Kelly signed it shortly after midnight, and White House staff then had to find, reactivate and return badges the Secret Service had taken when the ban was imposed, PBS News reports.

Two of the three names need explaining. MS NOW is the cable network formerly called MSNBC, and Politico is a Washington political news site.

One dispute survived the order. CNN and MS NOW both said their journalists were kept out of the arrival for the Chinese president’s state dinner, PBS News reports.

The White House set the terms of that exclusion. CNN said it allowed a photographer and an audio technician in and refused entry to a reporter and a producer, PBS News reports.

The President’s account of the same evening is different. He wrote that the networks “refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years”, his capital letters, PBS News reports.

The state visit ended on Friday in a reading room, the Washington Times, a conservative Washington daily, reports. Xi Jinping’s last stop was the National Archives, where the Archivist showed the two couples the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, CBS News reports.

The substance was thinner than the guest list. Xi announced that two pandas from China would soon go to Atlanta’s zoo, and the White House has said little about what the visit achieved, CBS News reports.

One deliverable has been promised rather than delivered, and it would cover a “relatively small subset of goods”. The United States Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, said on Fox News on Monday that there would be an announcement establishing a United States–China board of trade, CBS News reports.

The sentence worth keeping came from the Chinese president. Xi said artificial intelligence should remain “under human control” and that competition “should be a healthy one, and should be kept within bounds”, CBS News reports.

Trump’s own summary was warmer and vaguer. He said on leaving that the two had had “a great meeting”, CBS News reports, and described a friendship with Xi going back to 2016.

Canada Rehearses The Unthinkable, And Says So Out Loud

Canada spent this week discussing in public the possibility of an American attack on it. Mark Carney told the New York Times, in an interview the paper published on Wednesday 23 September, that he had examined the risk as a matter of risk management.

His words were careful rather than agitated. Carney said a leader has “a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk”, Global News, a Canadian broadcaster, reports.

He then took the drama out of it twice. The exercise was “just risk management” and “not a base case”, he said, but it would be irresponsible not to prepare, Global News reports.

The government spent the next day making that sound routine. Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Thursday that it is normal and that “all militaries in the world spend time analyzing risk scenarios”, CP24, a Toronto news channel, reports.

He would not say what had actually been prepared. The Prime Minister had indicated that was “the kind of detail that we would not get into”, McGuinty said, CP24 reports.

A second minister defended the habit rather than the scenario. Evan Solomon, the minister for artificial intelligence, said running any scenario is prudent and that “that’s the way every government functions”, CP24 reports.

Not everyone in Canada thought saying it aloud was wise. Peter MacKay, a Conservative former defence minister, criticised Carney’s candour as counterproductive during tense negotiations, CP24 reports.

The invasion line was the smallest part of a larger turn. Carney told the paper that Canada would cut both its military and its technological reliance on the United States, CTV News reports.

Two names made that concrete. He included Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service among the dependencies to be reduced, and said Canada would expand economic ties with China, CTV News reports.

The hardest test of that is sitting on a runway in Texas. Canada’s first F-35 fighter made its maiden flight at Fort Worth on 23 September, and the first aircraft are expected in Canada in 2028, CTV News reports.

The aeroplane is not yet a settled purchase. Canada agreed to buy 88 of them in January 2023 and has committed to only 16 under a review ordered in March 2025, 19FortyFive, an American defence publication, reports.

Carney describes the choice as a real one. It is “a real decision because of differing capabilities, because of strategic dependencies, and because of economic return”, he told the paper, CTV News reports.

The turn has an unhappy labour market behind it. Canada’s unemployment rate was 6.4 per cent in August against 4.1 per cent in the United States, CTV News reports, and the economy shed roughly 42,000 jobs that month, BNN Bloomberg reports.

Washington’s answer has been dismissive rather than reassuring. Trump said last week that reports Canada might become an associate member of the European Union were “laughable”, and that a hostile act would bring “very serious tariffs” on Europe, Fox News reports.

Investors in Toronto are not behaving as though any of this were imminent. The S&P/TSX Composite was reading 35,626.52 at 14.07 UTC on Friday, down 79.98 or 0.22 per cent on Thursday’s close, with the session still open.

Quebec Shops For A Government, Alberta For A Message

Quebec votes on 5 October wanting something different, without agreeing what. The polling firm Léger put the Parti Québécois on 29 per cent, the Liberals on 23, the governing Coalition Avenir Québec on 20 and the Conservative Party of Quebec on 17.

The appetite for change is larger than any party’s share of it. Léger found 65 per cent of Quebecers wanting a change of government, up four points, from 1,001 people questioned online between 18 and 21 September.

What they want changed is not the constitution. Cost of living and housing ranked first among the issues likely to decide the vote, named by 53 per cent, Léger reports.

The parties are answering with money rather than with sovereignty. The Parti Québécois leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, has promised to halve Quebec’s sales tax on petrol for at least a year, CP24 reports.

His rivals are bidding in the same currency. The Conservative leader Éric Duhaime would lift the basic personal allowance to C$35,000 (about US$24,749), and the governing party would put C$1,000 (about US$707) into every newborn’s education savings plan, CP24 reports.

Québec Solidaire, a left-wing party, is running on precariousness, CP24 reports. Alexandre Boulerice said young people “need to regain hope for the future, to regain the conviction that it is possible to live well without being in a state of constant precariousness”.

The party in front is nevertheless the one that wants to leave Canada. The Parti Québécois seeks independence for the French-speaking province, and it stood at 37 per cent among French-speaking voters in the same survey.

Alberta votes on 19 October on ten questions, among them whether to stay in Canada. Two pollsters put the stay side well ahead and disagree about by how much.

Research Co, a Canadian polling firm, found 74 per cent of Albertans would vote to remain and 22 per cent to begin a legal separation, from 750 likely voters between 24 and 26 August. The Angus Reid Institute, a Canadian not-for-profit polling foundation, had 61 per cent for staying and 33 per cent for starting the process, from 1,017 Albertans questioned between 10 and 13 August.

Angus Reid does not read the leave vote as a wish to leave. It found that two in five of those choosing to leave described the exercise as sending a message to Ottawa rather than wanting separation.

The premier running that referendum is against leaving. Danielle Smith has said she wants a “sovereign Alberta within a united Canada” and has declined to call separatists fringe extremists, the Lethbridge Herald, a southern Alberta daily, reports.

British Columbia will vote twice in October, which is a statement of its own. Municipal elections fall on 17 October and the provincial election Premier David Eby called early falls on 24 October, Daily Hive, a Canadian news site, reports.

The premier is running on continuity and on the American threat. Eby called it “an existential moment” and said that “at a time when Donald Trump is creating more uncertainty, the last thing we need is to rip up what’s working”, Daily Hive reports.

His opponents are running on sawmills. The British Columbia Conservatives said that “at least 21 B.C. lumber mills have closed since 2023, with roughly 15,000 forestry jobs lost since 2022”, Daily Hive reports.

The Greens object to the election itself. Their leader, Emily Lowan, said the early vote “will be costly, it isn’t wanted” and continues a record of putting the government’s interests first, Daily Hive reports.

American duties on Canadian softwood lumber are the background, and Ottawa is paying to keep mills running. The federal finance department committed a C$30 million loan (about US$21.2 million) on 18 September to Conifex Timber, which supports 260 direct jobs at Mackenzie in northern British Columbia.

The ministers framed it as defence rather than subsidy. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said the government is “strengthening the forest sector in the face of U.S. tariffs”.

The department put the industry’s weight beside the loan. It counted nearly 200,000 forest-sector workers, more than 11,000 of them Indigenous, and more than C$20 billion (about US$14.1 billion) of national output.

The American industry calls the same money a subsidy. The U.S. Lumber Coalition, an alliance of American sawmill owners, said on 2 April that Canada had announced C$2.1 billion (about US$1.5 billion) of new forestry subsidies in seven months.

The coalition put the total pledged at C$9.9 billion (about US$7.0 billion), in its own statement of 2 April. Its executive director, Zoltan van Heyningen, said that answering American trade enforcement “by doubling down on Canada’s unfair trade practices is both reprehensible and counterproductive”.

Ontario’s answer to the cost of living arrives on 1 October and is small. The province’s general minimum wage rises from C$17.60 to C$17.95 an hour, about US$12.44 to US$12.69.

The size of the rise is set by formula rather than by argument. It is indexed to a 1.9 per cent movement in provincial consumer prices, the employment law firm Hicks Morley reports, and the student rate goes to C$16.90 (about US$11.95).

A workers’ group called that inadequate on Friday, in a statement carried by BNN Bloomberg. Deena Ladd of the Workers’ Action Centre, a Toronto advocacy group, said the average two-bedroom flat in the province “still costs more than $2,100 a month” (about US$1,485).

She also priced the alternative. Had the C$20 an hour (about US$14.14) her group first demanded in 2021 been adopted then, Ladd said, the rate taking effect on 1 October would be C$24.10 (about US$17.04).

What This Means From Latin America

The war’s clearest export to this hemisphere is the price of a barrel. November Brent settled at US$106.60 on Thursday and was reading US$105.35 at 13.58 UTC on Friday, dearer fuel for importers such as Chile and Peru and better receipts for Brazil, Colombia and Guyana.

The next move in that price is being decided in New York rather than in a market. If Iran’s seven-day offer is taken up the freight premium has a reason to unwind, and if it is not, buyers keep paying more for oil now than for oil in December.

The removal fight is the item with the most direct regional consequence. The vast majority of people removed to third countries have gone to Mexico, and Guyana is among more than two dozen other destinations, the Associated Press reports.

The ballot case is the sequence a Latin American reader will recognise fastest. An elected county sheriff took more than 650,000 ballots on the strength of an outside fraud claim his own county’s registrar called a misreading, and a unanimous court made him give them back.

Canada’s search for other partners keeps a door open to this hemisphere. A middle power saying out loud that it will reduce its military and technological dependence on Washington is a natural counterpart for governments here making the same calculation.

What We Are Watching

Replies at the Supreme Court on third-country removals — Monday. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson set 4 p.m. Eastern time for the challengers’ answer, and the court had not ruled by 14.55 UTC on Friday.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson set 4 p.m. Eastern time for the challengers’ answer, and the court had not ruled by 14.55 UTC on Friday. Iran’s seven-day offer on the Strait of Hormuz — from 25 September. Washington had not accepted it by 14.55 UTC on Friday, and Rubio declined to call this week’s contacts a breakthrough.

Washington had not accepted it by 14.55 UTC on Friday, and Rubio declined to call this week’s contacts a breakthrough. The White House request to Congress — no date set. PBS News reports that US$87.6 billion has been sought for the war, American farmers and an Ebola response, and Congress has not voted on it.

PBS News reports that US$87.6 billion has been sought for the war, American farmers and an Ebola response, and Congress has not voted on it. Compliance at 26 Federal Plaza in New York — from 24 September. Judge Kaplan’s permanent injunction sets space, temperature, food and lawyer-access requirements, and the department had said nothing about it by 14.55 UTC on Friday.

Judge Kaplan’s permanent injunction sets space, temperature, food and lawyer-access requirements, and the department had said nothing about it by 14.55 UTC on Friday. The return of the Riverside County ballots — from 24 September. Bianco says he wholeheartedly disagrees with the ruling but would comply while exploring the federal courts; no federal filing had been reported by 14.55 UTC on Friday.

Bianco says he wholeheartedly disagrees with the ruling but would comply while exploring the federal courts; no federal filing had been reported by 14.55 UTC on Friday. The hearing on a longer press-access injunction — by 8 October. Judge Kelly’s restraining order of 24 September runs 14 days, and the badges were handed back that morning.

Judge Kelly’s restraining order of 24 September runs 14 days, and the badges were handed back that morning. Ontario’s minimum wage increase — 1 October. The general rate goes from C$17.60 to C$17.95 an hour, about US$12.44 to US$12.69, by statutory indexation.

The general rate goes from C$17.60 to C$17.95 an hour, about US$12.44 to US$12.69, by statutory indexation. The Quebec general election — 5 October. Léger has the Parti Québécois on 29 per cent and 65 per cent of Quebecers wanting a change of government.

Léger has the Parti Québécois on 29 per cent and 65 per cent of Quebecers wanting a change of government. British Columbia’s municipal elections — 17 October. The province votes twice this month, a week before its provincial election, Daily Hive reports.

The province votes twice this month, a week before its provincial election, Daily Hive reports. The Alberta referendum on staying in Canada — 19 October. Research Co had 74 per cent for remaining and the Angus Reid Institute 61 per cent, from separate August surveys.

Research Co had 74 per cent for remaining and the Angus Reid Institute 61 per cent, from separate August surveys. The British Columbia provincial election — 24 October. Eby called it early and is running on continuity; the Conservatives are running on closed sawmills.

Eby called it early and is running on continuity; the Conservatives are running on closed sawmills. The second reading of Canada’s building bill — date not set. Bill C-39, which would compress approval of major projects into a decision within a year, has had debate and no vote, and is not law.

Bill C-39, which would compress approval of major projects into a decision within a year, has had debate and no vote, and is not law. The American midterm elections — 3 November. The NPR, PBS News and Marist survey found 45 per cent of registered voters calling their vote opposition to Trump.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Senate vote on, and what did the result change?

It voted on a war-powers resolution. That is the instrument by which the American Congress can instruct a president to withdraw forces from hostilities it has not authorised. Stars and Stripes and CBS News both record the count on Thursday 24 September as 49 in favour and 50 against. Four Republicans crossed to support it — Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Rand Paul and Thom Tillis — and one Democrat, John Fetterman, crossed the other way. Nothing changed in law, because Stars and Stripes describes the measure as non-binding, and the House had passed the same resolution in July. The signal is what matters. Stars and Stripes records this as the fourteenth such resolution considered since the fighting began on 28 February. NPR reports that seven House Republicans now support withdrawal, up from four over the summer.

How could a sheriff take 650,000 ballots, and what happens to them now?

Chad Bianco is the elected sheriff of Riverside County in southern California. He obtained warrants and seized the ballots from the November 2025 special election, Fox News reported in March. The claim behind it came from a group calling itself the Riverside Election Integrity Team, which said it had found about 45,000 excess votes. The county’s own registrar of voters, Art Tinoco, said the group “had misinterpreted how votes are counted on Election Day” and put the final gap at 103 votes, Fox News reported. California’s Supreme Court held unanimously on 24 September that he had broken state election law. It ordered the ballots returned and the investigation stopped, with Chief Justice Patricia Guerrero writing that the statute “unambiguously prohibits the removal of ballots from an elections official’s custody”, KQED reports. The court did not rule on whether the fraud claim had merit. Bianco said in a video statement that he was “very disappointed and wholeheartedly disagree with the court’s ruling”, CalMatters reports, and called the inquiry “a lawful and legal investigation into potential election fraud”. KQED reports that he would nonetheless comply while exploring options of assistance from the federal courts, and no federal filing had been reported by 14.55 UTC on Friday.

What did the New York judge order, and what does the government say?

Judge Lewis Kaplan of the federal district court in Manhattan issued a permanent injunction on 24 September. It governs the immigration holding rooms at 26 Federal Plaza in lower Manhattan. It requires at least fifty square feet a person, temperatures between 68 and 74 degrees Fahrenheit, and three meals a day with bottled water. It also requires hygiene supplies, clean bedding, medical staff on site and unmonitored calls to lawyers, Axios reports. Kaplan found that the rooms, built for stays of twelve hours or less, had held people far longer. The number of people held rose from fewer than ten to upward of a hundred between May and August 2025. He wrote that the building “essentially was a black site” before his earlier orders, Newsweek reports. The Department of Homeland Security has not said what it will do about this ruling, and had made no statement by 14.55 UTC on Friday. Its position when the first order was made in August 2025 was that “26 Federal Plaza is not a detention center” but a processing centre, ABC7 New York reported. The agency’s political defence has been made elsewhere and not about these rooms. Tom Homan told the first Attorney General’s Summit on Victims of Violent Crime on Thursday, addressing the reporters present: “We’re gonna keep pushing. We’re not gonna apologize. The media back there, you can hate us all you want, we’re not going anywhere,” The Hill reports.

Why is Canada’s Prime Minister talking about an American invasion?

Because he was asked, and chose to answer. The New York Times published the interview on Wednesday 23 September. Mark Carney said a leader has “a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk”. He called the exercise “just risk management” and “not a base case”, and said it would be irresponsible not to prepare, Global News reports. He would not say what had been prepared. His defence minister, David McGuinty, said on Thursday that it is normal and that “all militaries in the world spend time analyzing risk scenarios”, CP24 reports. The remark sits inside a wider turn. Carney told the paper Canada would cut its military and technological reliance on the United States, including Elon Musk’s Starlink service, and expand economic ties with China, CTV News reports. Not all Canadians think the candour helps. Peter MacKay, a Conservative former defence minister, called it counterproductive during tense negotiations.

Europe Intelligence Brief — Friday, 25 September 2026

The Gran Vía in Madrid. The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the flat her family had rented since 1956 has put an anti-eviction decree on the Spanish cabinet’s table for Tuesday. Photo: Felipe Gabaldón, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Europe Intelligence Dossier — Friday, 25 September 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web. Read the web dossier → · All Europe dossiers →

Spain — Shamed by one eviction, and legislating from it. Italy — Policing the classroom, and arguing with its own head of state. Poland — Rehearsing the worst without panic, and printing the instructions. Hungary — Rewarded for undoing old habits, and told the money is not yet in hand.

Europe’s mood on Friday was defensive and domestic. In Madrid, Rome and Warsaw the week’s hardest arguments were not about Russia or the euro but about who belongs in a flat, in a classroom and in a shelter.

The temper is not fear so much as boundary-drawing. Four governments moved this week to say who sits inside a protected circle, and each was at once asked by its own institutions to justify the line.

Spain found its boundary in a single photograph. Police carried an 87-year-old woman out of the Madrid flat her family had rented since 1956 on Wednesday, and by Friday the cabinet had a housing decree written for next week.

Italy drew its line through the school register. Its cabinet approved a decree on Thursday that turns a limit written as guidance in 2010 into a binding 30 per cent ceiling on pupils who do not know Italian well, and fines a covered face at the school gate.

Poland’s line is physical, and it published the map. The interior ministry issued a step-by-step guide on Friday to what a citizen should do when something comes out of the sky, counting 85,000 places to shelter for 23.7 million people.

Hungary’s is bureaucratic, and it is being paid for. The European Commission proposed on Wednesday to release €4.2 billion (about US$4.79 billion) it had withheld from Budapest since 2022, and the member governments have a month to agree.

Key Facts — Madrid’s evicted pensioner. María del Carmen Abascal, 87, was removed from the Madrid flat her family had rented since 1956 on Wednesday 23 September, the news site Spain in English reported. — Spain’s fivefold rent rise. Spain in English and The Local both put the new rent at €2,650 a month (about US$3,022) against about €500 (about US$570) before, more than five times as much. — Italy’s cap made binding. A 30 per cent limit on pupils who do not know Italian well has existed since a 2010 circular, and a decree of 24 September makes it binding, Il Post reported. — Italy’s face-covering fine. The decree sets a fine of €200 to €1,000 (about US$228 to US$1,140) for a covered face at school, and President Sergio Mattarella has still to sign it. — Poland’s shelter arithmetic. Poland has identified 85,000 shelter points for 23.7 million people, 64 per cent of the population, in guidance its interior ministry published on Friday. — Hungary’s unfrozen money. The European Commission proposed on 23 September releasing €4.2 billion (about US$4.79 billion) in regional aid to Hungary, which the Council must approve within a month. — Serbia’s published polling. A Faktor Plus survey put Aleksandar Vučić’s list at 48.6 per cent and the Student List at 37.1, with fieldwork from 16 to 20 September, the Bulgarian state agency BTA reported. — Germany’s fuel-tax cut. The Bundesrat approved a cut of 14.04 cents a litre in energy tax (about US$0.16) on 25 September, after the Bundestag passed it by 434 votes to 128.

Madrid Finds Its Face For A Housing Crisis

Spain has spent three days arguing with one photograph. Police carried María del Carmen Abascal, who is 87 and uses a wheelchair, out of a flat in Madrid’s Retiro district on Wednesday, the English-language site Spain in English reported.

Her family had held the flat since 1956 under one of Spain’s old controlled tenancies, which pass from parent to child. She was taken out on a stretcher and driven to hospital, and hundreds of people had gathered in the street to stop it.

What the landlord asked for is the figure that made the case national. Spain in English and The Local both put the new rent at €2,650 a month (about US$3,022) against about €500 (about US$570) before, which is more than five times as much.

One wire figure does not fit that base. Agence France-Presse, a French wire service, put the increase at 275 per cent and printed no euro amount, and that percentage does not reconcile with a move from €500 to €2,650 (about US$570 to US$3,022).

Her income sets the scale of what was demanded. Spain in English put her pension at about €1,400 a month (about US$1,596), roughly half the new rent.

The company rejects the label its critics use. Urbagestión Desarrollo e Inversión said it is neither an investment fund nor a vulture fund but “una sencilla pyme”, a simple small business, eldiario.es, a left-leaning Spanish news site, reported on 23 September.

It also denies the scale the word fund implies, saying “No somos propietarios de ninguna otra vivienda”. It owns no other home, on that account.

Abascal answered from her hospital bed at the Gregorio Marañón. In a video released by the Madrid tenants’ union and carried by eldiario.es on Friday she said: “No he logrado defender mi casa. Pero sí he luchado para que los demás aprendan a luchar por la suya”.

That is a defeat claimed as a lesson. She had not managed to defend her home, she said, but she had fought so that others learn to fight for theirs.

Her second line names the target rather than the landlord. She said in the same video: “Lo que quiero es que este problema con los fondos buitre se elimine de una vez”. What she wants is for this problem with vulture funds to be got rid of once and for all.

The row inside Spain is about who is to blame rather than who should be ashamed. Pedro Sánchez called the eviction an unacceptable “social tragedy” and blamed Madrid’s conservative-led city and regional governments, Agence France-Presse reported.

The housing minister pointed the same way. Isabel Rodríguez described Wednesday as a “sad and dramatic day” and called on Madrid’s regional president and the city’s mayor to act, The Local and Spain in English reported.

A centre-left daily refused to let the law off. El País wrote in an editorial: “The law was upheld and the market worked. But it is the law of the jungle in a broken market, and it is a failure”, in Agence France-Presse’s account.

The government’s answer is a decree it does not yet have the votes for. A moratorium on evicting people with no suitable alternative accommodation is expected to form part of a royal decree-law going to the cabinet on Tuesday 29 September.

The text is not settled. Spain in English reported that it is still under negotiation, and that the People’s Party has so far distanced itself from the talks.

The housing minister named the obstacle herself. The government can approve it, she said, but “without the support of the groups it will not become law”, in that site’s translation.

Its own partners want more than it is offering. Sumar, the left-wing junior party in the coalition, wants the flat compulsorily bought, and Yolanda Díaz, the second deputy prime minister and labour minister, called for “the expropriation of Maricarmen’s home and a package to freeze rents”.

The votes it needs come from two directions at once. Junts per Catalunya, a Catalan pro-independence party, has offered tax breaks for landlords, while Podemos, a party to the government’s left, will negotiate only if changes to land law are left out.

The right refuses the premise of the appeal. Cuca Gamarra of the conservative People’s Party was blunt on the public radio network RNE that the government cannot make anyone else responsible for its own lack of a housing policy, the Spanish political site Moncloa.com reported.

The leader of the opposition asks for the job rather than defends a record. Alberto Núñez Feijóo said on Friday, after closing his party foundation’s summer campus in Madrid, that the government has had eight years and has not been able to solve the problem, Moncloa.com reported.

He put his own claim in one clause. Feijóo asked for a chance to solve the housing problem, “yo pido una oportunidad para solucionar el problema de vivienda”, and said the government cannot hold anyone else responsible for its lack of a housing policy.

He also put a number on the scale of it. Feijóo said there were about 25,000 evictions in Spain last year, 11 per cent more than the year before, in the same account.

Madrid’s regional president answers with the chain of command. Isabel Díaz Ayuso noted that the eviction was carried out “por orden de un juez y con presencia de la Policía Nacional”, by order of a judge and with the National Police present, Moncloa.com reported.

Her point is about who writes the law. Ayuso said that whoever can change the rules governing these procedures is whoever has been in government for eight years: “Quien puede cambiar las leyes que regulan estos procedimientos es quien lleva ocho años en el Gobierno”.

The party’s other argument is that the decree would not have helped this tenant. Moncloa.com reported that the housing decree Congress rejected in March was aimed at tenancies governed by the urban rental law of 1994, and Abascal’s dated from 1956.

The same account carries the party’s measure of the market. It says the price of rent has accumulated an increase of 44 per cent.

Ayuso is blunter about the government’s response. She accused it of “demagoguery” and of “not doing anything” during Sánchez’s eight years in office, the same French wire service reported.

Separately she widened it into a quarrel about maps. Ara, a Catalan daily, reported her saying the case was one of the 25,000 evictions that happen every year, and that for every eviction in Madrid there are five in Catalonia.

The judicial figures in that report do not carry the ratio. Ara reported 25,540 evictions in 2025, of which 6,814 were in Catalonia and 2,267 in Madrid, which is about three to one rather than five to one.

Ara also carries what cuts the other way. It notes that Madrid has about a million fewer inhabitants than Catalonia and a median household income about 8 per cent higher.

The lawyer’s complaint is about the law and not the landlord. Beatriz Duro, who acts for Abascal, said there is no legal umbrella that enables the suspension of the eviction of vulnerable people, the same wire service reported.

The background numbers explain why one eviction became national. Average prices a square metre have risen about 50 per cent in ten years, in the same wire report.

The public alternative is very small. Spain’s stock of public housing is 1.2 per cent of the total on the figures of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, in the same wire report, carried by Courthouse News.

Money was offered and refused before the police came. An unnamed Spanish writer offered to pay the €2,150 difference (about US$2,452) for the rest of her life so that she could go on paying €500 (about US$570), and the company rejected it, Spain in English reported.

By Friday the company had moved twice, in opposite directions. It offered the flat to Madrid City Council so that the municipal housing company could let it back to her at a social or affordable rent through the council’s Reviva scheme, eldiario.es reported.

It also went to court against her supporters. Urbagestión is claiming €10,000 (about US$11,403) from the Sindicato de Inquilinas, the Madrid tenants’ union, for calling it a “fondo buitre”, a vulture fund, in the same account.

What steadies Spain is that the landlord has moved and the cabinet has a date. What could stop the law is arithmetic, because the text is still being negotiated, the People’s Party has so far stayed out of the talks, and an earlier housing decree was already voted down in March.

Rome Draws A Line Through The Classroom

Italy has made an old rule binding rather than written a new one. The 30 per cent limit was set by a circular of 2010 issued by the then education minister, Mariastella Gelmini, the Italian news site Il Post reported.

The decree-law approved on Thursday follows that circular closely. Il Post says it “lo ricalca quasi interamente”, traces it almost entirely, and that the difference is that the circular allowed exemptions and left schools their autonomy while the decree does not.

The same report doubts the effect, writing “Nei fatti però potrebbe cambiare poco”. In practice, it says, little may change.

The cap is narrower than it first sounds. It bites on the first class of each stage rather than on every classroom, and it counts pupils without an adequate school background rather than every foreign child, in that site’s account.

The penalties fall on adults. A covered face at school carries a fine of €200 to €1,000 (about US$228 to US$1,140), and the parents pay when the pupil is a minor, the Italian news agency ANSA reported.

The rule names what it means by a covered face. It takes in the burqa and the niqab, and a surgical mask worn by a pupil who is not ill, in the same account.

Parents are given homework too, and only some of them. The obligation to attend free Italian courses bites where the child does not know Italian and “anche la famiglia non conosce l’italiano”, the family does not know it either, ANSA reported.

Money follows the obligation. A fund of €17.5 million (about US$19.96 million) is set aside for schools that cannot meet the cap, in the same report.

How much of Italy this touches depends on what is counted, and both figures are the minister’s own. Giuseppe Valditara said at Palazzo Chigi that “sono 34mila le classi che hanno numero di stranieri che supera il 30%”, 34,000 classes in which foreign pupils exceed 30 per cent, ANSA reported.

He gave attainment as the reason for acting. Implicit dropout, meaning the failure to reach the expected competences, runs at 5.7 per cent for Italian pupils and 10 per cent for foreign ones, he said, in the same report.

That count is not the threshold the decree uses. Valditara said the new rule would touch about 1,000 classrooms, or 0.3 per cent of the total, Al Jazeera, the Qatari state-funded broadcaster, reported, because it reaches only first-year classes and only pupils without adequate prior schooling.

The ministry’s own background figures are modest. Non-citizen pupils were 11.2 per cent of Italy’s school population in 2022-23, and classes with more than 30 per cent foreign pupils were 7.6 per cent of the total, on education ministry data quoted by Al Jazeera.

The minister frames it as language rather than origin. Valditara said the objective is to put the Italian language at the centre as a great instrument of integration, and that knowing Italian means integrating, in quotations printed by ANSA.

He also drew a line against the past. Old circulars, he said, were only recommendations and had no binding force as a law does, ANSA reported, which is an answer to the charge that his own head of state once did the same thing more gently.

The prime minister put it as common sense. Giorgia Meloni wrote on her own account that the tools to learn Italian and to stop burqas and niqabs in schools were “common sense that do not divide”, that broadcaster reported.

She described the aim in the same post. It was, she wrote, “a school that integrates without giving up on rules”, in that outlet’s translation of her Italian.

The president had already said something else about schools. Sergio Mattarella, opening the school year at Amatrice, said the school is the most effective lever of integration for those who come from other countries, the same Italian news site reported.

He warned in the same speech against forming ghettos and raising barriers. Meloni replied that when Mattarella was education minister he wrote circulars urging that foreign pupils be spread out, in a television interview on 22 September quoted by that same site.

The unions call it a flag rather than a policy. Gianna Fracassi, general secretary of the left-leaning FLC CGIL teaching union, called it “l’ennesimo intervento propagandistico”, one more propaganda measure, in quotations printed by ANSA.

Her second objection is about what the decree leaves out. She said turning access to education into an ideological banner to chase easy electoral consent is a very grave act.

The union’s own priorities are elsewhere. The decree, she said, ignores the two decisive questions for those who work in schools, which are pay and job insecurity.

The head teachers doubt it can be done at all. Attilio Fratta, president of DirigentiScuola, the head teachers’ union, called it propagandistic and in the final analysis unrealisable, and said measures of this weight are not adopted once the school year has begun, ANSA reported.

A second body of principals accepts the problem and not the remedy. Antonello Giannelli, president of the National Association of Principals, said the issue is well-founded and valid from an educational point of view but difficult to turn into a practical solution, Al Jazeera reported.

The opposition reads it as a distraction. Elly Schlein, leader of the centre-left Democratic Party, called it “a shameful decree that seeks to hide the government’s inability to address the real problems of the public school system behind a new ideological banner”, in that account.

There is a party further to the right of Meloni’s nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy. The National Future party of the former general Roberto Vannacci, which campaigns for what it calls remigration, demanded a crackdown on burqas in schools in July, in the same report.

What steadies Rome is that a decree-law takes effect at once and the money is named. What could unpick it is that parliament has 60 days to ratify it and President Mattarella has still to sign it, Al Jazeera reported.

Warsaw’s old town. The interior ministry published guidance this week on what a citizen should do in an air attack, counting 85,000 places to shelter for 23.7 million people.

Warsaw Rehearses The Worst, Calmly

Poland spent Friday teaching itself a drill. Its interior ministry published guidance on where to take cover in an air attack and how to prepare a home, Notes From Poland, an English-language site covering Polish affairs, reported.

The guidance covers where a person happens to be. It sets out what to do if the sirens sound at home, at work, outdoors or in a car, in the same report.

The instructions are domestic and unglamorous. People are told to take an evacuation rucksack and their medicines, to use the stairs rather than the lift, and, if reaching a shelter would mean too long in the open, to stay in a central room without windows.

The state has also chosen how to deliver it. The guidance goes on ministry websites, out through the regional governors to local councils and into mObywatel, the Polish government’s own citizen app, the Polish security-affairs site infosecurity24.pl reported on Thursday.

A deputy minister described the point of it plainly. Magdalena Roguska called it “nowa część, którą dajemy mieszkańcom”, a new part that is being given to residents, and said the aim is that people should know in advance where it is safe to go, in the same account.

The scale of it is now counted. Poland has identified 85,000 shelter points able to hold 23.7 million people, which is 64 per cent of the population, and 17 million households were sent safety handbooks earlier this year, Notes From Poland reported.

The minister’s tone was deliberately flat. Marcin Kierwiński said: “When a threat arises, we warn the Polish people and defend our security. It is only natural that we prepare for worst-case scenarios, while deeply believing that they will never come to pass.”

He was careful about what does not yet exist. Evacuation plans are being prepared and lean heavily on the strength of the whole crisis-response system, he said, and the more that system is strengthened the more precise the plans become.

The foreign minister was blunter about the reason. Notes From Poland reported him saying that multiple sources suggested that “Russia is planning something big this year”, and that President Vladimir Putin may need a pretext for mobilisation, so Russia might carry out a false-flag attack.

The week gave that argument a small and precise illustration. A Russian Mi-8 military helicopter crossed from the Kaliningrad exclave into Polish airspace on Wednesday, about 350 yards deep and for 42 seconds, the American forces newspaper Stars and Stripes reported.

Where it happened is not in dispute. It was near Braniewo in the Warmia region, close to the Vistula Lagoon, at an altitude of 300 metres, Breitbart, a right-wing American news site, reported, and Polish fighter aircraft were sent up while ground units stood by.

Poland’s military read the flight as a test. Its operational command said fighter aircraft were scrambled and ground-based forces and assets remained on standby, and described the flight as meant to test the air-defence preparedness of NATO, the Western military alliance, Stars and Stripes reported.

The defence minister put it in a sequence. Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said: “These are not isolated incidents, but an element of constant pressure.”

The list behind that sentence is short and recent. Stars and Stripes recorded a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft intercepted about 30 miles off the Polish coast over the Baltic Sea.

Romania had its own alarm the following morning. It scrambled two F-16 fighter jets early on Thursday after an unidentified aerial target crossed into the country from Ukraine, its defence ministry said, in the same report.

Not everyone on that border reads it the same way. Stars and Stripes reported that some regional officials warned against unnecessary panic, and that Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, said on Wednesday there are no indications of a looming Russian attack on NATO.

His reason is what his own frontier looks like. “It’s empty on the other side of Estonia’s border because Russia’s troops are in Ukraine. Therefore, all the talk about Russia potentially attacking NATO soon is simply not supported by what we see on the ground”, he said.

The president is pressing a different answer, and it is American. Karol Nawrocki said in a Bloomberg interview on 22 September that “I think that this matter is for sure confirmed because President Trump is famous for keeping his word”, Notes From Poland reported.

Washington had made no formal confirmation of the base by 14.40 UTC on Friday. Mr Trump had said that “if this happens, the location [of the base] will be announced very soon”, Notes From Poland reported.

The cost is a floor, and it is Poland’s share. The deputy defence minister, Stanisław Wziątek, said it would “definitely be more than 15 billion zloty” (about US$3.91 billion) but would depend on the level of involvement of the United States, in the same report.

What steadies Poland is that the preparation is public and dull. What is unfinished is the physical part, because the shelters themselves are to be marked only by the end of 2026, Notes From Poland reported.

A Polish Legend Is Cleared, And Nobody Is Satisfied

The same country spent Friday closing a quarrel about its own founding story. Warsaw prosecutors discontinued the case against Lech Wałęsa, the shipyard electrician who led the Solidarity movement and became Poland’s first freely elected president, Notes From Poland reported.

The charge was about words, not about the past itself. He was accused of lying when he denied that documents said to show he had informed for the communist secret police were his, in the same report.

The file at the centre of it was found in a general’s house. Papers carrying Wałęsa’s apparent signature, including a commitment to collaborate, payslips and an informant’s notes, turned up in the home archive of Czesław Kiszczak, the communist interior minister, and Wałęsa has always said they were forged.

The prosecutors’ reason is technical, and it is about handwriting. They found methodological errors in the attribution and said there was no evidence to assume with 100 per cent certainty that the comparative material actually came from Lech Wałęsa, Notes From Poland reported.

Their second reason is harsher on him than an acquittal. The evidence, they said, clearly indicated that Wałęsa did not write long manuscripts during his life, and some witnesses explicitly stated that at that time he was a secondary illiterate.

The government treated the decision as a verdict on its predecessor. Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, said a politicised state apparatus hounded the legend of Solidarity, deliberately ignoring facts and basic logic, and that truth has triumphed over an attempt to rewrite history.

The historian who assembled the file rejects the reasoning. Sławomir Cenckiewicz, a former national security adviser, said he had never read a bigger lie, and asked how a secondary illiterate could have led Solidarity and then governed Poland, Notes From Poland reported.

Polish opinion on him has been less evenly split than the case. A 2017 poll found 62 per cent of Poles calling Wałęsa a national hero against 28 per cent who did not, Notes From Poland reported.

What steadies the matter is that a prosecutor, not a politician, ended it. What keeps it open is that the decision rests on a judgement about one man’s handwriting, and both sides read the same reasoning as proof of bad faith.

Budapest Is Paid For Its Conversion

Hungary is being rewarded for dismantling machinery it spent a decade building. The European Commission, the Union’s executive, proposed on Wednesday to unlock €4.2 billion (about US$4.79 billion) in regional aid frozen since 2022.

It would also reopen two programmes to Hungarian academics. Access to the Erasmus+ exchange and the Horizon Europe research programme would be restored for students and researchers from universities maintained by Hungarian Public Interest Trusts.

The change of government is the reason. Péter Magyar’s administration, which replaced Viktor Orbán’s after the April election, notified Brussels on 9 September of new rules on public procurement, asset declarations, conflicts of interest and judicial review of prosecutors’ decisions.

The Commission president chose careful praise. Ursula von der Leyen said: “Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the Union’s financial interests.”

Hungary also joined the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Union’s own fraud prosecutor. The Commission listed that beside stronger powers for Hungary’s Integrity Authority and tighter control of public procurement as the steps that changed its mind.

The money is not in Budapest’s hands. The Council of the European Union, where the member governments sit, must approve the proposal within a month, the Brussels agency Agence Europe reported, and EUobserver reported technical discussions set for 24 September and 1 October.

The Council had announced no decision by 14.40 UTC on Friday. Whether it will adopt the proposal unchanged is not yet known.

The wider sum explains the politics. Reuters reported that €16.4 billion (about US$18.70 billion) of recovery and regional money had been frozen, and that the Union said in May it would release it as Hungary passed its reforms.

Some of it has gone for good. Agence Europe, a Brussels agency, and Hungarian Conservative, a right-wing Hungarian magazine aligned with the former governing party, both record that about €2 billion (about US$2.28 billion) was lost permanently when deadlines expired.

Brussels was more cautious than Budapest when the outline deal was struck in May. A senior Commission official told POLITICO Brussels: “We haven’t agreed to disburse the funds. We’ve agreed on a list of commitments which, if completed by 31 Aug, will trigger the payment of those funds”, Hungarian Conservative reported on 30 May.

Budapest did complete them, which is why Wednesday happened. The Commission acted on 23 September, a fortnight after Hungary notified its remedies.

The Hungarian right’s objection is about the price rather than the paperwork. Viktor Orbán said of Mr Magyar in May: “We know this. What we do not know is what he promised in exchange”, in the same report.

He put it as concealment. It is time to stop the deception and honestly tell Hungarians what was handed over from Hungarian interests, he said then, and his party has not withdrawn the charge since.

Some money stays frozen for reasons the proposal does not touch. More than €530 million (about US$604.36 million) remains blocked over disputes on migration, asylum and questions concerning lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer people, Hungarian Conservative reported in May.

What steadies Budapest is that the conditions are written down and the Commission has signed them off. What could reverse it is that the mechanism which froze the money can freeze it again, and the Council has not yet voted.

Belgrade Votes While Its President Steps Aside

Serbia is running an election that a year of protest forced on it. Aleksandar Vučić dissolved the National Assembly on 9 September and called a parliamentary vote for 25 October, after more than a year of street protests led by students demanding exactly that, the Italian European-affairs outlet Eunews reported.

His stated reason was clarity. Serbia needs results that can clearly define and demonstrate the will of its citizens about the direction the country intends to follow, he said in a televised address, in that outlet’s account.

The president has put a date on his own departure. Vučić has announced that he will step down on Sunday 27 September, the Bulgarian state news agency BTA reported on Friday.

He spent Thursday evening in New York on other business. He said there that he had discussed energy agreements and the sale of Russia’s majority stake in the Serbian oil company NIS, and the work of Russian Railways in Serbia, in the same report.

The published polling describes a race he can still win. A survey by Faktor Plus taken from 16 to 20 September put the list headed by Vučić at 48.6 per cent and the Student List at 37.1, BTA reported on 21 September.

Both numbers moved, and the challengers moved faster. The president’s list gained 1.4 percentage points on the previous survey and the students gained 5.6, which BTA attributed in part to several opposition parties withdrawing from the race.

The pollster hedged in public. Vladimir Pejić, executive director of the Serbian polling firm Faktor Plus, said the campaign was heating up and the figures could change as it progressed.

He also read the governing party’s position as solid. It was retaining its electorate, he said, and could reach an absolute majority if conditions held, BTA reported.

He also intends to change jobs rather than leave politics. His party nominated him as its candidate for prime minister on 6 September, which would move him from the presidency to the office that governs, the Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.

Three opposition parties have cleared the field for the students. BTA reported the withdrawal from the race of the People’s Movement of Serbia, Ecological Uprising and New Face of Serbia, which consolidated the opposition vote.

No statement from the Student List had been published in English by 14.40 UTC on Friday. What steadies Belgrade is that a date now exists where a year of protest had produced none, and what unsettles it is that the man who set the date leaves the presidency on Sunday.
