World.title: Azerbaijani boxers finish European Championship with record medal haul
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 25. Another Azerbaijani boxer has become European champion. Following Subhan Mammadov (50 kg), Saidjamshid Jafarov also won the gold medal at the tournament as part of the Azerbaijani team.

This was reported by the Azerbaijan Boxing Federation.

According to the information, the national team representative, competing in the 75 kg weight category, defeated Ismail Mutsolgov (Russia) 5:0 in the final (29:28, 29:28, 29:28, 29:28, 29:28).

Thus, the Azerbaijan national team finished the European Championship, which featured 406 boxers from 43 countries, with a record haul of five medals. The team led by head coach Ravshan Khojayev won two gold, one silver and two bronze medals.

It should be noted that before Jafarov, Subhan Mammadov (50 kg) also reached the top step of the podium at the European Championship. Nabi Iskenderov (70 kg) won the silver medal, while Amin Mammadzade (55 kg) and Mahammad Abdullayev (+90 kg) claimed bronze medals.

World.title: How the Dockers went from perpetual underdogs to top of the game
World.content:
It's a Dockers dream 32 years in the making — Fremantle are just one win away from premiership glory.

To their fans, the Dockers are the perpetual underdogs, a team that — according to historian Les Everett — was started to "dilute the West Coast Eagles".

Victorian clubs feared the Eagles were "getting too powerful" following their 1991 grand final appearance and premierships in 1992 and 1994.

There were many names put forward for Western Australia's second team, all with links to the port and sea, including the Pirates, Pelicans, Sharks, Dolphins and even the Doctors after Perth's famous sea breeze, the Fremantle Doctor.

The Dockers joined the competition in 1995, with futuristic purple footy shorts that were the "roomiest shorts in the AFL" compared to the tight fits of the 1980s.

Fremantle played their first AFL game in April 1995, taking on the Richmond Tigers at the MCG. (Supplied: Fremantle Football Club )

The purple origin

Coach Gerard Neesham paraded the team on the Fremantle Cappuccino Strip, telling reporters at the time "one of our briefs was to be innovative and we have definitely been that."

It was future thinking, with a nod to the past: the purple was inspired by the woollen hats historically worn by port workers, while the red and green colours on the kit came from the maritime signals for port and starboard.

The Dockers' identity is steeped in the maritime history of Fremantle and its dock workers, nicknamed wharfies. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

On the docks of Fremantle, wharfies still wear those purple beanies but in 2026, they have club logos.

As for the spirit of Wharfie Time, "it's passion, resilience and having that fight to never give up," said wharfie Jenson Chattaway.

"There will be tears if we win, I'll be crying for sure," added Port Services Officer Mike White.

Wharfies, including Jenson Chattaway (second from left) and Mike White (second from right), show their support for the Dockers. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Frustration forging greats

The early years were tough, with very little in the way of funding. The football club instead relied on 1000 donations of $1,000 each from their original fan group, the Harbour Masters.

Fremantle and West Coast quickly became fierce rivals. (Getty Images: Mandatory Credit: ALLSPORT/Tony McDonough)

But finally purple reigned in 1999. The club won its first game at the hallowed MCG and its first Western Derby, officially stepping out of the Eagles' shadow.

"In round 10, 1999, one of the Victorian newspapers said Melbourne only had to turn up to win the game at the MCG," historian Everett said.

"Fremantle played brilliantly, Tony Modra kicked 10 goals.

" The first derby win the same year was important, after losing the first nine to the Eagles, it was just a great relief really after being trapped as the little sibling to the Eagles. "

A year later, in 2000, Matthew Pavalich joined the Dockers. Through his career, he kicked 700 goals and as captain he took the team to its first decider in 2013.

Matthew Pavlich (centre) leads his teammates onto the MCG for the AFL grand final in 2013. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The famous all-rounder played alongside dual Brownlow Medal winner Nathan Fyfe. But it was not to be, and the Hawks shattered the Dockers' premiership dream by 15 points.

Fremantle lost to Hawthorn in the 2013 grand final. (AAP Image: David Crosling)

Daring to dream again

A new generation of players has taken the Dockers to the decider once again, and for Mr Everett, this is best team Fremantle has ever fielded.

Justin Longmuir's Dockers won the minor premiership and are now seeking their first flag. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"There is something about the way this team operates, there is a connection that makes it better than any team before," he said.

"It's been organically grown — it doesn't have any father-son gifts in it. Forged through good drafting, good trading, good development.

" That's been the story of Fremantle right from the start, it has been left to its own devices and if it wins the premiership it has done so itself. "

Even before the game began, the town was painted purple, and the team immortalised with a massive mural.

WA artist Jerome Davenport is painting the mural on the facade of Sailing for Oranges on the Cappuccino strip. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

But the players will achieve living legend status if they can take home the club's first ever premiership flag.

"If we do win it, I'll be watching the game again, again and again. I'll know every minute of it," Mr Everett said.

" Fremantle supporters, we've put ourselves through some misery, but I have never called myself a long-suffering Fremantle supporter, I have loved it. "

World.title: AI data centre company starts development work without a permit
World.content:
AI infrastructure company Firmus Technologies appears to have conducted illegal work at its site in north-west Tasmania, a local council says.

Firmus submitted a development application to build a 52-megawatt AI data centre in Wesley Vale at the old paper mill site, but Latrobe Council has deferred making a decision — instead asking the Tasmanian government to assess it as a major project.

But now, it seems Firmus has begun work without a permit.

"We're concerned that some of the works may be occurring beyond the scope of the approved forest practices plan for the site," Latrobe Mayor Peter Freshney said.

"If it's outside of that then there'll be stop work issued," he said.

Peter Freshney says Firmus has agreed to stop work while council conducts further assessments. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden)

He said Firmus had agreed to cease work while council conducted further assessments.

"We're seeking to understand and confirm whether or not that work is illegal," he said.

Cr Freshney said the approved forest practices plan allowed activities such as tree felling, stump removal, mulching and weed suppression.

"What we're seeing now though, I would suggest, is excavation to an extent that is not within the approved plan," he said.

Firmus is building two other AI data centres in Tasmania — in Launceston and Long Reach, in the state's north. (Supplied: Firmus Technologies)

Cr Freshney said there were transportable buildings, piles of dirt and blue metal on site.

In a statement, a Firmus spokesperson said the works were part of general site maintenance, separate from the development application.

"These activities do not require planning approval and will take approximately four weeks to complete," the spokesperson said.

" No main works associated with the broader projects will commence until all required approvals are in place. "

Issue causing 'further angst' in community

Cr Freshney said Firmus had committed in writing to working with the council.

"I suggest undertaking work without permits isn't consistent with that written commitment," he said.

"We will make this a priority and we expect the proponent to work with us to put this to bed and to ensure our community and our councils are respected and the processes are adhered to.

"This issue has now caused even further angst in our community, which is detrimental to community health and wellbeing, but also concerns held more broadly around data centres, evolving technologies and the like.

" Proponents more broadly need to be working with planning authorities and local government. "

Tabatha Badger praised Latrobe Council for "following proper process and intervening". (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Greens MP Tabatha Badger praised the council for intervening.

"Despite the lack of AI infrastructure guardrails, there are still laws in the state that must be complied with," she said.

"If Firmus is indeed pushing ahead at Wesley Vale before having the right approvals, what else will they get up to?

"Do Firmus think just because they sponsored the Tassie Devils they can get a free kick?"

Planning minister considering major project request

Councils and residents have raised concerns that the planning framework does not allow councils to adequately assess AI data centres.

In coming to a decision about Firmus's 288-megawatt facility at Long Reach in northern Tasmania, George Town Council's planners told residents their concerns about issues such as power and water use fell outside of its scope.

Those limitations led Latrobe Council to ask Planning Minister Kerry Vincent to consider assessing the Wesley Vale proposal as a major project.

Latrobe Council has asked the state government to assess the Wesley Vale proposal as a major project. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Premier Jeremy Rockliff has previously rejected the idea, stating the current planning process was adequate.

But residents in the Wesley Vale area this month received a letter from Planning Minister Kerry Vincent stating he was considering the request.

"As the proposal was referred from the Latrobe Council and not the proponent, Firmus Technologies, there is still further information to be provided before I can further consult with you on this matter," he wrote to residents.

"After a complete major project proposal has been provided to government, further consultation will occur, including providing you with a copy of that major project proposal and allowing 28 days to provide any comments."

Firmus announced last week it wanted to build a research and development facility at Wesley Vale, which would go through a separate approval process to the proposed AI data centre.

"The facility will be used to test new battery energy storage and power management technologies, with a particular focus on reducing reliance on conventional diesel backup generation," the company said in a statement.

World.title: Mason Cox chases second premiership after his AFL career was all but over
World.content:
Mason Cox still remembers arriving at the MCG for his first AFL grand final back in 2018.

"I took an Uber to the grand final and it ended up being like a Toyota Prius. So I was stuffed in the back of that, which is real humbling to start off the day," he said.

It may have been a humbling experience for the 211-centimetre American, but it was also not his last on the AFL's biggest day.

He returned in 2023 as the Magpies won the flag for the first time since 2010, and he will be back there again today, in what is a remarkable turn of events for the veteran.

Cox became a cult hero after winning an AFL premiership with Collingwood in 2023. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

In October last year he was delisted by Collingwood after 139 games, and at age 34, it appeared his remarkable career, which saw him plucked out of the United States and arrive at one of the biggest clubs in the land, was over.

But a month later, a lifeline came his way.

From disaster to destiny, it's taken a decade to rebuild the Dockers Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers, who crashed and burned in 2016 and are now on the cusp of winning their first-ever premiership 10 years later.

"It wasn't like I had a huge selection of people chasing after me once it all kind of happened and transpired with Collingwood," Cox said.

"I think Fremantle have been trying to get me for [a while], this is probably the third time they tried to get me."

Door opens in Dockers line-up

Cox arrived very much as backup for the established ruck pairing of Luke Jackson and Sean Darcy, before he found himself in the mix for a game.

Luke Jackson (centre) and Cox were once opponents but now make up Fremantle's ruck duo. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

Darcy missed the round six western derby due to concussion, opening the door for the American.

He took the opportunity with both hands, going on to play 19 of the next 21 games and becoming a constant in Justin Longmuir's side.

"Being an older guy, I was probably more relying on a bit of experience and just kind of seeing where the chips fall," Cox said of his expectations going into the season.

Cox kicked the go-ahead goal in last week's win over Sydney as the Dockers grabbed a grand final berth. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"At the end of the day, some things have to go your way and sometimes some things don't go your way.

"Over 12 years I think I've been playing now, I've kind of gotten used to that a bit."

Cox praises talent, 'big dogs'

While Cox admitted he was not batting away offers to play on, the culture at Fremantle still impressed him.

"Day one of getting here, just seeing how hard they work and they're a young team and they've got a lot of talent," he said.

" I thought this was the best list in the comp. "

Beyond the talented playing list, which saw the Dockers finish as minor premiers with a club-record 19 wins, including a streak of 14 straight, Cox became aware of the history of the club, which struggled in the early years and is yet to taste the ultimate glory.

For Cox, it is Fremantle's culture that made an early impression on him. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"A lot of us are understanding of just how much we're in this situation because of the people that came before us," he said.

"You talk about the big dogs before us that have set this club up to be where it's at, and the fans and supporters have kind of supported them through thick and thin.

What keeps Fremantle's purple army going? After the club's long struggle for success and on the cusp of what might be a maiden flag, Fremantle supporters reflect on why they keep coming back for more.

"We understand that we don't exist and we don't get to this position without them, and I think that's a real kind of thought process for a lot of the guys on the team.

"I think they kind of realise just how big of a deal it is for not only us but everyone around us, and then who's been able to kind of get us to this position."

If Fremantle beats Brisbane, Cox will become part of an immortal Dockers team, and will join the small list of players to have won AFL premierships at two different clubs.

Remarkable from the most unlikely of AFL players.

World.title: Domestic violence perpetrators are going undetected. Here's why
World.content:
A horror week of five suspected domestic violence deaths has exposed a key gap in the system: if the offender isn't known to police, who is meant to spot them?

Four people, including three women and a child, were killed in suspected domestic violence attacks in New South Wales in the space of 24 hours last weekend.

Police said none of the alleged offenders were known to them.

By Thursday, that number had climbed to five, after a one-year-old stabbed in the Blue Mountains died in hospital.

The deaths have raised questions about how authorities can act when alleged offenders aren't on the police's radar.

Two children have now died as a result of a stabbing in the Blue Mountains. (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

The latest Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR) results show more than 38,800 domestic violence-related assaults in the 12 months to June 26, up 3.4 per cent over the past decade.

Domestic Violence Death Review Team data shows that since 2000, 351 women, 230 men and 137 children have been killed in domestic violence-related homicides in NSW.

But police can't investigate what isn't reported. So how do you intervene when no-one knows there's a problem?

What happened last week? A mother allegedly stabbed three children in the Blue Mountains, killing a five-year-old boy. A one-year-old later died in hospital. She is facing two murder charges. Sergei Mitnik allegedly stabbed his grandmother, 90, in her Bondi Beach home. Phillip John Denton allegedly killed his mother at Mole River, in the Northern Tablelands. And Adam Mark Perrim, 31, allegedly stabbed his domestic partner, aged 23, at Kooringal in Wagga Wagga.

Why aren't police aware of DV offenders?

Despite improvements in recent years, under-reporting of domestic violence is still rife.

The 2021-23 Domestic Violence Death Review found half the men who killed a female partner had a history of using DV that had never been reported to police.

Macquarie University criminologist and former police detective Vince Hurley believes the number of offenders unknown to police is much higher.

"This notion that police always know who the offender is, is a bit of a misconception," he said.

"I would say probably 75 per cent, if not more, of domestic violence offenders are not known by police."

Macquarie University criminologist Vince Hurley is a former police negotiator. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

Dr Hurley said that information may be recorded by other agencies but not shared with police.

"It might be known to health officials, such as hospitals or GPs, but that information is not necessarily passed on to police because of privacy regulations.

"It's impossible to police what you don't know."

As part of Dr Hurley's research into domestic violence, he has reviewed hundreds of cases, with three key underlying issues identified: alcohol, drugs and mental health.

He said untreated mental health conditions could contribute to offending, and services were often out of reach.

"Most people who are wealthy might be able to afford to make a psychologist appointment and pay $300 an hour," he said.

"But for the bulk of the population, particularly in low socio-economic demographics, that is just not an option to them."

It is not known if mental health played a role in any of the deaths last weekend.

NSW Mental Health Minister Rose Jackson said it was important to distinguish between antisocial behaviour and people suffering from mental ill health.

"Failing to do so may inadvertently diminish the personal responsibility of those who perpetrate violence. It also risks unfairly stigmatising people living with genuine mental ill health," she said.

Rose Jackson says a distinction needs to be made between antisocial behaviour and mental ill health. (ABC News: Warwick Ford)

What's missing from the DV response?

Spotting the signs early and intervening is key to stopping domestic violence before it escalates, according to national peak body No to Violence.

But the body said that isn't where the funding is going.

General manager Chris Lacey said just 3.6 per cent of national domestic violence funding was spent on early intervention.

He said the system was heavily focused on helping victim survivors, but it should also invest in engaging men earlier.

The response to domestic and family violence is split into two areas — prevention and response.

Mr Lacey said there was a big gap in between, with very few early intervention programs on offer.

"That's the space where we need to be stepping into," he said.

"When someone at a hospital has a man present and they can identify that this man is at risk of committing or being violent, that there is a referral pathway directly from there for that man to get to tap in to services.

"At the moment, those services are very hard to find and very hard to get into.

" We need to be filling that massive gap. "

What are the warning signs?

The NSW Domestic Violence Death Review Team, which analysed more than 20 years of domestic violence homicides in a report tabled in parliament in 2024, found two in three women killed were killed by an ex-partner or at the point of separating from their partner.

The same report found three-quarters of the men who killed a female partner had used three or more different types of domestic violence against her during the relationship, behaviour that is often controlling rather than physical.

Coercive control became a criminal offence in NSW in July 2024.

According to BOCSAR's latest coercive-control data, police have recorded 682 incidents since the offence was criminalised, and 42 charges have been laid.

The report found nearly half the victims (47 per cent) had a prior history of domestic violence recorded by police, and 31 per cent had previously experienced domestic violence involving the same alleged offender.

Chris Lacey says there is a significant shortfall in funding for early intervention. (Supplied: No to Violence)

Mr Lacey said early warning signs of escalating behaviours can emerge during visits to a GP, hospital or other services.

"There are signs around drinking heavily, or going through a major life event, which can put more pressures on them," he said.

"That is generally a critical opportunity to identify the risk that exists and try to intervene before it escalates."

He said men who recognised those patterns in themselves could act on them.

"It's up to us as men to seek that help when we feel we need it, that is really important," he said.

Dr Hurley said families were often the first to notice something was wrong, but noticing was not the same as being able to fix it.

"It's OK for members of the family to look at the nuanced behaviour of members having a mental health episode, but that isn't easily equated into solving the problem," he said.

How do we break down those barriers?

Last weekend's deaths have renewed calls to look beyond the crisis response.

Getting various government departments talking to each other is a key part of the solution, according to Domestic Violence NSW CEO Delia Donovan.

"We need to make sure anyone responding to anyone impacted by domestic violence … really understands the nuance of domestic and family violence and it has to sit within every organisation's work plan," she said.

Delia Donovan wants government departments talking to each other. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

For Ms Donovan, this includes sporting codes, schools, corporate businesses and early childhood centres.

"We still don't have a society that really understands domestic and family violence, and we still have a society that victim-blames," she said.

" Until we can all look inwardly, government top-down, all the way through to community, we won't change this. "

Ms Donovan said there had been 52 women killed this year and without proper resourcing, "we're not going to touch the sides of it".

World.title: A new love, an old obsession and the final weeks of Jesse Baird's life
World.content:
The memory of being sent a photo from her son, Jesse, at a concert with a message that Luke Davies was now his boyfriend in early 2024 is a memory that causes Helen Baird's eyes to well up.

The two were "smitten" with each other, from her observations during a visit home to Melbourne weeks earlier.

At that point it was "early days" and they were "great together", she told the NSW Supreme Court this week.

" I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'. "

The mother of Jesse Baird told the court the pair were "smitten" with each other. (Instagram)

She was very close with Mr Baird and they spoke frequently, including about his personal life and relationships.

She recalled him expressing concern to her in 2023 about a person he had been somewhat romantically linked to, who Mr Baird believed was becoming obsessive.

Family and domestic violence support services: NSW Domestic Violence Line on 1800 656 463

Lifeline on 131 114

Men's Referral Service on 1300 766 491

Mensline on 1300 789 978

Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578

Emergency services on Triple Zero (000) if you need immediate care

Beau Lamarre-Condon would go through his phone and delete contacts, the court heard, and Mr Baird told his mum that in late 2023, he had told the then-NSW Police officer he did not want to see him again.

Not long after Ms Baird received the concert photo, Mr Baird and Mr Davies were allegedly murdered by Mr Lamarre-Condon with the officer's service pistol inside Mr Baird's Paddington terrace, in Sydney's east.

Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and lawyers intend to argue, during the trial, that it was a case of self-defence involving two separate struggles with the gun.

On the prosecution's case, the now-31-year-old's "obsessive and jealous infatuation" with Mr Baird spanned months, despite Mr Baird's belief that what happened between them was casual.

Mr Baird was close to his mother, Helen, and they spoke frequently. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

'I never heard him so scared'

During an opening address, Crown Prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC outlined a series of escalating behaviours, including monitoring Mr Baird's relationships and interfering with his phone and Instagram account.

Mr Hatfield alleged Mr Baird was stalked and his home broken into by the defendant "at least" twice.

Several of Mr Baird's friends gave evidence that he had expressed concern to them and sought advice.

According to Corey Dean Thorpe, Mr Baird's previous long-term partner, the television presenter was "petrified".

"I woke up at 11:30 last night to a guy standing over my bed, he stole my phone and wallet," Mr Baird told his ex in an August 2023 message.

"I was fast asleep. It was so weird, I sensed someone was there."

The Crown says that person was Mr Lamarre-Condon, who used a stolen or secretly-obtained key before jamming a bobby pin into a lock to make it look like it was picked.

The Crown says Mr Lamarre-Condon put a bobby pin into a lock to make it look like it was picked. (Supplied)

Mr Lamarre-Condon's defence counsel told jurors he had a key provided by Mr Baird. He denies a charge of aggravated break-and-enter over the incident.

In a November 2023 phone conversation with Mr Thorpe, Mr Baird spoke about the defendant using social media to give the impression they were together, the court was told.

"I've never heard him so scared in his voice before," Mr Thorpe testified.

"He just kept repeating, 'He has a gun'."

Mr Thorpe told the jury his former partner, Mr Baird, appeared "petrified". (ABC News: Monish Nand)

'I'm not going to stand for it anymore'

Mr Baird's decision to firmly break things off that month, according to the Crown opening, in part related to an Instagram "close friends" story showing a bouquet of flowers posted by Mr Lamarre-Condon.

"When he's in Melbourne but still sends you these…" read the caption.

The court heard when Mr Baird confronted the accused in a message about the post, Mr Lamarre-Condon said they were from someone else to his mother, Coleen.

The jury saw a photograph of Coleen Lamarre with a bunch of flowers, which the defendant sent to a friend he was asking advice from.

The court was told that Mr Lamarre-Condon said a post of a bouquet of flowers were from someone else to his mother, Coleen. (Supplied)

The Crown says the defendant had rushed to a florist, asked them to replicate the bouquet in a picture from the internet that he had posted, and lied about it being a misunderstanding.

On the Crown's case, Mr Lamarre-Condon would use Instagram's "close friends" feature, which allows users to limit visibility to specific accounts, to target perceived romantic rivals and give the impression Mr Baird was unavailable.

In a message seen by jurors, Mr Baird told Mr Lamarre-Condon there were examples of him acting "in a way that's completely inappropriate".

"I'm not going to stand for it anymore," Mr Baird wrote, requesting they part ways with no further contact.

Mr Baird told Mr Lamarre-Condon in messages there were examples of him acting "in a way that's completely inappropriate". (Supplied: Rocco Fazzari)

Rubina Shrestha, a PCYC colleague of Mr Lamarre-Condon, told the court he had spoken to her about his use of the "close friends" function to ward off people he thought were close to Mr Baird.

One was a man from Canberra, another was a young dancer who casually dated Mr Baird, she recalled.

Asked whether she "discouraged" her colleague's actions, she recalled her response to him: "That's crazy. He said, 'It works'."

Accused has done 'stupid things' but was self defence

The evidence in the first week of the trial, which is expected to run for up to three months, has largely focused on what Mr Baird told relatives, friends and colleagues about Mr Lamarre-Condon, and things the accused said to his friends or colleagues about Mr Baird.

Double murder-accused acted in 'self defence' Former Sydney police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon will argue he acted in self defence on the day he is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, a jury has been told.

Defence counsel John Stratton SC has urged jurors not to reach final conclusions until they have heard all of the evidence.

In his opening address, Mr Stratton said his client had done some "stupid things" like looking through Mr Baird's phone, deleting contacts of other men and wiping text messages.

He flagged a self-defence case in relation to the events of February 19, 2024.

Mr Stratton said he did not anticipate any evidence of any threats from the accused, who admits entering the Paddington terrace.

According to the opening address, the defence will argue Mr Lamarre-Condon, who was "very upset" about the final break up, went there to retrieve possessions.

He disguised himself as an Uber Eats driver because he did not expect anyone to be home, but if they were he would be able to "masquerade" as a delivery person, the jurors heard.

Loading...

Inside, Mr Stratton said his client was "surprised" by Mr Baird, who failed to recognise him due to a helmet he was wearing.

The barrister said it was his client's case that there was a struggle involving the police pistol which Mr Lamarre-Condon was carrying because his training prohibited it being left unattended in vehicles.

The gun went off twice and fatally wounded Mr Baird, according to the defence case, and the weapon was "flung" into the lounge room before Mr Lamarre-Condon called Triple Zero (000) from a mobile phone.

It is the accused's case that as he started moving to the door, he encountered Mr Davies and in a second struggle also involving the gun, Mr Davies fatally shot himself.

The two deaths were "a tragedy", Mr Stratton said.

14,000 hours of CCTV tracks accused's movements

The Crown has foreshadowed evidence about what it says was Mr Lamarre-Condon's alleged planning to murder Mr Baird.

According to the lead investigator, police obtained some 14,000 hours of CCTV footage showing his movements, including at a gun safe at a police station and stopping at ATMs.

On the morning of February 19, he used a hire car, activated a burner phone, and waited near the property for three hours until two housemates had left, the Crown said.

CCTV footage shows Mr Lamarre-Condon at a gun safe at a police station. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

The planning is also alleged to have included the cash purchase of a surfboard bag days prior, which prosecutors allege he intended to use to dispose of a body.

In CCTV of a sports store, Mr Lamarre-Condon is seen holding up a surfboard bag next to a friend.

The Crown anticipates evidence from that friend that the defendant asked whether he would fit inside.

It is alleged when the friend said "No", Mr Lamarre-Condon replied: "I'll grab this one instead, it should be big enough."

Loading...

In CCTV footage from another Brown Street home, the sound of three gunshots echoed through the neighbourhood that morning; the first two were four seconds apart, the third, about 50 seconds later.

The Crown alleges Mr Baird was murdered with the first two shots. Mr Hatfield described the second as an "execution-style" shot.

The Crown's case is that Mr Davies was allegedly murdered with a shot through a bedroom door as he called Triple Zero to ensure there was not a witness to Mr Baird's alleged murder.

Mr Hatfield told jurors the defendant immediately began to clean the crime scene — a process "complicated" by the presence of two bodies instead of one.

The court heard Mr Lamarre-Condon made multiple trips to Bunnings for items initially including gloves, double-sided tape, cleaning cloths, cable ties, garbage bags and bleach.

He is alleged to have left the couple's bodies in surfboard bags in the courtyard, where a housemate thought a red substance staining the ground underneath was rust.

The court was told Mr Lamarre-Condon made multiple trips to Bunnings. (Supplied: NSW Supreme Court)

According to the Crown's case, the then-senior constable returned to the property in a hire van and travelled with a witness to a farm known to him, near Goulburn.

There, it is alleged he unsuccessfully attempted to sink the victims' bodies in a dam using quick-set cement and weights with the surfboard bags as the witness was left waiting near the entrance gate.

The young men's bodies were found eight days after the alleged murders at a fence line near a monastery, about 20 kilometres away. The Crown says Mr Lamarre-Condon had returned alone to relocate them.

The defence team will argue Mr Lamarre-Condon's actions after the events in Brown Street, including the cleaning, were those of a panicked man who "knew the gravity" of the situation and how it looked.

He dumped bloodied items and personal possessions of the couple in a skip bin at Cronulla, which were discovered by a grounds keeper and prompted the police investigation, the Crown says.

Mr Edwards described the couple as the "real deal". (ABC News: Monish Nand)

Mr Baird's friend, Matthew Edwards, recalled seeing Mr Baird in February 2024, when his new relationship was solidifying.

He had never seen his friend happier, he told the court, and there was something about Mr Davies that "just lit Jesse up".

" They were the real deal. "

Mr Baird's sister, Kourtnee Baird, told the court she had heard her brother speak about his fear of Mr Lamarre-Condon and his job meaning he had access to a gun.

During her evidence, she was also asked if she ever met Mr Davies.

"No, I didn't," she replied, with a gentle smile.

"I wish I did."

World.title: Caged egg rule change delayed in Victoria due to spread of bird flu
World.content:
The Victorian government has delayed the imposition of stricter regulations on egg and poultry production because of the H5N1 bird flu outbreak.

In April the government announced it would legislate new poultry welfare standards as part of a plan to ban conventional laying cages by 2036.

Tougher rules for new cages were set to be implemented by the middle of this year, but this week the government said the changes would be pushed back until the middle of 2027.

Victorian Agriculture Minister Michaela Settle said the 12-month delay would allow producers "more time to prepare for new poultry welfare regulations" amid the bird flu outbreak.

“With H5 bird flu in Australia, poultry producers need to be able immediately focus on preparing for the disease,” she said.

Brian Ahmed says the delay gives farmers and the government more time to discuss the welfare changes. (Landline: Tim Lee)

Farmers 'never consulted' on changes

Victorian Farmers Federation egg group president and caged egg producer Brian Ahmed welcomed the move.

"We've had no input into these new regulations," he said.

"There's a lot of stuff in those documents that farmers have never been consulted with and have never agreed to."

The regulations were designed to align with national welfare standards agreed to in 2023.

Mr Ahmed said the delay gave farmers and the government more time to debate the issue.

"We're not going to get rid of a farming system that we believe is positive for our birds and our animals," Mr Ahmed said.

"[The government] had an ideological view that we need to get rid of cages and that's all they've stuck to."

Michaela Settle says poultry producers need to focus on preparing for bird flu. (ABC News)

The government said the decision to delay did not affect its commitment to phase out conventional unfurnished cages by 2036.

“These changes are about ensuring farmers, industry and government can focus on preventing H5 bird flu from entering the sector while developing new animal welfare standards that protect the wellbeing of poultry,” Ms Settle said.

The delay also means the changes will not come into effect until after the state election in November.

"As farmers, we're going to dig our heels in and if we have to fight this, we will," Mr Ahmed said.

Poultry producers in Victoria's south have been ordered to keep their birds indoors until at least the middle of October. (Supplied: Providore Farm)

Southern poultry housing order extended

Victoria has recorded nearly 200 H5 bird flu events since the first confirmed case in Portland in July.

In early August, poultry producers in southern Victoria were ordered to house their birds inside.

The lockdown has been extended several times and is now in place until the middle of October.

Poultry producers in southern and coastal Victorian regions with flocks of 50 or more are required to confine their birds to prevent contact with wild animals.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission gives producers 90 days to change their free range labelling, after a lockdown is announced.

World.title: How young officer's brief interaction left 'big impression' on Sydney local
World.content:
An inner-Sydney resident only had a brief interaction with a young officer who was killed in a police car crash on Friday, but the local said the female constable left a lasting impression.

Twenty-year-old Constable Mia Lay was in the passenger seat of a marked police vehicle, responding to reports of a car theft, when it crashed into a tree in Redfern in the early hours of Friday morning.

The young officer, who was only 16 months into her policing career, died in the collision.

The driver, a 24-year-old male constable, suffered leg and head injuries and was taken to Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in a stable condition.

In the hours after the incident, Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon paid tribute to Constable Lay and described her as a "promising" officer who was "loved" within the South Sydney Police Area Command.

Mal Lanyon said Mia Lay showed exceptional promise as a police officer. (ABC News: Ethan Rix )

Redfern resident Tim Cochran said that was exactly the type of officer he encountered when he called for assistance earlier this year.

Mr Cochran told the ABC he noticed an unresponsive man lying in the park in January this year and when he called Triple Zero (000), Constable Lay was at the scene within minutes.

"I just remember thinking to myself how confident and capable this young woman was," he said.

"And here I am, like [a] middle-aged dude with really no clue how to help this man.

"She was answering all the [emergency operator's] questions that I couldn't answer, and doing all the things to make sure that this guy was OK."

Mr Cochran said the man gradually became responsive with the help of the young officer and that she waited patiently with the man as an ambulance arrived.

Tim Cochran remembered Constable Lay fondly. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

He said in an area, where some residents have a "strained relationship" with police, he felt like the female constable made his community "better".

"I just remember feeling very thankful to have somebody like that in my community who is literally seconds away," Mr Cochran said.

"She left a really big impression on me that day for those things and because of that, I never forgot her.

" When I saw her picture this morning on Facebook … it was just like gut punch. "

Tragedy ahead of force's remembrance day

Constable Lay's death comes as officers around the country prepare for Police Remembrance Day next week.

The 20-year-old had returned from a holiday just last week with her partner, who is also a member of the force.

The pair had been stationed together when she had a brief stint at the Eastern Beaches Police Area Command.

The young constable's death sent shockwaves through the force. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

Her auntie also works for NSW Police State Crime and was described as a "mentor" figure for her niece.

"I guess she left that kind of impression on me as just a complete stranger," Mr Cochran said.

"I just can't imagine the impact that this woman would have had on the people in her life."

A critical incident investigation into the circumstances of the fatal crash remained underway.

At a press conference on Friday, Commissioner Lanyon said the investigation was still in its infancy.

"When officers are actually travelling on urgent duty, when they have lights and sirens on, they are exempt under the Australian road rules so they can exceed the speed limit," he said

"But we need to understand the circumstances and as the commissioner, what I'm keen to do is make sure our officers are as safe as possible."

World.title: Push to stop girls having to suffer pelvic pain in silence
World.content:
Endometriosis can be excruciatingly painful for the about one in seven Australian girls and women with the condition.

For teenagers dealing with changing bodies and raging hormones, it can be difficult to identify symptoms of the disease.

Polly Levinson has been delivering the hour-long Periods, Pain and Endometriosis Program (PPEP) Talk program to teenage students across schools for almost four years, helping young people understand more about pelvic pain.

Polly Levinson says students prefer learning about pelvic pain and menstrual issues from an external provider. (Supplied)

"Australian teachers are not super comfortable teaching about puberty, because it goes beyond biological processes," she said.

" We often find students appreciate not having to divulge really deeply personal information about their reproductive health to their potentially male PE teacher, who they're going to see for basketball tomorrow. "

Now, independent state MP for Murray Helen Dalton is sponsoring a parliamentary petition to get specialist endometriosis education classes for boys and girls funded across NSW public high schools.

The Period, Pain and Endometriosis Program, dubbed PPEP Talk, began in 2019 following the launch of the National Action Plan for Endometriosis. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

The PPEP Talk program currently runs in independent and Catholic schools across the country, and in state schools in Queensland, South Australia and Western Australia.

The NSW Department of Education will next year launch a pelvic health and endometriosis education program, which aims to support teachers discussing the condition.

But Ms Dalton said it made more sense to support the existing PEPP Talk program offered by the Pelvic Pain Foundation.

Her petition, which calls for the specialist class to expand into public high schools across the state, has gained more than 1,700 signatures since it was launched in August.

Helen Dalton is supporting a petition to have the PEPP Talk program in NSW public high schools. (Four Corners: Craig Hansen)

Ms Dalton said it could be particularly challenging for male teachers to deliver education around endometriosis.

"I think that they would find it a little bit difficult to speak to the girls about that, and the girls obviously would be probably hesitant to speak to a male about that," she said.

" Whereas the program is run by women that understand women's issues. "

A peer-reviewed 2022 study on menstrual health education in Australian schools found personal discomfort meant some Personal Development, Health and Physical Education (PDHPE) teachers lacked confidence when teaching puberty and menstruation.

Ms Levinson said clinical educators have been able to pick up on congenital conditions in conversations with students after the classes.

"That opportunity for students to talk one-on-one with the educator at the end of the session is something teachers have really told us they find immensely helpful, as well as the students themselves," she said.

Early intervention

Trudi Beck co-founded an endometriosis and pelvic pain clinic in Wagga Wagga.

She said young women often spent too long tolerating pain before seeking medical intervention.

Trudi Beck from Wagga Wagga says women in the regions have to travel hundreds of kilometres for pelvic pain support. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

"They are suffering these things often in silence, and only present when they get iron deficiency, which is a direct result of the heavy periods that's causing them to miss a lot of school," Dr Beck said.

She said awareness from an early age could prevent further health issues in later life, which was especially important in regional areas where access to support was limited.

"Some of the women in this region are travelling 200 to 300 kilometres each way to access care," Dr Beck said.

World.title: Ed Sheeran concerts cancelled in fresh blow to tour
World.content:
CultureMusicLive music Ed Sheeran concerts cancelled in fresh blow to tour India McTaggart September 26, 2026 — 7:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ed Sheeran’s two US concerts this weekend have been cancelled in a further blow to the embattled artist. The English singer-songwriter’s Friday and Saturday performances at the Gillette Stadium were pulled because of “severe weather warnings” as a storm approached Massachusetts. It comes as another setback to Sheeran’s US Loop tour, which has been beset by controversy since Macklemore, a supporting artist, was dropped over his “Free Palestine” chants. While on stage in Philadelphia last weekend, the tearful singer said his family and friends had “abandoned” him amid the furore. In a statement confirming the cancellation hours before the show was due to start, the tour promoter Messina Touring said: “Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium.



“The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.” Ticket holders would be refunded, it added. The two concerts had been due to take place at the stadium owned by Robert Kraft, the US billionaire, who Sheeran has said was responsible for cutting Macklemore from the tour. The Shape of You singer has broken down while performing amid the row about Palestine, which had led all his supporting acts to quit the US tour. While on stage in Philadelphia last weekend, the tearful singer said his family and friends had “abandoned” him amid the furore, which has seen fellow singers accuse him of choosing “capitalism over doing the right thing”.



More recently, his estranged rapper cousin has joined the online chorus against Sheeran, labelling him a “coward” because he refused to back his opening act’s pro-Palestine sentiments. Jethro Sheeran – who records music as Alonestar – also claimed his younger cousin was “shady” and that he was “embarrassed” by an old photograph of them together. Macklemore performs in Austin. AP Photo/Jack Plunkett Sheeran has apologised onstage for “making mistakes” in how he handled the Macklemore situation, saying last week that he could no longer “hide how I feel” about “this humanitarian issue”. He said: “I’m used to my music being criticised … This week the criticism was about something much more important ... I am making mistakes and I am so so sorry. I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important, compassionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet. “But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it any more.”



The musician said he sympathised with both sides of the Israel-Hamas war, telling the audience: “What happened in Israel, and at the Nova music festival on Oct 7, it was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain.” Related Article Opinion

Ed Sheeran Ed Sheeran made an art of being inoffensive: Here’s why it didn’t work this time Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist “What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate,” he added, stating: “My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation, loss of civilians’ lives. Children’s lives. At this systemic injustice, [what] we’re seeing unfolding in the West Bank cannot be overlooked.” The musical acts who pulled out of his tour – including Irish folk band Beoga and Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother – said they were acting in solidarity with Macklemore. Macklemore has since announced that he will be holding a “Free Palestine” tour, kicking off in Dublin on Monday, October 26.



The American rapper, whose real name is Benjamin Hammond Haggerty, led a pro-Palestine chant during two of Sheeran’s concerts in New Jersey on September 4 and 5. The chants led to Kraft, the pro-Israel owner of Gillette Stadium and the New England Patriots American football team, demanding his removal from Sheeran’s Loop tour. Loading Taking to Instagram, Macklemore said there had been a “collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now”. “Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work any more. People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment,” he wrote.



Macklemore’s actions labelled ‘inflammatory’ Responding to the announcement that the OVO Arena Wembley would host Macklemore’s upcoming Free Palestine tour, the Campaign Against Antisemitism labelled the rapper’s past actions as “inflammatory”. Writing to the arena through their X account, they said: “We are writing to Wembley Arena about its decision to host Macklemore. “Macklemore is not just a musician advocating for human rights. He is a multi-millionaire with a large audience who chooses to defend rabid anti-Israel protesters and has appeared on stage in Germany and said that the only way for society to atone for the Holocaust is by calling for a “free Palestine”. “Inflammatory actions like these only stoke the fires of anti-Semitism globally. This is not an underdog speaking truth to power. This is a celebrity using the current trendy cause – the war between Israel and Hamas – to their advantage, and claiming to speak for the victims of the Holocaust in a truly repulsive way.”

World.title: The ‘striking’ difference in how Trump and Xi used their invisible summit
World.content:
The many American business and technology titans invited to the White House state dinner on Thursday night - Jeff Bezos, David Ellison and Jamie Dimon among them - mostly had each other for company. There was no delegation of Chinese business executives on the trip, as there was on Xi Jinping’s last state visit to Washington in 2015. Apple’s Tim Cook, seated near Chinese President Xi Jinping at the state dinner. Annabelle Gordon - Pool via CNP It was one of the many signs that this summit was unlikely to elicit substantial outcomes - commercially at least - other than photographs. That has largely proven to be true. Little change has emerged from the meetings so far, except for a two-month extension to the trade truce brokered last year in Busan (it now expires in January) and a renewed AI dialogue.



US trade ambassador Jamieson Greer promised more announcements on Monday, while Donald Trump signalled good news for American farmers, though he has said that before. He also continued his pitch to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence”, but there was no obvious outcome on AI regulation. The White House had not provided an official readout at the time of writing. The summit was high on ceremony and low on substance - for now at least - which was predicted by most analysts. Bloomberg Evan Feigenbaum, vice president of studies at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, and a leading voice on Asia, said the affair was “long on performance, short on substance”. But, he added, “that doesn’t mean there won’t be substance, because they’re going to meet two more times this year. That’s really unprecedented.”



Having already met in Beijing in May, Trump and Xi are due to see each other again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November, and at the G20 in Miami before Christmas. Feigenbaum said one would ordinarily expect more tangible outcomes and co-operation from so much face-to-face time. The absence of this may mean they are still negotiating; the summit schedule gives them more time. Trump gifted President Xi and Madam Peng a bald eagle statue - a gift he has bestowed on others this term. Bloomberg Or it could mean, as Feigenbaum intuits, that “neither side wants that much out of the relationship any more that’s realistic and workable”. What they do get is an opportunity to cast US-Sino relations in their own terms. For Trump, as always, it is personal. He showered Xi and Madam Peng Liyuan with superlatives, and reiterated how great they get on. Showing off the White House, including the helipad and the forthcoming ballroom, was of great importance.



Xi was also complimentary but never missed an opportunity to reinforce Beijing’s geopolitical message. No clearer was this than during a tea ceremony in the White House’s Red Room on Friday morning. Trump praised his visitors and thanked the media for its “fair coverage”. Xi, meanwhile, made a short speech about “two people charting the course for the great ship of China-US relations”. The leaders concluded the summit with tea at the White House and a visit to the National Archives on Friday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin He repeated Beijing’s preferred framing of the relationship as one of “strategic stability”, and said the summit had added more substance to this notion - though how remained a mystery. He spoke of respect, fairness and reciprocity. Ryan Hass, a China scholar the Brookings Institution in Washington, said the contrast between the two leaders’ approaches was “pretty striking”.



“For Trump, the pageantry appears to be the point,” he wrote on X. “The focus is on forging personal bonds with Xi and signalling that both leaders can keep competition under control.” Meanwhile, “Xi spoke mostly in terms of state-state relations and national power … [He] seemed bemused by Trump’s entertaining approach to hospitality.” Chinese President Xi Jinping rarely missed an opportunity to reinforce Beijing’s geopolitical message. Annabelle Gordon - Pool via CNP While in Washington, the Chinese president repeatedly cast China and the US as two “major countries” who shouldered special responsibility to not just steer their own relationship, but to chart a course for the world. Implicit therein is the positioning of Beijing and Washington on an equal footing. Zhao Minghao, a professor of Sino-US relations at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said Beijing would be happy with the summit and the way it projected Xi as Trump’s equal, though it would have preferred a six-month or yearlong extension to the trade truce.



“If US–China summit meetings can help preserve channels and avoid a new shock, it is of great worth,” Zhao said. “Beijing measures success by process, symmetry and de-escalation, not by comprehensive agreements that were never expected.” But it was not just policy that was invisible at this meeting. While there was plenty of pomp, circumstance and goodwill, most of it was not broadcast to Americans. Donald Trump showed off his new helipad to Xi Jinping, including its granite. AP That’s because the five major TV networks - Fox News, ABC, CBS, NBC and CNN - did not participate in the “pool” that films presidential events and distributes footage to other stations around the country. They had refused to take part in solidarity with CNN, which Trump had banned from the White House and the pool. The ban was fully lifted on Friday (Washington DC local time), and their participation resumed. But it meant reduced exposure of an event crafted with visuals front of mind.



On Friday, the Chinese Communist Party’s official newspaper, the People’s Daily, splashed its front page with six photos of Xi’s US visit, featuring him being greeted by Trump on the tarmac, the red carpet welcome at the White House, and the two leaders shaking hands in the Oval Office. The optics matter immensely for the Chinese, says Dylan Loh, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. First Lady Melania Trump took her counterpart Peng Liyuan to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian American Art. Finn Gomez/POOL Getty Images North America via AP “It allows Beijing to demonstrate to their domestic audiences - and really to the rest of the world - that they are the US’s peer,” says Loh. “And to say: the US is giving us the respect that we have historically not necessarily gotten. We have arrived.” Zhao said China now saw itself as a co-equal great power that could withstand US economic force, and had been surprised by how quickly Trump had shifted from extreme confrontation and tariff brinkmanship to accepting Beijing’s framework of “constructive strategic stability”.



“Beijing does not believe rivalry is over,” Zhao said. “Tech decoupling, Taiwan and military mistrust remain. But it judges the balance of psychological initiative to have shifted. China can afford patience and incremental truce management.” Related Article Updated

Foreign relations ‘Major countries’ US and China must co-operate on the world’s problems: Xi Feigenbaum, who is also a former deputy assistant secretary of state for south and central Asia under George W. Bush, reached a similar conclusion. China is aware of Trump’s propensity to say almost anything. They also know that whatever Trump says or does, it does not necessarily commit the next US president. “The Chinese objective is just to ringfence the worst outcomes with the US, park the Americans in a corner and then pursue their opportunities elsewhere, where they actually have them,” Feigenbaum said. “That’s their view of it.”
