World.title: Rock and roll, fantasy and Silicon Valley fascism: 10 new books
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This week’s fiction includes a moving work set in the aftermath of the American Civil War to a world filled with magical animals, while non-fiction ranges across the local rock scene, the heroes and villains of history and WWII fighter pilots. Fiction The Newer World by Sebastian Barry (Allen & Unwin $34.99) Some may quibble that as a white Irishman, Sebastian Barry ought not to have the authorial right to adopt the voice of Tennyson Bouguereau, a black man navigating the messy aftermath of the Civil War. But if anyone can perform this act of cultural ventriloquism well, it’s Barry. The Newer World navigates the world of Tennyson, who, alongside his twin sister, was born into slavery but eventually freed, only to discover that freedom is not necessarily equivalent to acceptance in the deep American South. The newer world is not that much shinier than the old one. From rural Tennessee to Nashville, where Tennyson, with his beautiful voice, is given a chance to join a choir, and then to England when he goes on tour, and then back to America, Barry recreates the 19th-century period with vividness and colour. Written in the first person, this historical fiction is elegantly wrought. Like his poetic namesake, Tennyson’s descriptive mannerisms are filled with rhythmic, lyrical touches that can seem grandiose at times. But the narrative balances racism and trauma with hope and transformation. Strange Familiars by Keshe Chow (Hachette, $34.99)



Two academic rivals at a College of Magical Veterinary Sciences battle it out: in the one corner is earnest and hard-working Gwendolynne Chan, and facing her is rich nepo baby Harrisford Briggs. The reader will be forgiving for thinking the novel will focus on cutesy and strange animals doing fantastic tricks before they become injured, but Keshe Chow leads the narrative elsewhere. Set in an alternate London, her world-building involves the pair trying to figure out why there’s excessive magic that turns the animal-familiars feral and also causes explosions in the city. They have to join forces to stop the surges. Strange Familiars is told through alternate viewpoints of the protagonists as they investigate competing organisations that distribute and oppose the global supply of magic. The enemy-to-lovers trope is predictable, with Chow at full rein in exploring the romantasy genre. It’s a fun read – the first instalment of a series of two, and Percy, Gwen’s snarky telepathic cat, is a joyful addition. If only there were more magical animals in the mix. Female Life on Planet Earth by Laleh Khadivi (Oneworld, $32.99) Set in Los Angeles, this novel is about secret lives and the relationships between mothers and daughters. It focuses on the year Heti spends after the death of her mother, Anahita. While she plans a large-scale mourning anniversary at the urging of her bossy traditionalist aunt, Heti receives a mysterious package containing photos of a younger Anahita, enveloped in a black veil and carrying a machine gun. The mother Heti knew and loved was sweet and nurturing – who was this fighter in combat mode? What follows is a series of conversational vignettes with strangers about what it means to be a woman. But too much time and energy are spent on such peripheral musings, with comparatively scant details about Anahita’s past only allowed to surface toward the end. Though the book obviously references revolutionary Iran, it’s odd that Laleh Khadivi refrains from mentioning the country. Perhaps she’s aiming for universality of themes about war, religious fanaticism, persecution, womanhood, diaspora, and immigration, but depersonalising the context does a disservice to the narrative. Midwest by Caitlin Maling (Upswell, $27.99) In this suite of poems, Caitlin Maling roams the coastal waters of Western Australia with a keen eye. Mailing grew up in and around Fremantle, and her love of the vistas around this port city is evident. Midwest, her sixth poetry collection, continues her exploration of the natural world, especially its watery depths and the animals that live or at least struggle to survive within or near the sea. As the Tour Guide at the Ocean Park Marina and Aquarium puts it, “Everything you see is food, sex or death.” Whether it’s sea eagles nesting, parrotfish pecking at coral, sea snakes copulating or crabs being cracked open to eat, Maling’s words are visceral and sometimes startling. There are shipwrecks, salmon farming and single-celled organisms called stromatolites among the mix. Among her descriptions of the birds and beasts, she also writes about motherhood and her young son. Sometimes Maling’s metaphorical reach will make you stop and consider the world anew – she describes rock as “breaking out of the earth like bones” and an octopus’ nodules like “Mardi Gras beads, but finer filigree.”



Gone Guru by Nadine Browne (Fremantle Press, $34.99) Noni has flown into New York from WA and barely settled in her Harlem apartment when she discovers that her new flatmate, Vincent, a self-styled transcendental meditation guru with millions of followers and millions in a trust fund, has disappeared. Maybe he’s too busy trying to find himself? Though Noni has distractions of her own – she’s failing to combat imposter syndrome at a prestigious writing program – she becomes invested in finding him. Noni’s trying to think of a story for her class while navigating the strangeness of a new city; the missing Vincent may just be the catalyst she needs. Gone Guru is an auto-fiction, with Nadine Browne drawing on her own experiences. Partly a sleuthing story, with the clamour, colour, vibrancy, and characters of New York as a background, and partly an exploration into the challenges of being a creative writer (particularly with someone as intimidating as Joyce Carol Oates as a teacher), the book is an enjoyable and funny romp that surveys serious issues (race, class, identity, literature, culture) with a light touch. Non-fiction A History of the World in 51 Heroes and Villains by Tom Holland & Dominic Sandbrook (Bloomsbury, $36.99)



History is, of course, about far more than heroes and villains, but they can be a lot of fun, as The Rest is History podcast team demonstrates in this collection of cameos. And they’re not all human, either. Like Wojtek, the Syrian brown bear adopted by the Polish army in exile during WWII, who lugged heavy crates of munitions up the slopes of Monte Cassino, Italy, during the Allied advance and made a highly valued contribution to the war effort. Much loved by the troops, and with a penchant for cigarettes and stealing women’s underwear, Wojtek eventually died in the Edinburgh Zoo, an undisputed hero with his own statue. Some of the other figures, however, aren’t so clear-cut. The mad monk, Savonarola, for example, lauded by some as a Reformationist hero combating excessive wealth and corruption, and reviled by others as a murdering, puritanical fruitcake. Then there are the mysteries, like Elizabeth 1. Was she really a virgin, or just good at “branding”? Incorporated into a tale that stretches from Roman times (Boadicea gets a guernsey) to the 20th century are potted biographies of the likes of US-born photographer, war correspondent and former model Lee Miller, who famously soaked herself in Hitler’s bath. Reading this is a bit like opening a packet of potato chips; once you start it’s really difficult to stop. In the Realm of the Last Man by Francis Fukuyama (Profile, $45) Francis Fukuyama is best known for 1989 essay The End of History, which, he argues in this combination of memoir and dissertation, was wrongly interpreted as a piece of neo-conservative triumphalism – at the same time, stating that he was part of the neo-conservative clique that included the likes of Irving Kristol. Since then, he’s changed his mind, left old alignments behind, and moved closer to the left. What happened? Two things: the Iraq invasion of 2003, which he opposed after concluding that the post-war period of reconstruction would be a disaster, and the GFC that followed not long after, and which led him to question and reject the twin neo-conservative precepts of largely unfettered marketplace capitalism and a strictly limited government role. He might still talk of “history” in quasi metaphysical, qualified Hegelian terms, but his engaging, plain-speaking essays demonstrate that the mind (not just history) is constantly evolving, that someone can break free of outmoded beliefs and world views to see things anew. The Nerd Reich by Gil Duran (Simon & Schuster, $36.99) Once upon a time, Silicon Valley was the home of nerdy, vaguely left-leaning liberals. All that has changed. These days it sits at Trump’s table and with sinister intentions. When Elon Musk waved a chainsaw around at a Conservative convention just after Trump’s second coming (the chainsaw symbolising ruthless cuts to government and bureaucracy), the New Yorker announced Techno Fascism comes to America. Journalist and political advisor Duran traces its rise from the late 1990s to the present day. And he paints a truly alarming picture of the world’s most obscenely wealthy men being invited into the Trump administration on a mass scale. These techno-oligarchs, he argues, aren’t content to work within the democratic system – they hate it, want to destroy and replace governments and countries with corporate city states. To counter it, he says, we need to “rethink our relationship with technology, which means rethinking what it means to be human”. Welcome to the new fascism and the “Nerd Reich”, funded by cryptocurrency, enabled by AI and run by oligarchs with deep-seated, anti-democratic, global ambitions.

World.title: Dune 3 will be a hit, but there’s one mad version we’ll never get to see
World.content:
Even the dreams of top directors get left on the cutting room floor. In some cases, it’s a blessing.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This year’s much-anticipated touchdown of Denis Villeneuve’s third Dune film coincides with the 50th anniversary of the most valiant yet doomed attempt to bring Frank Herbert’s science-fiction epic to the screen. This earlier quixotic quest eclipsed even the interstellar ambitions of Villeneuve and his team. In the 1970s, Chilean-French auteur Alejandro Jodorowsky embarked on an unhinged mission to shoot a Dune film equivalent to an acid trip. His assembled cast included Orson Welles, Gloria Swanson and Mick Jagger; Pink Floyd were on soundtrack duties; French illustrator Moebius and artist H.R. Giger (of Alien fame) designed the psychedelic visuals. Even surrealist grandmaster Salvador Dali signed on, demanding an hourly rate of $100,000. Jodorowsky’s script was 14 hours long, and the production “bible” he created stretched to almost 300 pages (a rare copy sold for $4.3 million – 110 times the expected figure – at Christie’s in 2021). The film was too ludicrous to manifest in reality but it did spawn Jodorowsky’s Dune (2013), a wildly entertaining documentary tracing the making of a film that wasn’t made. Has there ever been another unrealised pipe dream so tantalising in its promise that other films have been made about it? Artist H. R. Giger in Jodorowsky’s Dune. Alamy Stock Photo As it happens, yes. Jon Schnepp’s The Death of ‘Superman Lives’: What Happened? (2015) offers a glimpse of the monstrosity that might have been had Tim Burton directed his Superman movie with Nicolas Cage as the Man of Steel. Christopher Walken, Courteney Cox and Sandra Bullock were picked for supporting roles, the script was penned by Kevin Smith (Mallrats) and the whole fiasco was produced by Jon Peters, a former hairdresser who insisted that his Man of Steel wasn’t allowed to fly or wear the red-and-blue outfit, and that the film end with Superman fighting a giant spider. Jon Schnepp with Tim Burton, who never got to make Superman Lives. These non-existent movies are just two of the countless unrealised projects that are like cinema’s dark matter: you’ll never see them but their sheer volume holds everything else together. Miles Davis is alleged to have said that great music is about the notes you don’t play; the films a director doesn’t make might be as important as those they do.



For most of his life Stanley Kubrick maintained an obsessive drive to create a film about Napoleon, even enlisting the support of 50,000 members of the Romanian People’s Army to re-enact battles. It wasn’t to be. For every Basic Instinct or Starship Troopers Paul Verhoeven has directed, there are dozens of films he’s had to abandon: Tom Cruise as Houdini, the early years of Adolf Hitler, a take on the life of Jesus. And who wouldn’t pay to see Luca Guadagnino’s American Psycho? Darren Aronofsky’s RoboCop? John Carpenter’s Top Gun, Fatal Attraction or Santa Claus: the Movie? In an alternate timeline all of these exist. But history is haunted by the spectres of films that don’t. Some are the victims of overreaching ambition, while others are vanity projects best left unrealised. A depressing number find themselves wallowing in “development hell”, the industry term for productions that sink into an eternal cycle of script rewrites, studio changes and funding sinkholes. Jon Peters – the aforementioned hairdresser-turned-producer (and one-time Barbra Streisand squeeze) – is the kind of colourful Hollywood character who can pave the way to development hell. After he attained the rights to Neil Gaiman’s classic Sandman series, he offered up what the author described as “quite easily the worst script I’ve ever read”. Again, there was the inexplicable inclusion of a giant spider (a dream Peters finally realised on 1999’s Wild Wild West, a film critics lambasted).



Some of the greatest hits (or likely misses) we can only imagine: Stanley Kubrick’s Lord of the Rings with Paul McCartney as Frodo and John Lennon as Gollum; Sofia Coppola’s The Little Mermaid, reportedly too dark and risky to finance; indie darling Lynne Ramsay’s unlikely foray into western territory on Jane Got a Gun, which was completed to lukewarm reviews by Gavin O’Connor; Spike Lee’s remake of Bruce Lee’s Enter the Dragon with comedian Ken Jeong in the kung fu king’s role; disaster master Roland Emmerich’s entry in the James Bond franchise. The list of off-kilter choices to direct Return of the Jedi is enough to induce whiplash. Terry Gilliam would likely have spun off the series in an odd direction but just imagine what Davids Lynch or Cronenberg would have done had they said yes to the job. Related Article The Verdict Other people’s dreams bore me rigid. So why are films and TV shows full of them? And picture the iconic Wolverine played not by Hugh Jackman but by the notably less ripped Bob Hoskins, who was originally slated for the role in the first X-Men adaptation, then to be directed by Kathryn Bigelow. Bigelow’s own filmography illustrates how the films that don’t get made are as illustrative as those that do. In the 1990s she headed up a string of genre classics, from erotic thriller Blue Steel to surfer heist caper Point Break. Post-9/11, though, she took a hard shift towards serious, politically provocative films such as The Hurt Locker and Zero Dark Thirty. Her catalogue of unrealised projects since that point drives home this career turn, full of titles such as Held by the Taliban, Mogadishu Minnesota and The True American. Australian directors might struggle to get projects up here but the difficulty can scale up exponentially when they arrive in Tinseltown. Jocelyn Moorhouse’s adaptation of Murray Bail’s Eucalyptus was production-ready in 2005, featuring a dream team of Nicole Kidman and Russell Crowe, before Fox Searchlight canned the project. Fellow Australian Peter Weir’s filmography may include Picnic at Hanging Rock, Dead Poets Society, The Truman Show, Witness and Green Card but many subsequent projects failed to gain traction and he eventually announced he was quitting the game.



Development hell is a place particular to big-name filmmakers, simply by virtue of their clout. Studios won’t pander to an up-and-comer whose ideas don’t wash but when a Kubrick or a Spielberg has a passion project, they’re not so easily dismissed. Ordering endless rounds of casting changes and screenplay revisions is a way to keep the big earners appeased without actually committing to their financially dubious hobby horses. Adam Driver and Nathalie Emmanuel in Francis Ford Coppola’s bloated Megalopolis. And sometimes the bean counters aren’t the villains of the story. Quentin Tarantino’s Star Trek, set in 1930s Chicago? Hard pass. Sylvester Stallone’s film about Edgar Allan Poe with himself in the lead? Nevermore! Francis Ford Coppola’s Megalopolis spent almost half a century in development hell; he ultimately financed the production himself, the result a sprawling mess that earned less than 10 per cent of its $120 million production budget. Sometimes a dream is better left that way. Zack Snyder’s bombastic Hollywood fare – 300, Man of Steel, Justice League – has been box-office dynamite but after decades in development hell he finally self-produced his dream project, The Last Photograph. It debuted at the recent Toronto International Film Festival, with critics dubbing it “supremely indulgent auteur gunk”, “boring, bloated, brutally violent” and “an utter disgrace from start to finish … Snyder at his most unfiltered, with no studio intervention”. It’s about the notes you don’t play, Mr Snyder, and the giant spiders you keep to yourself. The cruellest cut It’s one thing for a passion project to go unrealised but another level of heartbreak awaits filmmakers who complete a work only for it never to see the light of day.



Coyote vs. Acme, completed in 2023, rated well with test audiences before Warner Bros Discovery decided to shelve it as a $30 million tax write-off. It took a concerted campaign by indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment (and a $50 million price tag) for the film to finally make it to screens. As of writing, it holds a 96 per cent score on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes. Related Article Cinema Warner Bros axed this Looney Tunes movie. But fans refused to accept defeat Few similar tales achieve such a happy ending. The DC superhero flick Batgirl featured a stacked cast including Leslie Grace (In the Heights), J.K. Simmons, Brendan Fraser and Michael Keaton returning to the suit he first squeezed into for Tim Burton’s 1989 Batman. The film was close to completion when Warner Bros Discovery cancelled its release and wrote off another $90 million tax-wise. Other films have been consigned to the vaults for less financial reasons. The most famous is probably Jerry Lewis’ The Day the Clown Cried, in which a clown sent to a Nazi concentration camp attempts to offer hope to the children imprisoned there. After viewing a rough cut the co-writer declared it was unfit for public viewing and denied all rights for release. James Franco’s The Long Home was completed in 2016, with a cast including Josh Hutcherson, Courtney Love, Ashton Kutcher and Josh Hartnett. Allegations of inappropriate sexual behaviour by Franco during the shoot, however, ensured that the finished film has never been publicly screened. In 2009 Tony Kaye (American History X) completed a rough cut of post-Hurricane Katrina crime drama Black Water Transit but the work became a hot potato in a series of legal disputes that culminated in one of the film’s producers being sentenced to eight years in prison for fraud. Some nearly finished films have been denied the fairytale rescue Coyote vs. Acme has enjoyed. The 2025 musical comedy-drama Golden had some serious talent flex: Michel Gondry directing, Pharrell Williams as co-producer and composer, and an all-star line-up including Janelle Monae, Missy Elliott and Andre 3000, but Universal Studios cancelled the film before it was released.

World.title: ‘Computer says no’: I asked AI the pitfalls of asking AI for money advice
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingAI Opinion ‘Computer says no’: I asked AI the pitfalls of asking AI for money advice Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor September 26, 2026 — 6:00am

September 26, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Managing money well can be, well, confusing. It can even be confronting. And how are many of us are solving such issues these days with the help of artificial intelligence “buddies”. Heck, I even have friends who use AI to draft replies to tricky text messages from their mum. AI can look well-reasoned and comprehensive, giving you a sense of security when you should have nothing of the sort. iStock So is it any surprise that more than three million Australians are already using AI to help manage their financial activity, with the highest number – 25 per cent – among Gen Z Australians, says a new Understanding Modern Australia report. Not that we necessarily – thank goodness – trust it. The report, by life insurer TAL with McCrindle, found only 22 per cent of us feel comfortable using AI to help make major financial decisions and only 20 per cent trust AI to recommend a financial product suited to their needs.



So, I thought I’d try an experiment: I asked AI the pitfalls of asking AI for money advice – and whoa. In an emphatic “computer-says-no”, here are the 10 reasons the AI gave me not to use it – and how I might. (I’ve grouped them where AI doubled and even tripled down.) ‘An LLM’s training data has a cut-off, and even with web search, it can miss nuance, fail to update thresholds, blend outdated and current rules without flagging the difference.’ An AI’s response 1. No accountability or duty of care Yep, good point Claude! No care and no responsibility does not make for the ideal economic confidante. The rules and requirements to give financial advice in Australia are strict. AI is not bound by any of them.



Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Want to learn how to invest? Here are three expert tricks and the rule of 72 Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor The education needed is also now extensive (part of why the profession is shrinking). But, mainly, a licensed financial adviser is bound by law to act in your best interest. In the candid confession, AI said: “An LLM has no such obligation and no licence that can be revoked if it gets things wrong.” 2. Regulatory grey zone You need an Australian Financial Services Licence to give personal financial advice – it’s illegal otherwise. Reputable AI tools build in disclaimers and stick to general information rather than personal advice. But how do you even tell the difference when it’s – you know – you asking?



3, 4 and 5. Lack of personalisation depth. Generic, one-size-fits-all framing. Data privacy Variables that factor into smart financial decisions include your age, income, debts, risk tolerance, tax situation, existing assets, super balance, insurance and goals. Does your AI know all of this about you? And, crucially, do you want it to? Where does that data go and how is it stored? “Even if they did, an LLM isn’t verifying any of it or cross-checking for inconsistencies the way a human adviser would,” confides the LLM itself. The “cookie cutter” alternative isn’t great, either. The advice might just be versions of old financial adages like diversify, pay off debt and invest for the long term. They may not fit with your financial affairs at that moment. 6. Currency and accuracy problems



This is a massive one. Legislation changes regularly. Even in the past year, we have seen changes to the first home buyer 5 per cent deposit scheme, an overhaul of capital gains and a ban on negative gearing. Um, I won’t be trusting AI with any related financial decisions thank you! Related Article Opinion

Superannuation The best retirement advice you can give your friends Bec Wilson Money contributor Then there are just the regular updates and indexation to things like tax brackets, super contribution caps, income thresholds and interest rates. Old information could easily sink your future. Need proof? “An LLM’s training data has a cut-off, and even with web search, it can miss nuance, fail to update thresholds, blend outdated and current rules without flagging the difference.” Thanks, Claude. 7 and 8. A false sense of diligence and confident-sounding errors (aka “hallucinations”)



We’ve all encountered this - AI intel that’s slightly insane! And the danger it poses in complex financial information or advice is: would you even recognise it? AI can look well-reasoned and comprehensive, giving you a sense of security when you should have nothing of the sort. How’s this for candour: “LLMs can state incorrect figures, invent products or rules that don’t exist, or misapply a rule from one country’s system (e.g., US 401k rules) to Australia’s superannuation system, all while sounding authoritative.” 9. No understanding of behavioural or emotional context Factor in your state of mind? That you might be responding based on your childhood “conditioning” rather than actual conditions? Or that you might have a different risk tolerance to the questions you are asking? An AI model can’t possibly do this. Indeed: “An LLM responds to the words in the prompt, not the psychology behind them.”



10. No ongoing relationship or follow-through A financial plan needs to evolve with you. But we’ve come full-circle to the point above about how much your LLM remembers, and whether you actually want it to. We’ve all encountered this – AI intel that’s slightly insane! The danger it poses in complex financial information or advice is: would you even recognise it? Nine Finally, I loved AI’s very watery disclaimer at the end of the list, compared with the one we are required to use (see below!). “AI can be a decent starting point for financial literacy and generating questions to ask a professional, but it’s a poor substitute for licensed, personalised advice.” So, would I use AI for financial information? Only while good primary sources of that information still exist and are disclosed so I can check the pedigree and recency. (And those days are numbered as AI drives such traffic-based sites out of business.)



But AI for financial advice? Not unless you could interrogate just the one trusted financial philosophy, teaching or expert. Why would you put your money where AI’s possibly hallucinating mouth is? Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. Expert tips on how to save, invest and make the most of your money delivered to your inbox every Sunday.

World.title: Pretty lies for an audience of one: life as a biographer for hire
World.content:
CultureBooksPublishing Pretty lies for an audience of one: life as a biographer for hire Like Pol Pot’s portraitist, the big man’s scribe is on shaky ground. Anson Cameron September 26, 2026 — 5:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Out of sight of the reading public, unbeknown to bibliophiles, unsuspected by the churners-through of this year’s Top 10 Must Read lists, ignored by the bookshops and poo-poohed by publishers, biographies and histories are being penned for sums of money so large their authors are J.K. Rowling in money. Almost every big man sitting, Mojito in hand, beside his own swimming pool outside his beach house in Byron eventually begins to worry that his extraordinary life will disappear, unrecorded, uncelebrated. It’s a galling realisation when, Lord knows, a quest as righteous as his has been might be used to instruct his grandchildren, currently mewling, unenlightened, in their $5000 Danish bassinets. Photo: Robin Cowcher Their thoughts go something like this: “My glory years controlling the firm must be captured for posterity. For the sake of the family – an important history recording the brave battles I fought and won, allowing us to dominate markets where lesser men and firms foundered.” Next thing, these poolside giants are looking for an amanuensis. A friend of mine hires himself out to write self-published biographies for ex-CEOs and other assorted big men, histories of famous families and renowned Australian companies. No surprise it’s generally men who recognise their lives must be mythologised or the world be poorer.



The trick, if you want to write a biography of an emeritus CEO, is to find a big-swinging dick who isn’t a dick. But it’s more likely you’ll write a biography for a yeti than that. Your client will be difficult – bordering on Stalinesque. These self-funded wannabe biographees have run worlds without recourse to manners, laws or morals. Related Article Opinion

Friendship Kev’s mates put a GPS tracker on his car. Then they discovered his awful secret Anson Cameron Spectrum columnist, The Age When you sign on to write a biography of Clarence Dinklinker AC you better realise he wants a story in which he is Galahad. Don’t be a fool and let your journalistic ethics, historian’s integrity, proven methodologies, or just plain old honesty lead you astray, towards objectivity and fact. You’re not writing this book for a readership – you’re writing it for a reader. Dinklinker wants a hagiography, plain and simple. He wants to look like Steve McQueen with cojones like cantaloupes and a halo like a truck tyre. No one who’s spent a life befuddling the ATO and battling unions to make a fortune against the odds wants to be cynically celebrated in amber ambiguity like Serrano’s Piss Christ. But... do you remember the first time you heard your recorded voice? It sounded like a stranger, didn’t it? You don’t sound like that. A biographee experiences a similar dissociation. Big, important fellows never recognise the self they know and idolise in the book they’ve paid someone to write about them. So writing a biography of a Dinklinker is as risky as being Pol Pot’s portraitist... “Are you suggesting, with your laboured draftsmanship, that my eyes are set so close together?”



I met my friend, the freelancing biographer, in a cafe last week. He was on brief furlough from a shitstorm – thin-faced and pale and his pinot gris a choppy puddle in a shaky hand. He currently has four books run aground on the reef-egos of big men. They don’t agree with what he’s written. They won’t pay for anything less than an anthem and he still has a homeopathic inkling of integrity that won’t let him deliver. He’s entangled in a history of a canning business where the three brothers who founded the company all insist on being the hero and that the other two coat-tail-riding layabouts be given mere walk-on roles. Another of his bespoke mires is a history of a mining company in which he’s serving a dozen different masters, all ex-directors and CEOs, who have got up a riot of contradictory narcissistic fabrications and exculpatory balderdash. Not only have they conflicting “memories” of who sired the company, they’re willing to sue if their paternity is questioned in print. There he sat in our little local cafe, the biographer for hire, cowed by the protagonists of his various works-in-progress, at war with balding gangs of once greatish men, holding on, trying to write something closer to true than they will swallow. I pitied him. He had mistresses to hide, bankruptcies to gloss over, prosecutions to de-emphasise, failed mergers to justify... It’s no easy thing writing history to order if you fancy yourself honest. Or once did. But the wealthy pay big for pretty lies, and a man’s got to eat. On our second bottle he mumbled, “What a joy it would be to write of an utter nobody, like you do.”

World.title: Ed Sheeran concerts cancelled in fresh blow to tour
World.content:
CultureMusicLive music Ed Sheeran concerts cancelled in fresh blow to tour India McTaggart September 26, 2026 — 7:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ed Sheeran’s two US concerts this weekend have been cancelled in a further blow to the embattled artist. The English singer-songwriter’s Friday and Saturday performances at the Gillette Stadium were pulled because of “severe weather warnings” as a storm approached Massachusetts. It comes as another setback to Sheeran’s US Loop tour, which has been beset by controversy since Macklemore, a supporting artist, was dropped over his “Free Palestine” chants. While on stage in Philadelphia last weekend, the tearful singer said his family and friends had “abandoned” him amid the furore. In a statement confirming the cancellation hours before the show was due to start, the tour promoter Messina Touring said: “Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium.



“The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.” Ticket holders would be refunded, it added. The two concerts had been due to take place at the stadium owned by Robert Kraft, the US billionaire, who Sheeran has said was responsible for cutting Macklemore from the tour. The Shape of You singer has broken down while performing amid the row about Palestine, which had led all his supporting acts to quit the US tour. While on stage in Philadelphia last weekend, the tearful singer said his family and friends had “abandoned” him amid the furore, which has seen fellow singers accuse him of choosing “capitalism over doing the right thing”.



More recently, his estranged rapper cousin has joined the online chorus against Sheeran, labelling him a “coward” because he refused to back his opening act’s pro-Palestine sentiments. Jethro Sheeran – who records music as Alonestar – also claimed his younger cousin was “shady” and that he was “embarrassed” by an old photograph of them together. Macklemore performs in Austin. AP Photo/Jack Plunkett Sheeran has apologised onstage for “making mistakes” in how he handled the Macklemore situation, saying last week that he could no longer “hide how I feel” about “this humanitarian issue”. He said: “I’m used to my music being criticised … This week the criticism was about something much more important ... I am making mistakes and I am so so sorry. I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important, compassionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet. “But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it any more.”



The musician said he sympathised with both sides of the Israel-Hamas war, telling the audience: “What happened in Israel, and at the Nova music festival on Oct 7, it was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain.” Related Article Opinion

Ed Sheeran Ed Sheeran made an art of being inoffensive: Here’s why it didn’t work this time Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist “What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate,” he added, stating: “My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation, loss of civilians’ lives. Children’s lives. At this systemic injustice, [what] we’re seeing unfolding in the West Bank cannot be overlooked.” The musical acts who pulled out of his tour – including Irish folk band Beoga and Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother – said they were acting in solidarity with Macklemore. Macklemore has since announced that he will be holding a “Free Palestine” tour, kicking off in Dublin on Monday, October 26.



The American rapper, whose real name is Benjamin Hammond Haggerty, led a pro-Palestine chant during two of Sheeran’s concerts in New Jersey on September 4 and 5. The chants led to Kraft, the pro-Israel owner of Gillette Stadium and the New England Patriots American football team, demanding his removal from Sheeran’s Loop tour. Loading Taking to Instagram, Macklemore said there had been a “collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now”. “Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work any more. People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment,” he wrote.



Macklemore’s actions labelled ‘inflammatory’ Responding to the announcement that the OVO Arena Wembley would host Macklemore’s upcoming Free Palestine tour, the Campaign Against Antisemitism labelled the rapper’s past actions as “inflammatory”. Writing to the arena through their X account, they said: “We are writing to Wembley Arena about its decision to host Macklemore. “Macklemore is not just a musician advocating for human rights. He is a multi-millionaire with a large audience who chooses to defend rabid anti-Israel protesters and has appeared on stage in Germany and said that the only way for society to atone for the Holocaust is by calling for a “free Palestine”. “Inflammatory actions like these only stoke the fires of anti-Semitism globally. This is not an underdog speaking truth to power. This is a celebrity using the current trendy cause – the war between Israel and Hamas – to their advantage, and claiming to speak for the victims of the Holocaust in a truly repulsive way.”

World.title: The ‘striking’ difference in how Trump and Xi used their invisible summit
World.content:
The many American business and technology titans invited to the White House state dinner on Thursday night - Jeff Bezos, David Ellison and Jamie Dimon among them - mostly had each other for company. There was no delegation of Chinese business executives on the trip, as there was on Xi Jinping’s last state visit to Washington in 2015. Apple’s Tim Cook, seated near Chinese President Xi Jinping at the state dinner. Annabelle Gordon - Pool via CNP It was one of the many signs that this summit was unlikely to elicit substantial outcomes - commercially at least - other than photographs. That has largely proven to be true. Little change has emerged from the meetings so far, except for a two-month extension to the trade truce brokered last year in Busan (it now expires in January) and a renewed AI dialogue.



US trade ambassador Jamieson Greer promised more announcements on Monday, while Donald Trump signalled good news for American farmers, though he has said that before. He also continued his pitch to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence”, but there was no obvious outcome on AI regulation. The White House had not provided an official readout at the time of writing. The summit was high on ceremony and low on substance - for now at least - which was predicted by most analysts. Bloomberg Evan Feigenbaum, vice president of studies at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, and a leading voice on Asia, said the affair was “long on performance, short on substance”. But, he added, “that doesn’t mean there won’t be substance, because they’re going to meet two more times this year. That’s really unprecedented.”



Having already met in Beijing in May, Trump and Xi are due to see each other again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November, and at the G20 in Miami before Christmas. Feigenbaum said one would ordinarily expect more tangible outcomes and co-operation from so much face-to-face time. The absence of this may mean they are still negotiating; the summit schedule gives them more time. Trump gifted President Xi and Madam Peng a bald eagle statue - a gift he has bestowed on others this term. Bloomberg Or it could mean, as Feigenbaum intuits, that “neither side wants that much out of the relationship any more that’s realistic and workable”. What they do get is an opportunity to cast US-Sino relations in their own terms. For Trump, as always, it is personal. He showered Xi and Madam Peng Liyuan with superlatives, and reiterated how great they get on. Showing off the White House, including the helipad and the forthcoming ballroom, was of great importance.



Xi was also complimentary but never missed an opportunity to reinforce Beijing’s geopolitical message. No clearer was this than during a tea ceremony in the White House’s Red Room on Friday morning. Trump praised his visitors and thanked the media for its “fair coverage”. Xi, meanwhile, made a short speech about “two people charting the course for the great ship of China-US relations”. The leaders concluded the summit with tea at the White House and a visit to the National Archives on Friday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin He repeated Beijing’s preferred framing of the relationship as one of “strategic stability”, and said the summit had added more substance to this notion - though how remained a mystery. He spoke of respect, fairness and reciprocity. Ryan Hass, a China scholar the Brookings Institution in Washington, said the contrast between the two leaders’ approaches was “pretty striking”.



“For Trump, the pageantry appears to be the point,” he wrote on X. “The focus is on forging personal bonds with Xi and signalling that both leaders can keep competition under control.” Meanwhile, “Xi spoke mostly in terms of state-state relations and national power … [He] seemed bemused by Trump’s entertaining approach to hospitality.” Chinese President Xi Jinping rarely missed an opportunity to reinforce Beijing’s geopolitical message. Annabelle Gordon - Pool via CNP While in Washington, the Chinese president repeatedly cast China and the US as two “major countries” who shouldered special responsibility to not just steer their own relationship, but to chart a course for the world. Implicit therein is the positioning of Beijing and Washington on an equal footing. Zhao Minghao, a professor of Sino-US relations at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said Beijing would be happy with the summit and the way it projected Xi as Trump’s equal, though it would have preferred a six-month or yearlong extension to the trade truce.



“If US–China summit meetings can help preserve channels and avoid a new shock, it is of great worth,” Zhao said. “Beijing measures success by process, symmetry and de-escalation, not by comprehensive agreements that were never expected.” But it was not just policy that was invisible at this meeting. While there was plenty of pomp, circumstance and goodwill, most of it was not broadcast to Americans. Donald Trump showed off his new helipad to Xi Jinping, including its granite. AP That’s because the five major TV networks - Fox News, ABC, CBS, NBC and CNN - did not participate in the “pool” that films presidential events and distributes footage to other stations around the country. They had refused to take part in solidarity with CNN, which Trump had banned from the White House and the pool. The ban was fully lifted on Friday (Washington DC local time), and their participation resumed. But it meant reduced exposure of an event crafted with visuals front of mind.



On Friday, the Chinese Communist Party’s official newspaper, the People’s Daily, splashed its front page with six photos of Xi’s US visit, featuring him being greeted by Trump on the tarmac, the red carpet welcome at the White House, and the two leaders shaking hands in the Oval Office. The optics matter immensely for the Chinese, says Dylan Loh, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. First Lady Melania Trump took her counterpart Peng Liyuan to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian American Art. Finn Gomez/POOL Getty Images North America via AP “It allows Beijing to demonstrate to their domestic audiences - and really to the rest of the world - that they are the US’s peer,” says Loh. “And to say: the US is giving us the respect that we have historically not necessarily gotten. We have arrived.” Zhao said China now saw itself as a co-equal great power that could withstand US economic force, and had been surprised by how quickly Trump had shifted from extreme confrontation and tariff brinkmanship to accepting Beijing’s framework of “constructive strategic stability”.



“Beijing does not believe rivalry is over,” Zhao said. “Tech decoupling, Taiwan and military mistrust remain. But it judges the balance of psychological initiative to have shifted. China can afford patience and incremental truce management.” Related Article Updated

Foreign relations ‘Major countries’ US and China must co-operate on the world’s problems: Xi Feigenbaum, who is also a former deputy assistant secretary of state for south and central Asia under George W. Bush, reached a similar conclusion. China is aware of Trump’s propensity to say almost anything. They also know that whatever Trump says or does, it does not necessarily commit the next US president. “The Chinese objective is just to ringfence the worst outcomes with the US, park the Americans in a corner and then pursue their opportunities elsewhere, where they actually have them,” Feigenbaum said. “That’s their view of it.”

World.title: Rock and roll, fantasy and Silicon Valley fascism: 10 new books
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This week’s fiction includes a moving work set in the aftermath of the American Civil War to a world filled with magical animals, while non-fiction ranges across the local rock scene, the heroes and villains of history and WWII fighter pilots. Fiction The Newer World by Sebastian Barry (Allen & Unwin $34.99) Some may quibble that as a white Irishman, Sebastian Barry ought not to have the authorial right to adopt the voice of Tennyson Bouguereau, a black man navigating the messy aftermath of the Civil War. But if anyone can perform this act of cultural ventriloquism well, it’s Barry. The Newer World navigates the world of Tennyson, who, alongside his twin sister, was born into slavery but eventually freed, only to discover that freedom is not necessarily equivalent to acceptance in the deep American South. The newer world is not that much shinier than the old one. From rural Tennessee to Nashville, where Tennyson, with his beautiful voice, is given a chance to join a choir, and then to England when he goes on tour, and then back to America, Barry recreates the 19th-century period with vividness and colour. Written in the first person, this historical fiction is elegantly wrought. Like his poetic namesake, Tennyson’s descriptive mannerisms are filled with rhythmic, lyrical touches that can seem grandiose at times. But the narrative balances racism and trauma with hope and transformation. Strange Familiars by Keshe Chow (Hachette, $34.99)



Two academic rivals at a College of Magical Veterinary Sciences battle it out: in the one corner is earnest and hard-working Gwendolynne Chan, and facing her is rich nepo baby Harrisford Briggs. The reader will be forgiving for thinking the novel will focus on cutesy and strange animals doing fantastic tricks before they become injured, but Keshe Chow leads the narrative elsewhere. Set in an alternate London, her world-building involves the pair trying to figure out why there’s excessive magic that turns the animal-familiars feral and also causes explosions in the city. They have to join forces to stop the surges. Strange Familiars is told through alternate viewpoints of the protagonists as they investigate competing organisations that distribute and oppose the global supply of magic. The enemy-to-lovers trope is predictable, with Chow at full rein in exploring the romantasy genre. It’s a fun read – the first instalment of a series of two, and Percy, Gwen’s snarky telepathic cat, is a joyful addition. If only there were more magical animals in the mix. Female Life on Planet Earth by Laleh Khadivi (Oneworld, $32.99) Set in Los Angeles, this novel is about secret lives and the relationships between mothers and daughters. It focuses on the year Heti spends after the death of her mother, Anahita. While she plans a large-scale mourning anniversary at the urging of her bossy traditionalist aunt, Heti receives a mysterious package containing photos of a younger Anahita, enveloped in a black veil and carrying a machine gun. The mother Heti knew and loved was sweet and nurturing – who was this fighter in combat mode? What follows is a series of conversational vignettes with strangers about what it means to be a woman. But too much time and energy are spent on such peripheral musings, with comparatively scant details about Anahita’s past only allowed to surface toward the end. Though the book obviously references revolutionary Iran, it’s odd that Laleh Khadivi refrains from mentioning the country. Perhaps she’s aiming for universality of themes about war, religious fanaticism, persecution, womanhood, diaspora, and immigration, but depersonalising the context does a disservice to the narrative. Midwest by Caitlin Maling (Upswell, $27.99) In this suite of poems, Caitlin Maling roams the coastal waters of Western Australia with a keen eye. Mailing grew up in and around Fremantle, and her love of the vistas around this port city is evident. Midwest, her sixth poetry collection, continues her exploration of the natural world, especially its watery depths and the animals that live or at least struggle to survive within or near the sea. As the Tour Guide at the Ocean Park Marina and Aquarium puts it, “Everything you see is food, sex or death.” Whether it’s sea eagles nesting, parrotfish pecking at coral, sea snakes copulating or crabs being cracked open to eat, Maling’s words are visceral and sometimes startling. There are shipwrecks, salmon farming and single-celled organisms called stromatolites among the mix. Among her descriptions of the birds and beasts, she also writes about motherhood and her young son. Sometimes Maling’s metaphorical reach will make you stop and consider the world anew – she describes rock as “breaking out of the earth like bones” and an octopus’ nodules like “Mardi Gras beads, but finer filigree.”



Gone Guru by Nadine Browne (Fremantle Press, $34.99) Noni has flown into New York from WA and barely settled in her Harlem apartment when she discovers that her new flatmate, Vincent, a self-styled transcendental meditation guru with millions of followers and millions in a trust fund, has disappeared. Maybe he’s too busy trying to find himself? Though Noni has distractions of her own – she’s failing to combat imposter syndrome at a prestigious writing program – she becomes invested in finding him. Noni’s trying to think of a story for her class while navigating the strangeness of a new city; the missing Vincent may just be the catalyst she needs. Gone Guru is an auto-fiction, with Nadine Browne drawing on her own experiences. Partly a sleuthing story, with the clamour, colour, vibrancy, and characters of New York as a background, and partly an exploration into the challenges of being a creative writer (particularly with someone as intimidating as Joyce Carol Oates as a teacher), the book is an enjoyable and funny romp that surveys serious issues (race, class, identity, literature, culture) with a light touch. Non-fiction A History of the World in 51 Heroes and Villains by Tom Holland & Dominic Sandbrook (Bloomsbury, $36.99)



History is, of course, about far more than heroes and villains, but they can be a lot of fun, as The Rest is History podcast team demonstrates in this collection of cameos. And they’re not all human, either. Like Wojtek, the Syrian brown bear adopted by the Polish army in exile during WWII, who lugged heavy crates of munitions up the slopes of Monte Cassino, Italy, during the Allied advance and made a highly valued contribution to the war effort. Much loved by the troops, and with a penchant for cigarettes and stealing women’s underwear, Wojtek eventually died in the Edinburgh Zoo, an undisputed hero with his own statue. Some of the other figures, however, aren’t so clear-cut. The mad monk, Savonarola, for example, lauded by some as a Reformationist hero combating excessive wealth and corruption, and reviled by others as a murdering, puritanical fruitcake. Then there are the mysteries, like Elizabeth 1. Was she really a virgin, or just good at “branding”? Incorporated into a tale that stretches from Roman times (Boadicea gets a guernsey) to the 20th century are potted biographies of the likes of US-born photographer, war correspondent and former model Lee Miller, who famously soaked herself in Hitler’s bath. Reading this is a bit like opening a packet of potato chips; once you start it’s really difficult to stop. In the Realm of the Last Man by Francis Fukuyama (Profile, $45) Francis Fukuyama is best known for 1989 essay The End of History, which, he argues in this combination of memoir and dissertation, was wrongly interpreted as a piece of neo-conservative triumphalism – at the same time, stating that he was part of the neo-conservative clique that included the likes of Irving Kristol. Since then, he’s changed his mind, left old alignments behind, and moved closer to the left. What happened? Two things: the Iraq invasion of 2003, which he opposed after concluding that the post-war period of reconstruction would be a disaster, and the GFC that followed not long after, and which led him to question and reject the twin neo-conservative precepts of largely unfettered marketplace capitalism and a strictly limited government role. He might still talk of “history” in quasi metaphysical, qualified Hegelian terms, but his engaging, plain-speaking essays demonstrate that the mind (not just history) is constantly evolving, that someone can break free of outmoded beliefs and world views to see things anew. The Nerd Reich by Gil Duran (Simon & Schuster, $36.99) Once upon a time, Silicon Valley was the home of nerdy, vaguely left-leaning liberals. All that has changed. These days it sits at Trump’s table and with sinister intentions. When Elon Musk waved a chainsaw around at a Conservative convention just after Trump’s second coming (the chainsaw symbolising ruthless cuts to government and bureaucracy), the New Yorker announced Techno Fascism comes to America. Journalist and political advisor Duran traces its rise from the late 1990s to the present day. And he paints a truly alarming picture of the world’s most obscenely wealthy men being invited into the Trump administration on a mass scale. These techno-oligarchs, he argues, aren’t content to work within the democratic system – they hate it, want to destroy and replace governments and countries with corporate city states. To counter it, he says, we need to “rethink our relationship with technology, which means rethinking what it means to be human”. Welcome to the new fascism and the “Nerd Reich”, funded by cryptocurrency, enabled by AI and run by oligarchs with deep-seated, anti-democratic, global ambitions.

World.title: Dune 3 will be a hit, but there’s one mad version we’ll never get to see
World.content:
Even the dreams of top directors get left on the cutting room floor. In some cases, it’s a blessing.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This year’s much-anticipated touchdown of Denis Villeneuve’s third Dune film coincides with the 50th anniversary of the most valiant yet doomed attempt to bring Frank Herbert’s science-fiction epic to the screen. This earlier quixotic quest eclipsed even the interstellar ambitions of Villeneuve and his team. In the 1970s, Chilean-French auteur Alejandro Jodorowsky embarked on an unhinged mission to shoot a Dune film equivalent to an acid trip. His assembled cast included Orson Welles, Gloria Swanson and Mick Jagger; Pink Floyd were on soundtrack duties; French illustrator Moebius and artist H.R. Giger (of Alien fame) designed the psychedelic visuals. Even surrealist grandmaster Salvador Dali signed on, demanding an hourly rate of $100,000. Jodorowsky’s script was 14 hours long, and the production “bible” he created stretched to almost 300 pages (a rare copy sold for $4.3 million – 110 times the expected figure – at Christie’s in 2021). The film was too ludicrous to manifest in reality but it did spawn Jodorowsky’s Dune (2013), a wildly entertaining documentary tracing the making of a film that wasn’t made. Has there ever been another unrealised pipe dream so tantalising in its promise that other films have been made about it? Artist H. R. Giger in Jodorowsky’s Dune. Alamy Stock Photo As it happens, yes. Jon Schnepp’s The Death of ‘Superman Lives’: What Happened? (2015) offers a glimpse of the monstrosity that might have been had Tim Burton directed his Superman movie with Nicolas Cage as the Man of Steel. Christopher Walken, Courteney Cox and Sandra Bullock were picked for supporting roles, the script was penned by Kevin Smith (Mallrats) and the whole fiasco was produced by Jon Peters, a former hairdresser who insisted that his Man of Steel wasn’t allowed to fly or wear the red-and-blue outfit, and that the film end with Superman fighting a giant spider. Jon Schnepp with Tim Burton, who never got to make Superman Lives. These non-existent movies are just two of the countless unrealised projects that are like cinema’s dark matter: you’ll never see them but their sheer volume holds everything else together. Miles Davis is alleged to have said that great music is about the notes you don’t play; the films a director doesn’t make might be as important as those they do.



For most of his life Stanley Kubrick maintained an obsessive drive to create a film about Napoleon, even enlisting the support of 50,000 members of the Romanian People’s Army to re-enact battles. It wasn’t to be. For every Basic Instinct or Starship Troopers Paul Verhoeven has directed, there are dozens of films he’s had to abandon: Tom Cruise as Houdini, the early years of Adolf Hitler, a take on the life of Jesus. And who wouldn’t pay to see Luca Guadagnino’s American Psycho? Darren Aronofsky’s RoboCop? John Carpenter’s Top Gun, Fatal Attraction or Santa Claus: the Movie? In an alternate timeline all of these exist. But history is haunted by the spectres of films that don’t. Some are the victims of overreaching ambition, while others are vanity projects best left unrealised. A depressing number find themselves wallowing in “development hell”, the industry term for productions that sink into an eternal cycle of script rewrites, studio changes and funding sinkholes. Jon Peters – the aforementioned hairdresser-turned-producer (and one-time Barbra Streisand squeeze) – is the kind of colourful Hollywood character who can pave the way to development hell. After he attained the rights to Neil Gaiman’s classic Sandman series, he offered up what the author described as “quite easily the worst script I’ve ever read”. Again, there was the inexplicable inclusion of a giant spider (a dream Peters finally realised on 1999’s Wild Wild West, a film critics lambasted).



Some of the greatest hits (or likely misses) we can only imagine: Stanley Kubrick’s Lord of the Rings with Paul McCartney as Frodo and John Lennon as Gollum; Sofia Coppola’s The Little Mermaid, reportedly too dark and risky to finance; indie darling Lynne Ramsay’s unlikely foray into western territory on Jane Got a Gun, which was completed to lukewarm reviews by Gavin O’Connor; Spike Lee’s remake of Bruce Lee’s Enter the Dragon with comedian Ken Jeong in the kung fu king’s role; disaster master Roland Emmerich’s entry in the James Bond franchise. The list of off-kilter choices to direct Return of the Jedi is enough to induce whiplash. Terry Gilliam would likely have spun off the series in an odd direction but just imagine what Davids Lynch or Cronenberg would have done had they said yes to the job. Related Article The Verdict Other people’s dreams bore me rigid. So why are films and TV shows full of them? And picture the iconic Wolverine played not by Hugh Jackman but by the notably less ripped Bob Hoskins, who was originally slated for the role in the first X-Men adaptation, then to be directed by Kathryn Bigelow. Bigelow’s own filmography illustrates how the films that don’t get made are as illustrative as those that do. In the 1990s she headed up a string of genre classics, from erotic thriller Blue Steel to surfer heist caper Point Break. Post-9/11, though, she took a hard shift towards serious, politically provocative films such as The Hurt Locker and Zero Dark Thirty. Her catalogue of unrealised projects since that point drives home this career turn, full of titles such as Held by the Taliban, Mogadishu Minnesota and The True American. Australian directors might struggle to get projects up here but the difficulty can scale up exponentially when they arrive in Tinseltown. Jocelyn Moorhouse’s adaptation of Murray Bail’s Eucalyptus was production-ready in 2005, featuring a dream team of Nicole Kidman and Russell Crowe, before Fox Searchlight canned the project. Fellow Australian Peter Weir’s filmography may include Picnic at Hanging Rock, Dead Poets Society, The Truman Show, Witness and Green Card but many subsequent projects failed to gain traction and he eventually announced he was quitting the game.



Development hell is a place particular to big-name filmmakers, simply by virtue of their clout. Studios won’t pander to an up-and-comer whose ideas don’t wash but when a Kubrick or a Spielberg has a passion project, they’re not so easily dismissed. Ordering endless rounds of casting changes and screenplay revisions is a way to keep the big earners appeased without actually committing to their financially dubious hobby horses. Adam Driver and Nathalie Emmanuel in Francis Ford Coppola’s bloated Megalopolis. And sometimes the bean counters aren’t the villains of the story. Quentin Tarantino’s Star Trek, set in 1930s Chicago? Hard pass. Sylvester Stallone’s film about Edgar Allan Poe with himself in the lead? Nevermore! Francis Ford Coppola’s Megalopolis spent almost half a century in development hell; he ultimately financed the production himself, the result a sprawling mess that earned less than 10 per cent of its $120 million production budget. Sometimes a dream is better left that way. Zack Snyder’s bombastic Hollywood fare – 300, Man of Steel, Justice League – has been box-office dynamite but after decades in development hell he finally self-produced his dream project, The Last Photograph. It debuted at the recent Toronto International Film Festival, with critics dubbing it “supremely indulgent auteur gunk”, “boring, bloated, brutally violent” and “an utter disgrace from start to finish … Snyder at his most unfiltered, with no studio intervention”. It’s about the notes you don’t play, Mr Snyder, and the giant spiders you keep to yourself. The cruellest cut It’s one thing for a passion project to go unrealised but another level of heartbreak awaits filmmakers who complete a work only for it never to see the light of day.



Coyote vs. Acme, completed in 2023, rated well with test audiences before Warner Bros Discovery decided to shelve it as a $30 million tax write-off. It took a concerted campaign by indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment (and a $50 million price tag) for the film to finally make it to screens. As of writing, it holds a 96 per cent score on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes. Related Article Cinema Warner Bros axed this Looney Tunes movie. But fans refused to accept defeat Few similar tales achieve such a happy ending. The DC superhero flick Batgirl featured a stacked cast including Leslie Grace (In the Heights), J.K. Simmons, Brendan Fraser and Michael Keaton returning to the suit he first squeezed into for Tim Burton’s 1989 Batman. The film was close to completion when Warner Bros Discovery cancelled its release and wrote off another $90 million tax-wise. Other films have been consigned to the vaults for less financial reasons. The most famous is probably Jerry Lewis’ The Day the Clown Cried, in which a clown sent to a Nazi concentration camp attempts to offer hope to the children imprisoned there. After viewing a rough cut the co-writer declared it was unfit for public viewing and denied all rights for release. James Franco’s The Long Home was completed in 2016, with a cast including Josh Hutcherson, Courtney Love, Ashton Kutcher and Josh Hartnett. Allegations of inappropriate sexual behaviour by Franco during the shoot, however, ensured that the finished film has never been publicly screened. In 2009 Tony Kaye (American History X) completed a rough cut of post-Hurricane Katrina crime drama Black Water Transit but the work became a hot potato in a series of legal disputes that culminated in one of the film’s producers being sentenced to eight years in prison for fraud. Some nearly finished films have been denied the fairytale rescue Coyote vs. Acme has enjoyed. The 2025 musical comedy-drama Golden had some serious talent flex: Michel Gondry directing, Pharrell Williams as co-producer and composer, and an all-star line-up including Janelle Monae, Missy Elliott and Andre 3000, but Universal Studios cancelled the film before it was released.

World.title: ‘Computer says no’: I asked AI the pitfalls of asking AI for money advice
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingAI Opinion ‘Computer says no’: I asked AI the pitfalls of asking AI for money advice Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor September 26, 2026 — 6:00am

September 26, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Managing money well can be, well, confusing. It can even be confronting. And how are many of us are solving such issues these days with the help of artificial intelligence “buddies”. Heck, I even have friends who use AI to draft replies to tricky text messages from their mum. AI can look well-reasoned and comprehensive, giving you a sense of security when you should have nothing of the sort. iStock So is it any surprise that more than three million Australians are already using AI to help manage their financial activity, with the highest number – 25 per cent – among Gen Z Australians, says a new Understanding Modern Australia report. Not that we necessarily – thank goodness – trust it. The report, by life insurer TAL with McCrindle, found only 22 per cent of us feel comfortable using AI to help make major financial decisions and only 20 per cent trust AI to recommend a financial product suited to their needs.



So, I thought I’d try an experiment: I asked AI the pitfalls of asking AI for money advice – and whoa. In an emphatic “computer-says-no”, here are the 10 reasons the AI gave me not to use it – and how I might. (I’ve grouped them where AI doubled and even tripled down.) ‘An LLM’s training data has a cut-off, and even with web search, it can miss nuance, fail to update thresholds, blend outdated and current rules without flagging the difference.’ An AI’s response 1. No accountability or duty of care Yep, good point Claude! No care and no responsibility does not make for the ideal economic confidante. The rules and requirements to give financial advice in Australia are strict. AI is not bound by any of them.



Related Article Opinion

Sharemarket Want to learn how to invest? Here are three expert tricks and the rule of 72 Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor The education needed is also now extensive (part of why the profession is shrinking). But, mainly, a licensed financial adviser is bound by law to act in your best interest. In the candid confession, AI said: “An LLM has no such obligation and no licence that can be revoked if it gets things wrong.” 2. Regulatory grey zone You need an Australian Financial Services Licence to give personal financial advice – it’s illegal otherwise. Reputable AI tools build in disclaimers and stick to general information rather than personal advice. But how do you even tell the difference when it’s – you know – you asking?



3, 4 and 5. Lack of personalisation depth. Generic, one-size-fits-all framing. Data privacy Variables that factor into smart financial decisions include your age, income, debts, risk tolerance, tax situation, existing assets, super balance, insurance and goals. Does your AI know all of this about you? And, crucially, do you want it to? Where does that data go and how is it stored? “Even if they did, an LLM isn’t verifying any of it or cross-checking for inconsistencies the way a human adviser would,” confides the LLM itself. The “cookie cutter” alternative isn’t great, either. The advice might just be versions of old financial adages like diversify, pay off debt and invest for the long term. They may not fit with your financial affairs at that moment. 6. Currency and accuracy problems



This is a massive one. Legislation changes regularly. Even in the past year, we have seen changes to the first home buyer 5 per cent deposit scheme, an overhaul of capital gains and a ban on negative gearing. Um, I won’t be trusting AI with any related financial decisions thank you! Related Article Opinion

Superannuation The best retirement advice you can give your friends Bec Wilson Money contributor Then there are just the regular updates and indexation to things like tax brackets, super contribution caps, income thresholds and interest rates. Old information could easily sink your future. Need proof? “An LLM’s training data has a cut-off, and even with web search, it can miss nuance, fail to update thresholds, blend outdated and current rules without flagging the difference.” Thanks, Claude. 7 and 8. A false sense of diligence and confident-sounding errors (aka “hallucinations”)



We’ve all encountered this - AI intel that’s slightly insane! And the danger it poses in complex financial information or advice is: would you even recognise it? AI can look well-reasoned and comprehensive, giving you a sense of security when you should have nothing of the sort. How’s this for candour: “LLMs can state incorrect figures, invent products or rules that don’t exist, or misapply a rule from one country’s system (e.g., US 401k rules) to Australia’s superannuation system, all while sounding authoritative.” 9. No understanding of behavioural or emotional context Factor in your state of mind? That you might be responding based on your childhood “conditioning” rather than actual conditions? Or that you might have a different risk tolerance to the questions you are asking? An AI model can’t possibly do this. Indeed: “An LLM responds to the words in the prompt, not the psychology behind them.”



10. No ongoing relationship or follow-through A financial plan needs to evolve with you. But we’ve come full-circle to the point above about how much your LLM remembers, and whether you actually want it to. We’ve all encountered this – AI intel that’s slightly insane! The danger it poses in complex financial information or advice is: would you even recognise it? Nine Finally, I loved AI’s very watery disclaimer at the end of the list, compared with the one we are required to use (see below!). “AI can be a decent starting point for financial literacy and generating questions to ask a professional, but it’s a poor substitute for licensed, personalised advice.” So, would I use AI for financial information? Only while good primary sources of that information still exist and are disclosed so I can check the pedigree and recency. (And those days are numbered as AI drives such traffic-based sites out of business.)



But AI for financial advice? Not unless you could interrogate just the one trusted financial philosophy, teaching or expert. Why would you put your money where AI’s possibly hallucinating mouth is? Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. Expert tips on how to save, invest and make the most of your money delivered to your inbox every Sunday.

World.title: Pretty lies for an audience of one: life as a biographer for hire
World.content:
CultureBooksPublishing Pretty lies for an audience of one: life as a biographer for hire Like Pol Pot’s portraitist, the big man’s scribe is on shaky ground. Anson Cameron September 26, 2026 — 5:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Out of sight of the reading public, unbeknown to bibliophiles, unsuspected by the churners-through of this year’s Top 10 Must Read lists, ignored by the bookshops and poo-poohed by publishers, biographies and histories are being penned for sums of money so large their authors are J.K. Rowling in money. Almost every big man sitting, Mojito in hand, beside his own swimming pool outside his beach house in Byron eventually begins to worry that his extraordinary life will disappear, unrecorded, uncelebrated. It’s a galling realisation when, Lord knows, a quest as righteous as his has been might be used to instruct his grandchildren, currently mewling, unenlightened, in their $5000 Danish bassinets. Photo: Robin Cowcher Their thoughts go something like this: “My glory years controlling the firm must be captured for posterity. For the sake of the family – an important history recording the brave battles I fought and won, allowing us to dominate markets where lesser men and firms foundered.” Next thing, these poolside giants are looking for an amanuensis. A friend of mine hires himself out to write self-published biographies for ex-CEOs and other assorted big men, histories of famous families and renowned Australian companies. No surprise it’s generally men who recognise their lives must be mythologised or the world be poorer.



The trick, if you want to write a biography of an emeritus CEO, is to find a big-swinging dick who isn’t a dick. But it’s more likely you’ll write a biography for a yeti than that. Your client will be difficult – bordering on Stalinesque. These self-funded wannabe biographees have run worlds without recourse to manners, laws or morals. Related Article Opinion

Friendship Kev’s mates put a GPS tracker on his car. Then they discovered his awful secret Anson Cameron Spectrum columnist, The Age When you sign on to write a biography of Clarence Dinklinker AC you better realise he wants a story in which he is Galahad. Don’t be a fool and let your journalistic ethics, historian’s integrity, proven methodologies, or just plain old honesty lead you astray, towards objectivity and fact. You’re not writing this book for a readership – you’re writing it for a reader. Dinklinker wants a hagiography, plain and simple. He wants to look like Steve McQueen with cojones like cantaloupes and a halo like a truck tyre. No one who’s spent a life befuddling the ATO and battling unions to make a fortune against the odds wants to be cynically celebrated in amber ambiguity like Serrano’s Piss Christ. But... do you remember the first time you heard your recorded voice? It sounded like a stranger, didn’t it? You don’t sound like that. A biographee experiences a similar dissociation. Big, important fellows never recognise the self they know and idolise in the book they’ve paid someone to write about them. So writing a biography of a Dinklinker is as risky as being Pol Pot’s portraitist... “Are you suggesting, with your laboured draftsmanship, that my eyes are set so close together?”



I met my friend, the freelancing biographer, in a cafe last week. He was on brief furlough from a shitstorm – thin-faced and pale and his pinot gris a choppy puddle in a shaky hand. He currently has four books run aground on the reef-egos of big men. They don’t agree with what he’s written. They won’t pay for anything less than an anthem and he still has a homeopathic inkling of integrity that won’t let him deliver. He’s entangled in a history of a canning business where the three brothers who founded the company all insist on being the hero and that the other two coat-tail-riding layabouts be given mere walk-on roles. Another of his bespoke mires is a history of a mining company in which he’s serving a dozen different masters, all ex-directors and CEOs, who have got up a riot of contradictory narcissistic fabrications and exculpatory balderdash. Not only have they conflicting “memories” of who sired the company, they’re willing to sue if their paternity is questioned in print. There he sat in our little local cafe, the biographer for hire, cowed by the protagonists of his various works-in-progress, at war with balding gangs of once greatish men, holding on, trying to write something closer to true than they will swallow. I pitied him. He had mistresses to hide, bankruptcies to gloss over, prosecutions to de-emphasise, failed mergers to justify... It’s no easy thing writing history to order if you fancy yourself honest. Or once did. But the wealthy pay big for pretty lies, and a man’s got to eat. On our second bottle he mumbled, “What a joy it would be to write of an utter nobody, like you do.”
