Spectrum Anson Cameron is a columnist for Spectrum in The Age and the author of several books, including Boyhoodlum and Neil Balme: A Tale of Two Men.

World.title: ACT promises noise cameras to combat boy racers in Tāmaki
World.content:
The ACT Party is pledging to crack down on noisy vehicles and hike fines for drivers causing a nuisance.

It wants to spend $2 million on buying and installing 20 relocatable noise cameras, initially rolling them out in Tāmaki.

ACT Tāmaki candidate James Christmas said his election campaign door-knocking missions had drawn consistent pleas to do something about noisy neighbourhoods.

"People should be able to sleep, relax and enjoy their homes, without having their street turned into someone else's racetrack," he said.

"I can see the attraction for boy racers to come to Tāmaki, but it's not fair on the families and working people who have their life disrupted, just because they live in a great location with nice streets."

Such disturbance was already illegal, but effective enforcement relied on a police officer being in the right place at the right time, Christmas said.

If elected, ACT would:

Introduce a fleet of relocatable noise cameras to be deployed in communities frequented by excessively noisy vehicles

Establish an objective noise limit measured by the cameras (86 decibels on roads with speed limits of 50 km/h or less and 90 decibels on roads between 50-70 km/h)

Increase penalties for excessive vehicle noise from $50 to $300, with the maximum court fine increasing from $1000 to $3000.

World.title: 'Disrespectful', 'unprofessional': Principal and education minister at odds over speech
World.content:
The Principals' Federation president and the education minister are firing insults at one another after Erica Stanford's speech at a recent conference.

The federation (NZPF) issued a bitter review of last week's speech to the International Confederation of Principals Convention, labelling it embarrassing, disappointing and disrespectful.

Stanford hit back, calling NZPF president Jason Miles' behaviour rude, aggressive and unprofessional.

Following the speech, Miles emailed members saying Stanford had exploited the opportunity.

"This was a significant global convention and it felt apt to invite Aotearoa New Zealand's minister of education to welcome the audience and acknowledge the convention's significance," he said.

"It was not, however, an opportunity for the minister to use the global stage to promote her party policies."

In the speech, Stanford highlighted the Government's education reforms designed to address flagging achievement, and pointed out its successes. She did not reference National Party policies.

Stanford acknowledged the hard work of principals and specified nine associations and groups that had been helpful to her - omitting her hosts, the NZPF.

Miles said the snub was divisive and showed Stanford did not value his organisation.

"Our work over the past three years to bring this event to New Zealand was ignored, and her decision not to recognise the International Confederation of Principals president and executive sitting directly in front of her was also extremely disrespectful," he wrote.

Miles said the convention coordinator had specifically outlined the intent of the speech to the minister's office.

"I quote: 'This is the opening of the convention only. It is not an opportunity for a policy or political speech. 5 - 10 minutes please'," he wrote.

"This was followed up with further correspondence and clarification to her office, including requests from me to the secretary of education to reiterate the non-political, welcoming intent of the speech."

NZPF president Jason Miles. Supplied / NZPF

Miles said after the minister's speech he asked why she continued to decline opportunities to meet with him, and she replied "because you go to the media".

NZPF is proposing an independent curriculum and assessment council, saying that could ensure changes are driven by experts rather than politicians and end what it believes is disruptive education reform.

Miles said he had sought meetings with Stanford to discuss it, but she had not found the time.

The NZPF's response comes amid accusations of a culture of secrecy surrounding curriculum changes.

Minister condemns sector leader's behaviour

Stanford said she used her speech to praise the progress of the education system lifting achievement.

She said she had thanked NZPF and acknowledged the work of other education groups.

"I was surprised and disappointed by Jason Miles' inappropriate behaviour towards me immediately after my speech, which was rude, aggressive and unprofessional," she said.

"His subsequent correspondence and comments do not accurately reflect the speech I gave, which is available online for anyone to read."

Stanford said she had met with NZPF before and appreciated it would like more opportunities but that was not possible given the volume of her commitments.

World.title: Crash blocks Waikato Expressway, injuries feared
World.content:
The Waikato Expressway is closed in both directions following a serious crash.

Police said the single-vehicle accident happened near Whangamarino, northbound, between the Rodda Road on-ramp and the Hampton Downs off-ramp.

"Initial indications are that one person may be seriously injured, and others may have sustained moderate injuries."

It was not clear when precisely the accident occurred.

Police said with all four lanes of SH1 closed, there could be "significant delays" and diversions were in place.

World.title: Oceania Rugby says no money to host Oceania Sevens Cup in Rotorua
World.content:
Oceania Rugby has cancelled the 2026 Oceania Rugby Sevens Cup planned for Rotorua on 31 October and 1 November.

General manager Frank Puletua said in a statement they do not have the funds to hold the event as announced two weeks ago.

"This is not the outcome anyone wanted, and I'm sorry for the disappointment it causes our players, teams, fans and the Rotorua community," Puletua said on Friday.

"We pursued every option to deliver this tournament. When it became clear we could not secure the funding needed in the time available, the responsible decision was not to proceed.

"We own that decision.

"Our focus now is on looking after the teams, ticket holders and partners affected, and on securing a qualification pathway for our players."

The 2026 Oceania Rugby 7s Cup was also scheduled to provide the regional qualification pathway for eligible Oceania men's and women's teams to the World Rugby SVNS 3 - third-tier - event.

Puletua said they have been unable to secure the funding required to deliver the event within the available timeframe, even though key stakeholders, including World Rugby, had made funding commitments in full.

"With the tournament only weeks away and significant financial and operational commitments now required to proceed, Oceania Rugby has made the difficult but responsible decision not to proceed... rather than take on further commitments without the funding certainty to meet them," he said.

"This decision has not been made lightly. We recognise the significant planning, preparation and commitment that has already gone into bringing international sevens rugby to Rotorua."

He acknowledged the work undertaken by RotoruaNZ and its local partners in preparing to host the tournament.

But he is hopeful that Rotorua will still put their hands up to host the 2027 event.

"Oceania Rugby understands the disappointment this cancellation will cause and sincerely appreciates the commitment and support shown by everyone involved."

World.title: Want to put a bounty on the head of a cyber criminal? Now you can
World.content:
A new international programme has put a $40,000 bounty on a group of hackers that attacked the health system in New Zealand last year.

It is the first bounty issued under Crime Stoppers International's scheme to help police crack down.

Glenn Maiden, who helped set it up, says the first target is a prolific group Inc Ransomware - if the criminals in it are prosecuted, the bounty can be paid to the informant.

"In the case of Inc Ransomware, they will get US$22,000 (NZ$37,000)," Maiden told RNZ.

"The bounty isn't limited to that US$22,000. So if you've got more or less than that you want to post a bounty, we'll absolutely look at it."

Inc Ransom has been hacking in Australasia and the Pacific, and last year raided data from a Wellington medical centre. The national cyber watchdog warned against the group.

Immediate warning

Hackers have grabbed worldwide attention this week by going after the FBI and after a break-in on Australian government agencies by an OpenAI swarm on its own volition.

The extortion group 'ShinyHunters' claimed to have breached the Federal Bureau of Investigation and stolen data on a huge number of its employees. ShinyHunters was named by Maiden as a group they wanted to go after.

In Australia advanced models broke out of OpenAI testbeds to get into health, justice and other government sites off their own bat, in what some researchers say is the first autonomous hack of government sites.

But OpenAI did not tell the government for weeks, and it is reported to be looking at legal options to punish OpenAI.

The NZ Government initially said only it was well aware of the issues of frontier or advanced AI and the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) was working on it.

Digitising Minister Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

When asked again by RNZ if he had considered what the Australia attack meant for New Zealand and if he would approach the big AI developers, Digitising Minister Paul Goldsmith said, "NCSC is in contact with its Australian counterparts about the Open AI incident.

"The NCSC is in contact with frontier AI companies and will be seeking assurance that any incidents affecting New Zealand government agencies are immediately reported to the affected agency and to the NCSC."

How bounties work

Maiden said the CyberCrime Bounty Programme could take the offer of a bounty from anyone - after some vetting - not necessarily a hacking victim but, say, from someone wanting to do a bit of good, as is the case with the Inc Ransom offer.

The programme then received anonymous tipoffs to identify the cyber criminals personally, and if they are prosecuted it paid out the tipster.

A company supporting it, Fortinet - Maiden is chief security officer for Fortinet Australia - pulled the tips together and assessed them before they go to police.

The scheme had echoes of FBI 'Most Wanted' posters but went further so that the likes of New Zealand organisations targeted by hackers had a means to support bounties to hit back, Maiden said.

"It raises some interesting questions for New Zealand," said Crime Stoppers.

"International ransomware groups can operate across borders and jurisdictions that local authorities cannot easily follow - will this kind of public-private model help close those gaps?"

Crime Stoppers International's chief security officer Glenn Maiden. Supplied / Crime Stoppers International

Prosecuting criminals in some countries might prove tough, said Maiden.

But it was already working with Europol and Interpol against non-cyber criminal groups in eastern Europe, so had experience.

"So it's not always a failure but it definitely is difficult."

As to the OpenAI Australia hack, RNZ asked the NCSC and Health NZ if they knew of similar incidents here. The NCSC did not say.

Goldsmith said the Government was already working with a number of partners and companies on the application of advanced AI tools, and was "actively strengthening our defences".

Health NZ said it was not aware of any instances of autonomous AI agents or AI companies gaining unauthorised access to Health NZ systems.

"Artificial intelligence is a rapidly evolving area, and we continually review our cyber security posture and defences to ensure they remain appropriate to the changing threat environment.

World.title: Country Life:150 years of Tinui School
World.content:
Back in 1876, children at Tinui School would make their way to school on horseback, now they ride in utes and SUVs.

Bright modern classrooms, walls adorned with children's artwork and education materials - all was on show on a sunny spring day when the school threw open its doors to welcome students past and present to celebrate 150 years.

Like the school itself, Tinui has changed a lot in that time, with a smaller school roll a reflection of changing land use.

Audio player for " 150 years of Tinui School " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/country/1583272%2Fcountry-life-150-years-of-tinui-school

150 years of Tinui School Country Life Download MP3 21m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

European settler farmers began moving into Tinui in the 1850s, and by the 1870s the village was established, and the first school was founded in 1876 - a combination master's residence and boarding school.

Attendance back then was spotty, local historian Caryl Forrest told Country Life.

"There was still a problem that went on for a very long time with children being [absent] when they did a big muster prior to shearing and during shearing. Boys of about 11 and 12 were expected to be on the farm helping.

"Farming was very labour intensive. They had really, really big paddocks compared with today."

Close to 200 people attended the weekend's celebrations, with multiple activities held over the three days - from class pictures across the decades, to drinks, dinners and of course a Sunday church service. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Former students gathered for the reunion and to have their class picture taken. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

That changed with the establishment of the rehab farms after the war, when the government purchased blocks of land from larger stations to offer to returned servicemen, whose names were drawn from a ballot.

Ian Perry's father was one of those who further developed the district, breaking in a new farm named Orere.

"My father was a rehab farmer here, and our family's been here ever since.

"These people put in the paddocks, broke them up. These people were going onto farms without houses, probably two or three paddocks, no stock, so it was a huge challenge."

Ian Perry's father was one of the returned servicemen who helped develop the surrounding farmland. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

At the end of the weekend a plaque was being unveiled to commemorate these early families, listing the 20 original rehab farmers, their wives, the farm names and locations, and where the men served.

"They contributed significantly to the social and the economic fabric of this district," Perry said.

A former pupil himself, he said the school had long been the heart of the community.

"That's changed significantly over the past probably 20 or 30 years with what's happened in agriculture, but the school still remains a buoyant part of the community.

"So we're celebrating 150 years and it's fantastic to have everybody here together and enjoy each other's company and reminisce about a lot of the times gone by."

Reverend Steve Thomson of Tinui's appropriately named, Church of the Good Shepherd. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Reverend Steve Thomson also noted the changes in the community.

He first came to the area in 1977, working the land his wife's family had farmed for generations, and later working closely with the neighbours through the Rural Support Trust and, as the Reverend at Tinui's appropriately named, Church of the Good Shepherd.

He told Country Life it had been an "amazing place" to bring up his children who all attended Tinui School.

"I've seen the pine trees move into the area and basically destroy the school. [It's] all planting now and nowhere near the farms around now that there was 30 or 40 years ago."

His own farm was sold into pine trees so he understands the tension well.

"I just think that communities like this are the backbone of this country. I think that's what we need more of today, is communities like this.

"Unfortunately they're getting smaller, but just look at all the people around here, they come from all around the world, the people that have come back today and all of them have got good jobs and it's just very special."

At 93, Phyllis French, née Cameron, is perhaps the oldest former student present. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The Tinui Hall featured photos and histories from past pupils. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Close to 200 people attended the weekend's celebrations, with multiple activities held over the three days - from class pictures across the decades, to drinks, dinners and, of course, a Sunday church service.

It's clear the school, and its community, mean as much to those who've lived there for generations as well as newcomers to the district, like former teacher and principal Duncan Smith who was at the school in the late 1980s.

Students flocked around him to look over his collection of photos and handwritten lesson plans from his teaching days, breaking into song when they saw the familiar words.

"We loved it," he said of his family's experience in the small farming community.

"We were brought into it for them to chuckle at our naivety, but we learnt the skills and did the processes and felt as if we were farmers."

Former teacher and principal Duncan Smith. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Now retired as an artist in Whanganui, Smith said he did some of his best work in the quiet hours of the night before teaching.

He said it had taught him how special country schools were.

"This seems to have been one of the few country schools that has three roads going off it and as the other country schools closed, then it's probably become a little bit special but I think that so much has changed in rural character that we were in a prime time."

Jenny Balfour who helped organise the weekend's festivities is another import - from Auckland no less.

The school was refurbished after being badly damaged during Cyclone Gabrielle. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Walls covered in children's artwork, it's a far cry from the half a metre high silt left behind which filled the classrooms. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

However, her roots run deep as her husband attended the now closed Mangapakeha School nearby and she worked at Tinui School's office from 2000 to 2015, including helping organise its 125th celebrations.

She said it was a great place to live and it had been special seeing so many people come back to celebrate.

"[I'm] really, really thrilled that we've had so many people and to just watch everybody talking and chatting and reminiscing and all those things, it's just amazing.

"When I was here there were about 70 children and now we only have about 20 and the impact of forestry, and a lot of the houses have gone to other people who do not have children.

"It really saddens me because it was such a thriving [community]... we are still thriving and we've got a lovely new principal who's doing her best here."

That principal is Amanda Aitken, who told Country Life she had big visions for the school.

Post-cyclone, the then 40 or so students continued to learn in makeshift classrooms in the hall up the road, before moving back into the refurbished classrooms.

"I mean, a lot of schools you're going to, they're quite outdated and behind the times, but we're really lucky.

"Everything's sort of new and modern and they don't go without here, that's for sure," Aitken said, finding the silver lining in the flood experience.

"We're very lucky to have such a nice school, especially out in these rural schools. Often they get a bit forgotten about."

Current Tinui School principal Amanda Aitken at the school bell. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

She's taught in a few schools and knows they're something special.

One of the big advantages is the lower teacher-to-student ratio. Another, she said, was the intergenerational connections between the families.

"One of the really cool things here is, you know, that's the relationships you get with these sorts of schools. Everybody knows everyone - we know the nanas, the grans, they all come in for reading."

Her hopes for the future?

"These little rural schools tend to disappear, but I don't think we'll go anywhere. I'd love to hope you'll see me in one of those photos in 150 years, and they'll be, 'oh, that was her 150 years ago'.

"I'd love to hope that it's still a cool, thriving little rural school, because they're something different, country kids."

World.title: Teen in government's bootcamp charged over two armed robberies
World.content:
A teenager taking part in the government's bootcamp for young offenders has been charged over two-armed robberies while he was on the community part of the voluntary programme, RNZ can reveal.

A rangatahi (young person) who was in the community phase of the second Military Style Academy (MSA) pilot was arrested following two-armed robberies earlier this month, and faces new charges of aggravated robbery with an offensive weapon, as well as unlawfully taking a motor vehicle.

A community provider connected to the programme says it should be emphasised these kids are "persistent offenders".

"These are the ones that everything's been offered to them in the community ... and then they continue to offend and seriously offend."

It comes after the government's bootcamp legislation passed its final legislative hurdle in Parliament, and after the Minister confirmed in August that two other participants had already left voluntarily during the in-residence phase.

The second intake of 10 youths at the military style academy began in March with the transition from residential into the community phase taking place in July, as part of a second pilot that took place ahead of the legislation being passed.

The third reading for the Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill took place last week, with Minister in charge Karen Chhour saying the legislation would "help create less victims and make our communities safer".

Karen Chhour RNZ/Marika Khabazi

The legislation gives the Youth Court the power to sentence serious young offenders to bootcamps. The pilot programmes had been voluntary.

RNZ approached the police about two separate robberies, one in Rotorua and one in Waitara, about a week apart.

A statement from Police confirmed they'd been called to an incident in Rotorua where a group of masked offenders entered a store armed with weapons, smashed display cabinets and stole items before leaving the area in two stolen vehicles. There were no reports of injuries.

Another statement from police confirmed three people were arrested in Waitara after a report of assault and robbery nearly a week later. A pursuit commenced before being abandoned, with three people later taken into custody.

"Two were charged with aggravated robbery with an offensive weapon and unlawfully taking a motor vehicle.

"They will go through a youth justice process. Enquiries are ongoing," police said.

Asked by RNZ about the charges Oranga Tamariki (OT) deputy chief executive Dean Winter said given there was a police investigation underway with matters before the youth court, "we are unable to comment on this matter."

Minister for Children Karen Chhour was also asked, but a spokesperson for the minister said it would be inappropriate to respond in this instance as "all offending is alleged until found otherwise by a court".

But Labour's spokesperson for children Willow-Jean Prime told RNZ "enough is enough".

Prime said the majority of participants went on to reoffend in the pilot, and now in the second iteration of the programme, there was more offending and participants voluntarily leaving.

"The re-offending rate for National's boot camps is about the same as the rest of the youth justice system. It's a wasteful political experiment and takes us back down a path of harm.

"This is what Christopher Luxon has made Kiwis pay tens of millions for by turning this chaos into law just last week."

Labour has promised to scrap the bootcamps if elected and invest in "evidence-based and trauma-informed wraparound approaches that are proven to work for young people".

Willow-Jean Prime. VNP / Phil Smith

Community provider

The head of a community organisation that has been involved in the MSA spoke to RNZ, on condition of anonymity.

He was frustrated with the use of the word 'military' to describe what he called an "intensive wraparound programmme in residence".

"The programme gets completely slated because of the use of the word military.

"There's obviously some political reason to use the word military because it's not. It's not actually a military programme at all."

He described the in residence component as having intensive support, therapy, counselling, "that should be standard practice" in youth residence, "but it's not because it's obviously expensive".

The in-residence programme reduced victimisation "hugely" because these kids who were doing "lots of crime" were now off the street.

"They are doing crime every single day of the week," he said, wanting to reiterate the word "persistent".

"These are persistent youth offenders who have failed community intervention," adding they continue to be prolific offenders.

He said the mandatory sentencing now available to the Youth Court was a good thing for this specific cohort because it was a targeted intervention.

They couldn't re-offend while they were effectively locked up, "...how many kids you know offend when they're in residence? None of them".

But the reoffending by the MSA participant this month took place while they were in the community phase of the programme.

That was a key issue.

"What failed last time," he said in relation to the first pilot, "was when they were placed back in the community. The community placements for some of the kids were awful".

He said it really mattered where the kids went after being in-residence, because for some of those young people they might be returning to families with drug addiction or gang affiliations.

"My feedback from last time was that there wasn't a lot of thought, or it was left till the last minute," and bad selections were made.

"This time, I think they put a lot more thought into the placements."

He likened it to drug rehabilitation, and being offered a residential placement where you remain clean for that period of time. But the question was whether someone could stay drug free a year later with very little support, he said.

"How does that support then get reinforced once you're actually back out in the community."

When it came to reoffending he said "if you had 10 drug addicts going to rehab, how many of them do you think would reoffend within a month of getting out".

Asked if he thought the MSA programme was successful, he said they'd been developed to address "what is clearly a need within the youth justice system and within society".

Normally, these young people would go to prison, where they wouldn't have intensive support he said.

Asked what went wrong for this young person, he said you'd have to question how much trauma had they had in their life, how young they were when they first started offending, their family background, whether there are gangs involved or family harm, and whether the young person was emotionally unregulated, "There's a whole list of things."

In response, OT told RNZ the second programme had built on the first, including a full evaluation that showed the the transition to community period, the first months after leaving the residence, was the "most high-risk for rangatahi to re-offend, whilst their new skills, habits and behaviours are still embedding".

World.title: Stunning free kick shows Irankunda's star is aligning for Socceroos
World.content:
With some players, there's always a moment in their career that, years into the future, you can look back on as a beacon of when they truly announced themselves.

Perhaps we will be able to point to a stunning free kick for the ages as that moment in the young career of Nestory Irankunda.

Those 25,440 people lucky enough to be in Townsville to see Socceroos 1-1 Brazil will certainly never forget it.

Neither, you suspect, will Chelsea wonder kid Estêvão.

The 19-year-old probably had the best view of anyone, lying at the base of the four-man wall looking back towards Hugo Souza.

He could see, with devastating precision, the ball fly over him and into the top corner, Souza skittishly crabbing across his line before admitting defeat.

It might be fun to wonder what was going through Estêvão's mind as he rolled onto his back to stare into the sky above the Townsville stadium.

Whatever he was thinking, Irankunda was already flipping towards the corner flag.

Nestory Irankunda celebrates in emphatic style after his magical free kick. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

"I mean, good goal, good goal," he told Channel 10, the confidence of youth oozing from his voice as he was asked about his free kick.

"I've done it before and to do it again today against a top team in Brazil, it's amazing.

"Sometimes [when I try it], the ball goes outside the training ground. Sometimes I miss completely.

"For it to go in today, it felt good. You see there, beautiful."

Estêvão already had first-hand experience of Irankunda's slipperiness: on the half hour mark the Sporting forward showed brilliant balance to turn the Chelsea man and then exploded with power to dance away up field.

That, almost as much as the goal, was a moment worth remembering, an Aussie displaying the audacity to spin a Brazilian in the middle of the pitch.

"There were some big stars out tonight," Irankunda said on Channel 10, marvelling at the crowds that had come out to support both Australia and Brazil.

"But we've got some big stars too."

That is true, but already Irankunda deserves to be considered one that could burn among the brightest.

Having made the move to Portuguese giants Sporting from Watford in the off-season, Irankunda has not quite had time to make his mark yet.

Nestory Irankunda scores a stunning free kick. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Only once in five games has he started in the Portuguese Primeira Liga, and he is yet to provide an assist or score a goal.

But given this moment against Brazil, a team that still carries the romance of an illustrious past despite a 24-year-and-counting absence from the World Cup final, one wonders whether the ripples through the lusophone world may just nudge those in power at the Lisbon giants to afford him greater chances to prove his worth.

It certainly caught the eye of the club's social media team, who slapped a "GOLAÇO" label on it within three minutes of the net rippling 16,844 kilometres away.

Of course there must be caveats.

Brazil were most certainly off-colour, "average" according to Bruno Guimarães's damning assessment post-match.

In the first half at least, it was the Socceroos who were bossing the game, charging forward, rampaging through a fragile Brazilian midfield that still seems bruised from its last-16 defeat at the World Cup a few months ago, crafting the chances, delivering the crosses and winning the corners.

Of course Brazil started to turn it on. With the quality up front that they had, how could they not?

Endrick of Real Madrid. Raphinha of Barcelona. Estêvão of Chelsea. Vinícius Júnior of Real Madrid. Despite an atrocious pitch, which rolled up like a cheap carpet at a shabby motel, Brazil's bevvy of stars began to knock the ball around with the playful nonchalance of men who are all too aware of their own brilliance.

But it was their lesser lights, Flamengo pair Samuel Lino and Pedro, as well as Bournemouth's Rayan who finally made the breakthrough.

And it was Irankunda who provided the stand-out moment of the game.

Hopefully, Tony Popovic is telling Nestory Irankunda that he will always play him on the left. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

It is his liveliness and confidence imbues in the Socceroos a dash of verve and belief in their own abilities.

Playing on the left, cutting back inside and posing a threat from set pieces, Irankunda has the sort of aura that few Socceroos players in recent years can command.

His ability to cut back inside and unleash with that right foot, just as he did inside the opening 10 minutes to force a fine save from Hugo Souza, is explosive.

Tony Popovic only made three changes from the side that started the game against Egypt in the World Cup but playing Irankunda left was so decisive, the pain of seeing him so wasted as a target man in Dallas surely enough to forever wipe that option from Popovic's mind.

Yengi played his part centrally as a willing runner and constant menace to an inexperienced Brazilian back four, while the Seleção's pitiful midfield was readily overrun by fullbacks Jacob Italiano and Aziz Behich, with Paul Okon-Engstler's driving runs from midfield the telling factor in winning the free kick that Irankunda so magnificently placed into the net.

Brazil may prove to be better in Brisbane.

A quiet night may have those who were singing Irankunda's praises on Friday bemoaning a lack of consistency by Tuesday.

But given he is showing himself repeatedly capable of such brilliance, it seems unlikely to be long before the next career-defining moment will come along.

World.title: Fremantle turns purple as Dockers attempt grand final history
World.content:
In the heart and home of the Dockers — the City of Fremantle — it's hard to escape the colour purple.

As history beckons for the AFL team, flags and signs line every wall and corner of the city centre, and purple scarves have become the uniform.

Purple reigns on the streets of Fremantle. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

People walking down the famous cappuccino strip this week watched in awe as artist Jerome Davenport painted a mural in honour of the Fremantle Dockers.

"I really do hope that this inspires a few people, and the players," he said after finishing the giant work in just four days.

Jerome Davenport finished the mural, which is painted on the facade of Sailing for Oranges. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"I sat here 13 years ago in this street and watched them the first time they were in the finals.

" What an honour to be here and be a part of it for the second time. "

As the Dockers head towards making what could be premiership history, business has been rife in purple cannolis, ice creams, beer and hot dogs.

Purple sausages are being sold at a butcher in Fremantle. (ABC News)

The local school has temporarily rebranded as the "Fremantle Dockers College" and allowed students to dress up in purple on Friday for a gold coin donation to one of the team's charities of choice, the Starlight Children's Foundation.

Principal Stan Koios said the city felt electric.

"We thought, let's get on board the euphoria that started with the Dockers and their success … let's get a bit quirky and crazy," he said.

To their fans, the Dockers are already winners. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Public screens have been set up at several locations across the city for a grand final watch party, with 40,000 people expected to attend.

Roads in central Fremantle have been closed, and public transport is free for the day.

Winners forever

Regardless of Saturday's result, there's no doubt in the minds of locals that the Dockers are winners.

Even Brandy, who belongs to fan Darren Reid, is dressed up in purple. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"They are the best team in all of Australia; nothing can compare to them," student Nathan Campisi said.

Another local, Juliet Kirsten, said the town had watched the team grow and was now ready to see them make their mark in history.

Regardless of the result, the Dockers are already immortalised in this mural. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"We've seen the club grow over the years, and Freo just responded over the years with the community vibe and everything, and it's just gone exponentially better and better," she said.

" We're going to win. "

World.title: Neale the common thread in Fremantle and Brisbane's eerie shared history
World.content:
When Fremantle coach Ross Lyon activated his sub in the fourth quarter of the 2013 grand final against Hawthorn, he scarcely could have believed the impact that player was going to have.

On the odd occasion, the sub would come in and make a serious impact, acting as a spark plug, while on other days, their impact would be negligible.

Fremantle's sub that day came on to replace ruckman Zac Clarke and picked up seven disposals, but it was ultimately in vain as an experienced Hawthorn side held the Dockers at bay.

Fremantle's sub that day was Lachie Neale.

Lachie Neale (fourth from right) was a 20-year-old substitute when Fremantle last made a grand final appearance. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Neale, then 20, would not have believed that he would have to wait 13 years to see the Dockers in another grand final.

He also would not have believed he'd be playing against them in Brisbane colours, looking for a third straight premiership.

It is funny how time works.

Fremantle and the Brisbane Lions both entered the AFL in the mid 90s as the league was undergoing an expansion boom into states outside of Victoria.

Three-time Brisbane premiership captain Michael Voss (pictured) won a Brownlow Medal in the Bears' last season of existence. (Getty Images)

Brisbane's entry occurred as the Bears back in 1987 alongside Fremantle's WA rivals West Coast, and while the Eagles found themselves in a grand final within four years and holding the premiership cup within five, the Bears struggled.

The Lions were eventually formed in 1996 when the Bears merged with the Fitzroy Lions, another club that had been haemorrhaging money for years.

West Coast's success saw the AFL expand further into WA with Fremantle chosen as the state's second team with its inaugural season played in 1995.

It is somewhat poetic that the Dockers and Lions are playing against each other in this year's grand final when you consider how closely they are tied together right at the inception of both clubs.

Fremantle's first ever win in the AFL came against the Fitzroy Lions in round 3, 1995, while Fitzroy's last ever AFL win came against Fremantle in round 8, 1996.

Fitzroy's last ever AFL game? You guessed it, against Fremantle in Perth in round 22 of the 1996 season.

Over the three decades that have followed, both Fremantle and Brisbane have had periods of dominance, but never really at the same time until recent years.

Leigh Matthews's arrival as Brisbane's coach at the end of 1999 immediately turned the Lions into a force to be reckoned with.

Brisbane won three premierships in a row between 2001 and 2003 before losing in the 2004 grand final. (Getty Images: Hamish Blair)

Matthews masterminded Brisbane to three straight premierships and four straight grand final appearances between 2001 and 2004 before his departure and the aging of that era of Brisbane players left the club in AFL purgatory for the best part of 15 years.

Fremantle had to wait until its ninth season in the AFL to make a finals appearance, and then had to wait another three seasons before it won a final.

Since 2000, Brisbane has made the finals on 14 occasions, while Fremantle has registered 10 post-season trips, yet Brisbane has five premierships to Fremantle's zero.

And tying them together through the last 13 years has been Neale, once the best midfielder for both clubs.

Neale made his AFL debut with Fremantle in round 4, 2012, picking up seven disposals in a win over St Kilda. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Neale was drafted 58th overall by Fremantle in the 2011 draft.

He was Fremantle's fourth selection that night. The three players selected before him — Tom Sheridan, Hayden Crozier and Alex Forster — played a combined 226 games.

The grand final will be Neale's 321st appearance.

His arrival coincided with Fremantle's first real period of contention under Lyon in the early 2010s.

In Neale's first four seasons, Fremantle won the third-most home and away games in the AFL behind Hawthorn and Sydney.

In that period, the Hawks won three premierships and played in four grand finals, while the Swans played in two grand finals and won one.

Fremantle's first era of premiership contention drew to a close after losing the 2015 preliminary final to eventual premiers Hawthorn. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Fremantle came away with the one unsuccessful grand final appearance.

While Fremantle was knocking on the door of its first premiership, Brisbane was going through one of the worst periods of its existence.

By 2012, Neale's debut season, just two of Brisbane's triple premiership-winning players — Simon Black and Jonathan Brown — remained on its list.

Memories of Brisbane being one of the AFL's most feared sides were disappearing fast and players on the list originally from outside Queensland wanted to be anywhere but at the club.

The infamous 'Paddle Pop Lion' logo remains a symbol of an era of struggle for Brisbane. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Even Brisbane's logo on its jumper had changed, going from the traditional Fitzroy passant lion to a lion with a front-facing head, infamously nicknamed 'The Paddle Pop Lion'.

Fremantle won the first minor premiership in club history in 2015, with Neale becoming one of its most indispensable players, but the Dockers were again denied by Hawthorn, this time in a home preliminary final.

The Dockers cratered spectacularly the following season, dropping from first to third-last, and would not make it back to the finals for another seven seasons.

In dire need of some stability, Brisbane turned to one of the figureheads behind Hawthorn's triple premiership dynasty, Chris Fagan, to be its head coach.

Chris Fagan's arrival at Brisbane at the end of 2016 helped turn the club back into a powerhouse. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Lions struggled in Fagan's first two seasons in charge, but Neale had seen the vision and requested a trade to the then-cellar dwellers.

Had Fremantle known what he was about to become, they'd have asked for double what they received in return for him from Brisbane.

Neale's move to Brisbane put him up in lights on Broadway.

The All-Australian jackets, the Brownlow Medal wins and eventually premierships all arrived, leaving him with a resume that undoubtedly has him in the conversation as one of the best players of his generation.

His departure from Fremantle, which looked like someone getting the last life raft out of a sinking ship, proved to be a pivotal moment in the Dockers' trajectory to the grand final as well.

The following year's draft proved to be a watershed moment for Fremantle, as it supercharged its rebuild with the selections of Hayden Young and Caleb Serong.

Luke Jackson (left) and Shai Bolton's (right) arrival at Fremantle has transformed the Dockers into a premiership threat. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Having seen Brisbane supplement its young core with shrewd recruitment of seasoned players such as Neale, Charlie Cameron, Josh Dunkley and others, Fremantle has done the same, adding Luke Jackson and Shai Bolton.

For both clubs, the addition of star talent from rival clubs has resulted in an immediate uptick in on-field fortunes.

All of it leads us here, to two teams inextricably linked from their inceptions and still connected by one man.

Now that he has been freed to play, don't be surprised if that one man, Lachie Neale, has a big say in who holds the premiership cup.

World.title: Why Sarah 4.0 needs no further upgrades following year of injury hell
World.content:
The path that any elite athlete travels to the top of their sport is rarely straightforward.

The most evangelical of adherents to their chosen regimens are still liable to succumb to the seemingly endless torment of injury hell.

As Australian cyclist Sarah Gigante prepares for the elite women's road race at the UCI World Championships on Saturday night, she can be certain that she knows this as much as anyone.

Gigante had just returned home to Spain after competing in her first race since the 2025 Tour de France Femmes, a 403-day absence from the professional peloton due to a badly broken femur.

She has previously spent time off the bike to have treatment for myopericarditis, inflammation of her heart, in 2021 and surgery to correct iliac artery endofibrosis in 2024.

"It has been a really unlucky streak," Gigante understatedly told ABC Sport.

"But on the other hand, I now know more and more how to deal with setbacks."

Sarah Gigante has fought through numerous setbacks in her career so far. (Getty Images: Szymon Gruchalski)

Cycling is a sport that litters broken bodies and dreams throughout its history.

How Matthews twice dodged death to line up at the Tour de France Michael Matthews has twice diced with death since he last rode in a Tour de France. The 36-year-old now wants to make up for lost time.

At Gigante's return race, the Faun Tour Femmes, half her AG Insurance-Soudal team was eliminated by crashes, the vulnerability of riders competing at lightning speeds with minimal safety equipment laid painfully bare.

Justine Ghekiere broke her knee on stage one in a crash that also eliminated SD Worx-Protime pair Mischa Bredewold, who broke her hip, and New Zealand's Mikayla Harvey who suffered concussion.

Then, on stage three, Urška Žigart broke her jaw.

"It was, I wouldn't say a rude awakening to how harsh cycling can be, because I know how harsh it can be," Gigante said.

"Definitely don't take it for granted when you're feeling good and you're healthy and things go right.

"Because often they don't."

The power of positivity — and meme-making

Sarah Gigante who won the blue mountain classification jersey at the 2025 Giro d'Italia Women, is one of the best pure climbers in the world. (Getty Images: Luc Claessen)

Despite theoretically being the most simple of her ailments, Gigante's latest break from riding has almost been the most difficult to wrap her head around.

Following a season in which she claimed sixth place overall at the Tour de France Femmes, backing up a third-place finish featuring two stage wins and Queen of the Mountains victory at that year's Giro d'Italia women, Gigante crashed during a training ride.

Surgery was required to pin her broken femur before recovery could begin, but the pin proved to be too long and was improperly placed, leaving her in as much pain as she was when she first fell for months on end, until a second surgery removed the offending metalwork.

"For sure this broken femur has been the hardest, most frustrating [injury]," Gigante said.

"When you're concussed, you don't know how long it will take to heal, or with the iliac artery you don't even know if it will work.

"It's not that I'd want a broken bone, but I'd always be like, 'oh, like give me a broken bone any day' over that uncertainty. And the time I actually did just have a broken bone, it ended up being way worse."

The pins in Sarah Gigante's leg were causing her extreme pain. (Supplied: Instagram/@slipstreamsarah)

It was not just the excruciating physical pain, but the psychological burden of a seemingly endless healing process that took its toll following those career-best performances in 2025.

However, thanks to an iron-clad support network that includes her mum and teammates, combined with Gigante's cheeky, good-humoured nature, the Australian climber took it in her stride.

She also had the most 21st century of all activities to take her mind off things — making memes.

"Actually it was really funny … It wasn't just for Instagram, it was like a coping mechanism," Gigante said.

Loading Instagram content

"Riding indoors all the time, it gets a bit boring, so because it was so easy I was on my phone making memes … and I really looked forward to it.

"When I had to have the second operation to get the metal out, people were like, 'oh, I can't wait for the memes to come back,' but I didn't need to make them.

"I think it took the point of me going kind of crazy to need that coping mechanism and I didn't need it this time.

"I'm really happy that now I can say I'm back to racing, not just a professional trainer and a professional meme maker."

Sarah Gigante was just thrilled to be back racing after 403 days out. (Getty Images: Billy Ceusters)

Gigante is fresh off signing a new contract that will keep her at AG Insurance-Soudal until the end of 2027, a testament to their continued belief in the young Aussie, even if Gigante has previously joked that following her many setbacks, she has had to be rebooted and is now a completely new version of herself.

Now, with this being her third major comeback, she'll be happy for no more upgrades.

"After the heart, I was Sarah 2.0, and then after the iliac artery it was version 3.0, now I'm up to 4.0," Gigante noted, counting out on her fingers as she did so.

"I'm not planning on changing again, I think Sarah 4.0 is enough. I think that will be the final update.

"Now I'm looking forward to what I can do."

A 'super open' elite road race

Sarah Gigante is capable of mixing it with the very best riders in the world. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

Gigante is part of a four-strong Australian team that will take to the start line in Canada alongside Georgia Baker, Lauretta Hanson and Amanda Spratt.

"It's only my my second time in the elite colours racing for Australia on the road … it's a real privilege and I'm really grateful," Gigante said.

"Given I only will have four UCI races this year, to have one be the world champs is incredibly special."

That team is smaller than it might be, Australia qualified six women riders but is only sending four, a situation Gigante noted was "a bit sad" — and that quartet will be up against it in a wide open field.

Amanda Spratt will ride in her 13th and final world road race for Australia. (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

The women's elite road race takes place over 180.4 kilometres in Montréal, the longest ever distance for a women's race at a world championships, including eight laps of a gruelling, 13.4km Mont Royal Circuit which comprises the majority of the route's 2,502 metres elevation gain.

"It is two-and-a-half thousand metres over 180K [km], but it's also two-and-a-half thousand metres over 120 kilometres because the first 60km is dead flat," Gigante said.

"So actually, for someone like me, that's even better. Obviously, I'd rather it were three-and-a-half-thousand metres … but I love that the climbing is really backloaded."

Tour de France Femmes and Giro d'Italia Women champion Demi Vollering leads a typically strong Dutch team who has plenty of backup options in its squad.

But in reality, the list of favourites could conceivably run into double figures: Belgium's two-time road world champion Lotte Kopecky, Spain's La Vuelta Femenina victor Paula Blasi, Italian firebrand Elisa Longo Borghini, 21-year-old Brit Zoe Bäckstedt, last year's silver medallist Niamh Fisher-Black of New Zealand, Polish pair Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney and Dominika Włodarczyk, and Swiss duo Marlen Reusser and back-to-back Tour Down Under winner Noemi Rüegg are all contenders.

Demi Vollering is the leader of Team Netherlands, but history says that does not always mean they will all work for her. (Getty Images: Billy Ceusters)

"A course like this is super open," Gigante said.

"Obviously I'm gunning for the Aussie team. We have a small but strong and definitely hopeful team, and I'm sure we'll give it our best shot against the bigger favourites.

"But [AG Insurance-Soudal teammate] Kim Le Court Pienaar, I won't be racing with her, but I'm definitely hoping she can have a really strong ride.

"I think the course suits her perfectly — I think it suits her more than it does Demi, probably.

"It's more that Demi has six super strong teammates alongside her and it's likely that Kim will be isolated quite early in the race.

"It is hard coming from a small nation like Mauritius, but then it also means it's even more special if she can win."

Kim Le Court Pienaar (left) is the pick of Sarah Gigante (right) for the upcoming world championships road race. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

Gigante acknowledges that she is in far from the best form of her life and is potentially more suited to what is expected to be a ferociously hilly course next year in the French Alps, but added that the women's field is so open that anyone can claim the win.

"Every person that lines up on the start line in any bike race has a chance. It's not just who's the strongest and that's really a fun part about the sport," Gigante said.

"After the success of last year's early breakaway with [Canadian dark horse] Magdeleine Vallieres taking an awesome win, I'm sure there'll be a fight for the breakaway.

"But also the big teams and favourites know what not to do as well, so it [the breakaway] will likely be kept on a leash, but who's going to walk the dog and become the leash?

"Even though the Dutch say they're all in for Demi [Vollering], it doesn't always go like you think it will.

"I think that's why cycling is so exciting."

World.title: A decades-old newspaper snippet gives blueprint of modern Knights
World.content:
The blueprint of a Newcastle Knight was inked in black and white before anyone wore the red and blue.

Newcastle's inaugural coach Allan McMahon spelled out his vision in a 1987 newspaper column, ahead of the club's 1988 debut.

"Our guidelines for recruiting players are that the major part of their football be in front of them," McMahon decreed.

"[Players] will have an in-built desire to win as well as strength, tackling ability, and speed.

"There's a fantastic nursery for rugby league around Newcastle and that will be looked after.

" Promising, strong players with their careers ahead of them — that's the only way to go. "

Allan McMahon's weekly column in the Canberra Times, the day after he was announced to be leaving the ACT for Newcastle in 1987. (Supplied: National Archives of Australia, The Canberra Times)

McMahon, who died in 2003, will undoubtedly be looking down on the 2026 Knights with a special brand of pride only Novocastrians know.

And if any player embodies every ounce of his dream-Knight, it's Phoenix Crossland.

"It's hard to put into words what this club means to me and the whole team," Crossland said.

2026 Danny Buderus medallist Phoenix Crossland, leading out the Knights at an open training session earlier this week. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

The 26-year-old half-turned-hooker was sourced from the Erina Eagles, at the border of Newcastle's nursery, crafted through the club's pathways, and unleashed into top-flight footy in 2019.

"We can do something special here; we just need to focus," he said.

"I've always been inspired and motivated to play for this club and to do my best for them and the fans."

Crossland said "Justo" (coach Justin Holbrook) gave him a simple to-do list at the start of the season.

"[He said] all you need to do, and make sure you're the best in the comp at it, is tackling, defending and turning up for your team."

Phoenix Crossland 2026 statistics Games played 23 matches Total tackles 1,055 (most in the NRL) Tackle efficiency (successful tackles) 93 per cent 40/20 kicks Four (most in the NRL) Pass receipts 1,835 Tries scored Three

Club identity

The motivation Crossland feels going into this weekend's preliminary final against the Penrith Panthers is a club-wide sentiment.

"There's a belief that whatever's thrown our way, we can overcome it," the Knights' director of football Chris James said.

"I reckon you can sense that, for these players, no opposition scares them, no situation in a game scares them.

"After winning in New Zealand, that very quickly turned to, 'Right, let's go after winning the comp.'"

James, a former NRL referee, joined Newcastle from the Roosters at the start of last season.

"A lot of the reasons that Allan McMahon put in that article is why I came here," he said.

He added one question has been asked by the coaching staff, and it's driving the players' hunger for success: "What is your 'why?'"

"If you can make that greater than an individual 'why', by representing this town and the region that's supported us for so long and playing in a style that would make them proud, then you've got something special."

Young and hungry

Half of Newcastle's extended 22-player squad named earlier this week wasn't born by the 2001 grand final, when the underdog Knights upset the Eels to snatch a second premiership.

Loading...

One of them is Fletcher Sharpe, the Cessnock boy who can play halfback, five-eighth, wing and centre.

He'd probably have a crack in the front row if things got desperate.

Fletcher Sharpe is a fan favourite amongst Newcastle supporters. (ABC News)

"We've enjoyed putting a bit of pressure on ourselves this year to go out there and represent the town and the community, and make them a part of the team," he said.

" We've put ourselves in a good position, and now it's about going out there and executing. "

In the context of this weekend, it's eerie to look back and see what Allan McMahon wrote about Penrith in his column.

He referenced a young Mark Geyer as an inspiration for what a Knight should and could be, a local junior moulded into a die-for-his-jersey Panther.

"That's the sort of thing we will be encouraging, the youth of Newcastle and young players from surrounding areas," he wrote.

Crossland is that. Sharpe is that. Maitland's Cody Hopwood, Lachlan Crouch and Tom Cant all fit that bill too.

20-year-old Cody Hopwood, a West Maitland Wallaroos junior, made his NRL debut in the final game of last season. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

And for the formidable Penrith, it is embodied in Nathan Cleary, Brian To'o, Lindsay Smith, Mitch Kenny, Moses Leota and several more.

The challenge

McMahon didn't mince his words in 87. He knew it was going to be a tough slog to build the Knights.

When Holbrook arrived at the end of the 2025 season, he didn't mince his words either.

He said he'd focus on connecting with the region's pathway clubs urgently, and connecting the players to the Hunter's real roots.

"It's a hard-working area, and you want to see that in your rugby league team," he said at his first press conference.

He took his squad underground into one of the Hunters' many coal mines during the pre-season, pulling them further than down-to-earth.

Loading Instagram content

He wanted to show them what scores of their fans do day-to-day, and show them how lucky they were to play footy for a living.

The top comment on the club's social media post of the visit, from Daniel Connors, summed it up.

"This is great, a lot of them needed a dose of reality, most of them seemed to be taking their positions for granted last year."

Even if the finals-versed Panthers do spell the end for the Knights' 2026 campaign, it's inarguable that Newcastle is the rugby league fairytale of the year.

Twelve months ago, the men in red and blue were the laughing stock of the NRL, ridiculed, mocked and pitied for what they did and didn't do.

Now, the players are warranted in asking a very satisfying question to the scores of naysayers.

Who's laughing now?

World.title: Everything you need to know ahead of today's AFL grand final
World.content:
The 2026 AFL grand final is almost upon us, as the Brisbane Lions look to make history with their second threepeat in 25 years, and the Fremantle Dockers look to win their first flag since joining the league in 1995.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

What time is the 2026 AFL grand final?

Here are the times according to which state or territory you're in:

2.30pm AEST: ACT, NSW, Queensland, Tasmania, Victoria

ACT, NSW, Queensland, Tasmania, Victoria 2pm ACST: Northern Territory, South Australia

Northern Territory, South Australia 12.30pm AWST: Western Australia

Which teams are playing in the grand final?

The Brisbane Lions are facing off with the Fremantle Dockers.

This is Brisbane's fourth grand final in a row, losing to Collingwood in 2023, before beating Sydney and Geelong in the following years.

Should they win, it would be the second threepeat in their history following 2001-2003, and it would see them join Melbourne (1939-41 and 1955-57) as one of the only two teams to record the feat twice in VFL/AFL history.

Meanwhile, Fremantle is yet to win a premiership after joining the league in 1995. This is the club's second grand final following its loss to Hawthorn in 2013.

Over their past six games against each other, the ledger is tied at 3-3, with the Dockers winning their most recent clash at the Gabba in round 13 this year.

Can I watch the AFL grand final on Kayo?

No. The grand final vision is exclusive to Channel 7 and won't be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It's a deal that catches out punters every year given Kayo and Fox have access to every single other game of the season.

The game can be streamed via the 7Plus app, while ABC Sport will be calling every moment and live blogging right throughout the day at abc.net.au/news/sport.

What time will Kylie Minogue be performing?

Australia's pop princess should be on stage from about 1.30pm. Again, be very aware that Minogue's performance is pre-game and is not halftime entertainment. There is no halftime entertainment.

G Flip, Kylie Minogue, Mike Brady and Michael Paynter will all perform before the grand final. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

Other performers will be G Flip, musical actor Michael Paynter on the national anthem, and of course Mike Brady doing Up There Cazaly during the retiree motorcade.

Who will be lining up for the Lions and Dockers?

Brisbane Lions FB: T.Gallop, H.Andrews, R.Lester HB: D.Zorko, D.Gardiner, D.Wilmot C: Z.Bailey, W.Ashcroft, J.Berry HF: C.Cameron, L.Morris, O.Allen FF: K.Lohmann, C.Rayner, E.Hipwood FOL: D.Fort, J.Dunkley, L.Neale IC: S.Draper, J.Fletcher, H.McCluggage, L.Ashcroft, C.McKenna EMG: N.Answerth, B.Reville, C.Curtin

Fremantle Dockers FB: J.Clark, A.Pearce, J.McVee HB: K.Worner, O.McDonald, H.Chapman C: M.Johnson, A.Brayshaw, N.Erasmus HF: M.Frederick, M.Reid, S.Switkowski FF: J.Amiss, J.Treacy, P.Voss FOL: L.Jackson, C.Serong, S.Bolton IC: I.Dudley, M.Cox, H.Young, C.Wagner, L.Ryan EMG: B.Cox, J.O'Meara, C.Scerri

Who will present the cup to the winners?

The Lions have picked Simon Black, a Brownlow medallist and champion midfielder from that first threepeat, while the Dockers have gone with Shaun McManus, who debuted in Fremantle's inaugural season before playing 228 games.

What are some questions I can drop into the conversation and sound smart as a result?

If this is the one time you watch the footy each year, we've got you covered for some conversation starters. Just reel off any of these:

"How good is Luke Jackson's work around the ground for a big man?"

"Doesn't Kai Lohmann just pop up at exactly the time the Lions need him?"

"Do you reckon Will Ashcroft is cementing himself as one of the all time great finals performers?"

"Do you think the Dockers went too top heavy given the conditions?"

"Is this Lions team better than the threepeaters in 2001 to 2003?"

"Should Lachie Neale even be playing?"

World.title: Man City guilty of breaching EPL financial rules, punishment still pending
World.content:
Global football heavyweights Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 beaches of the English Premier League's financial regulations, according to multiple reports, after a years-long investigation.

In a decision that will send shockwaves through the sport, the club is now expected to face yet-to-be-determined penalties, which could range from reprimands and fines, to being docked competition points or expelled from the Premier League completely.

City were charged in 2023 with 115 breaches of the EPL's financial laws between 2009 and 2018.

A hearing last year, which lasted several weeks, saw an independent find the club guilty on all but one of the charges, according to The Athletic.

Man City have always maintained they have done nothing wrong, and are expected to appeal.

Roughly two thirds of the charges related to breaches concerning financial reporting, profit and sustainability rules. The other third related to failing to cooperate with the EPL's investigation.

While the independent panel's decision was widely reported in British media, the EPL has so far declined to comment or confirm it.

Manchester City released a statement on Friday, local time, which said the process "remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed".

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence," it said.

The club, based in northern England, has a significant global following. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

During the period in question, City won three EPL titles, as well as the FA Cup and three League Cups.

This period of success was driven by massive financial investment from Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates's ruling family, who bought the club in September 2008.

Man City is consistently rated among the most valuable football clubs globally, and have an enormous international fanbase.

It's understood other EPL clubs have been informed about the decision.

Clubs found to have breached the Premier League's financial rules have previously been docked competition points.

If City had titles taken off them, it would be a bitter pill to swallow for the club's fans. When they finished top of the league in 2011-12, arch rivals Manchester United were runners-up.

That could mean the Red Devils are given the trophy retrospectively, something already being floated by some former Man U players, including Rio Ferdinand, who posted on social media on Friday: "Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet."

World.title: Late Brazil goal denies Socceroos famous win after stunning Irankunda free kick
World.content:
Nestory Irankunda's stunning free kick had the Socceroos just seconds away from a famous victory against Brazil in Townsville.

However, Brazilian substitute Rayan slammed a header in off the underside of the crossbar in the 95th-minute to salvage a 1-1 draw, dashing the Socceroos hopes of recording just a second ever victory against the Seleção.

Irankunda later told Channel 10 that his goal was "beautiful" and it would be hard to disagree.

Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti bemoaned what he described as a "not so good" pitch that made it hard to play good football.

But Irankunda's goal was everything that is beautiful about the game.

Lining up a free kick 20 metres from goal, Irankunda punched the ball over the four-man wall, and into the top corner of the goal.

"I mean, good goal, good goal," the 20-year-old told Channel 10.

"I've done it before and to do it again today against a top team in Brazil, it's amazing."

The goal, and lead, was exactly what the Socceroos deserved after a superb first half, running the number five-ranked Brazilians ragged through midfield and creating a number of chances.

Brazil looked shaky and uncertain in possession, turning over the ball in dangerous areas in a throwback to the worst aspects of their faltering 2026 World Cup campaign.

"I think we should do so much, much better," Bruno Guimarães said,

"The pitch was a little bit difficult … we couldn't pass the ball properly.

"We got a draw and I'm hopeful we can perform better in the next game, because the level that we have in the squad, we can definitely play better."

Both Australia's fullbacks found themselves in acres of space, rushing forward and laying the ball off to attacking threats Tete Yengi and Irankunda, who forced a fine save from Hugo Souza with a 20-metre driven shot inside the opening 10 minutes.

Nestory Irankunda had a fine effort saved early in the first half. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Brazil grew into the game towards the end of the half, even putting the ball in the back of the net in first half stoppage time when Estêvão slotted home after Harry Souttar was caught in possession.

However, VAR ruled that Bruno Guimarães had grabbed the giant centre back's leg, leading to the goal being overturned.

Brazil also felt they could have had a penalty when Lucas Herrington was seen to grab a fistful of Endrick's shirt as he raced into the penalty area.

In the second half Brazil continued to build the pressure right up until the moment Irankunda turned on the style with his magical free kick.

The remaining 20 minutes saw the Socceroos retreat deeper and deeper into their shells, with all 11 players within 20 metres of the goal line at times as Brazil camped on the edge of the penalty area.

Souttar and Herrington both made tremendous blocks in outstanding performances, but neither could stop a bullet header from Rayan, which kicked up off the pitch and through the palms of Pat Beach, going in off the base of the crossbar.

The two teams will resume hostilities in Tuesday night at Brisbane's Lang Park.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

Tech.title: Phones don’t have lights
Tech.content:
Mark Zuckerberg has a new defense of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses: They’re actually doing more to signal they’re taking a photo than phones do. He’s brought this up in at least two recent interviews, noting that the glasses have a light that comes on to signal when a photo is being taken, while phones do not. In one of the interviews, Joanna Stern notes that, while phones do not always emit a light, someone does have to hold a phone up in the air, which is itself pretty noticeable.

On today’s Vergecast, we’re talking about Meta Connect, the Muse AI assistant, all the new smart glasses hardware, and Zuckerberg’s response to the privacy uproar around wearable cameras. First, we spend time diving into Muse, which has quickly turned the vibes around on Meta’s progress in AI by making agentic features vastly more accessible than others have in the past. That ties right into Meta’s glasses problem and the question of whether people will trust Meta enough with their privacy to link all their services up to Muse.

There’s also a ton of hardware to discuss. We have thoughts on the new audio-only Ray-Ban Meta glasses and the new Meta VR Glasses. Then it’s onto Googlebooks, which arrived this week with surprisingly refined hardware and compelling integrations between desktop and mobile. It’s going to be a big hurdle to convince people to switch from Windows, but the laptops are full of interesting enough ideas that we’re excited to check them out.

Finally, everyone’s favorite podcast within a podcast returns after a brief hiatus. And then it’s on to the Lightning Round, where we’re discussing the Paramount settlement, YouTube’s embrace of AI tools, the state of Xbox, and Rode hooking its users up with 4K.
